**The interpretation of His words, may His remembrance be exalted:** ﴿Praise be to God, who sent down the Book to His servant and did not make in it any crookedness﴾ (1)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Praise be to God, who singled out Muhammad with His message and chose him to convey it from Him. He sent him to His creation as a prophet and messenger, and sent down to him His Book, upright (qayyiman), and did not make in it any crookedness.

By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, ﴿qayyiman﴾ He means: moderate and straight. It has also been said that He means: it is upright over the other books, confirming them and preserving them.

**Mention of those who said that it means moderate and straight:**

* Ali ibn Dawud related to me, he said: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, he said: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness, upright﴾, he said: He sent down the Book as just and upright, and did not make in it any crookedness. Ibn Abbas, with this statement and his explanation of the meaning of qayyim, indicated that qayyiman is placed after His words "and did not make in it any crookedness," and its meaning is brought forward: He sent down the Book upon His servant as upright.

* I was told from Muhammad ibn Zayd, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿qayyiman﴾, he said: straight.

* Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, regarding ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness, upright﴾: that is, moderate, with no disagreement in it.

* al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness, upright﴾, he said: God sent down the Book upright, and did not make in it any crookedness.

* Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿Praise be to God, who sent down the Book to His servant and did not make in it any crookedness, upright﴾.

He said: In some readings it is: "but He made it upright" (wa-lakin ja'alahu qayyiman).

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is what Ibn Abbas said, and what those who agree with his statement said, because of the evidence of His words ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness﴾. He, may His praise be exalted, informed that He sent down the Book that He revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) as ﴿upright﴾, straight, with no disagreement in it and no inconsistency, but rather some of it confirms other parts, and some of it bears witness to others, with no crookedness in it and no deviation from the truth. The ayn in His words ﴿ʿiwajan﴾ is pronounced with a kasra (ʿiwaj), because the Arabs say it this way for every crookedness that exists in religion, or in something whose form is not seen standing upright, so that it is perceived standing erect, like ʿiwaj in religion. For this reason the ayn is pronounced with a kasra in this place. Likewise ʿiwaj in a road, because it is not an upright, standing form. As for crookedness in upright, standing forms, its ayn is pronounced with a fatha, as in ʿawaj in a spear, a piece of wood, and the like. Ibn Abbas used to say, regarding the meaning of His words ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness﴾: and did not make in it anything ambiguous (multabis).

**Mention of those who said that:**

* Ali related to us, he said: Abdullah related to us, he said: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness, upright﴾, and did not make in it anything ambiguous.

There is also no disagreement among the scholars of Arabic that the meaning of His words ﴿qayyiman﴾, although placed after, is "brought forward" to be beside "the Book." It has been said that...

Almighty God opened this sura by mentioning Himself with what befits Him, and by informing about the sending down of His Book to His Messenger, as a declaration to the polytheists of Mecca that Muhammad is His Messenger (ﷺ). This is because the polytheists had asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about things that the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir had taught them, and they had instructed them to ask him about them. They said: If he tells you about them, he is a prophet; and if he does not tell you about them, he is a fabricator. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) promised them an answer about them at a set time. Revelation was delayed somewhat, and the coming of Jibril (peace be upon him) was late beyond the appointed time for the people. The polytheists talked, saying that he had broken his promise to them, and that he was a fabricator. So God sent down this sura as an answer to their questions, and opened its beginning with His mention, and with the refutation of the polytheists in the rumors they spread among themselves.

**Mention of those who said that:** Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Yunus ibn Bukayr related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, he said: A shaykh from the people of Egypt related to me, who had come [to Medina] some forty-odd years earlier, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, as Abu Ja'far al-Tabari narrates [[The apparent meaning: the phrase "as Abu Ja'far al-Tabari narrates" is the author's reference to himself, not to another person, nor is it a phrase from one of his students about him.]], he said: Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina. They told them: Ask them about Muhammad, describe his attributes to them, and inform them of what he says, for they are the People of the First Book, and they have knowledge that we do not have of the knowledge of the prophets. So the two set out until they reached Medina. They asked the rabbis of the Jews about the Messenger of God (ﷺ), described his affair and some of what he said to them, and said: You are the People of the Torah, and we have come to you so that you may inform us about this companion of ours. He said: The rabbis of the Jews said to them: Ask him about three things that we command you about. If he informs you of them, he is a sent prophet; if he does not do so, the man is a fabricator, so judge his affair as you see fit. Ask him about youths who went out in the earliest age, what their affair was, for they had a wondrous story. Ask him about a wandering man who reached the eastern and western parts of the earth, what his account was. And ask him about the Spirit, what it is. If he informs you of that, then he is a prophet, so follow him; and if he does not inform you, then he is a fabricator, so do with his affair what you see fit.

Al-Nadr and Uqba set out until they came to Mecca to Quraysh, and said: O assembly of Quraysh, we have come to you with a decisive matter between you and Muhammad. The rabbis of the Jews have instructed us to ask him about certain matters, so inform them of them. They came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, inform us. They asked him about what they had been instructed to ask. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: I will inform you tomorrow of what you have asked about, and he did not add "if God wills." So they turned away from him. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained for fifteen nights, with God not sending down any revelation to him about this, and Jibril (peace be upon him) not coming to him. The people of Mecca spread rumors, saying: Muhammad promised us for tomorrow, and it has been fifteen days, and we have awakened in them, and he has not informed us of anything of what we asked him. The delay of revelation saddened the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and what the people of Mecca said weighed heavily upon him. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him from God, Mighty and Majestic, with the sura of the People of the Cave, in which there is a rebuke to him for his grief over them, and the account of what they had asked him about the affair of the youths and the wandering man, and the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾. [Ibn Ishaq said: It reached me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began the sura by saying ﴿Praise be to God, who sent down the Book to His servant﴾, meaning Muhammad: you are My messenger, in establishing what they asked about of his prophethood, ﴿and did not make in it any crookedness, upright﴾: that is, moderate, with no disagreement in it.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 2–3:

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿Upright, to warn of severe punishment from Him, and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, [in which] they will remain forever﴾

His exalted remembrance says: He sent down upon His servant the Qur'an, moderate and upright, without any crookedness in it, in order to warn you, O people, of severe punishment from God. By "punishment" (ba's) He means swift torment, immediate retribution and might. His saying ﴿from Him﴾ means: from the presence of God.

Commentators of the interpretation (ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said about this. Those who said so:

* Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq: ﴿to warn of severe punishment﴾: a swift penalty in this world and a torment in the Hereafter. ﴿from Him﴾: that is, from the presence of your Lord who sent you as a messenger.

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, similarly.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿from Him﴾: that is, from His presence.

If someone says: where is the object of His saying ﴿to warn﴾? Its object is omitted, relying on the indication of what appeared in the speech from its mention, and it is an implied pronoun connected to "warn" before "punishment," as if it were said: "to warn you of punishment," just as it is said: ﴿He frightens His allies﴾ [Al 'Imran: 175], which means: He frightens you with His allies.

* *

As for His saying ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers﴾

It means: and to give good tidings to those who affirm God and His messenger, ﴿who do righteous deeds﴾, which is acting upon what God has commanded to be acted upon, and refraining from what God has forbidden. ﴿that they will have a good reward﴾ means: a great reward for them from God for their faith in God and His messenger, and their righteous deeds in the world; and that reward is the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised.

* *

As for His saying ﴿in which they will remain forever﴾

Abiding eternally, not moving away from it, nor being moved from it. And "remaining" (makithin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from His saying ﴿that they will have a good reward﴾; in this state, they remain in that reward.

Commentators of the interpretation have said the same as what we have said about this. Those who said so:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds, that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever﴾: that is, in an abode of eternity in which they will not die, those who affirmed you regarding what you brought from God and acted upon what I commanded them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 4–5:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Enormous is the word that comes out of their mouths. They say not except a lie.﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance: "And [Muhammad] also warns the people ﴿who say, 'Allah has taken a son'﴾, among the polytheists of his people and others, of the punishment of Allah, His swift vengeance, and His delayed torment, for their saying that."

As [it has been reported]:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, regarding ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾: he means the Quraysh in their saying, "We only worship the angels, and they are the daughters of Allah." And His saying ﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾ means: the speakers of this statement have no knowledge of it, meaning their saying ﴿"Allah has taken a son"﴾. ﴿Of it﴾: meaning, of Allah, there is no knowledge. The pronoun in His saying ﴿of it﴾ refers to the remembrance of Allah.

The meaning of the speech is: those who utter this statement about Allah have no knowledge that it is permissible for Him to have a son; rather, out of their ignorance of Allah and His greatness, they said that.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿nor did their fathers﴾:

It means: nor did their forefathers who passed away before them, upon the same [creed] as what they hold today, have any knowledge of Allah and His greatness.

As for His saying ﴿Enormous is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾, the reciters differed in its recitation. The majority of the reciters of Medina, Kufa and Basra recited ﴿kabura kalimatan﴾ with the accusative on "kalimatan", meaning: "Enormous is their word that they spoke, as a word [of distinction]," as in the idiom "ni'ma rajulan 'Amr" and "ni'ma l-rajulu rajulan qama" and "ni'ma rajulan qama". Some grammarians of Basra said: "kalimatan" is put in the accusative because it carries the sense of "Enormous is this word," as the Exalted said, ﴿and evil is it as a resting place (wa sa'at murtafaqan)﴾. And he said: In the accusative it is like the verse of the poet:

*"And indeed I know, when the milch-camels return at dusk, [their] gait is the gait of the young ostriches, the winds overturning them to the north."* [[The verse is unattributed. Liqah are she-camels giving milk, which bear in early spring and remain liqah until summer passes from them. Tarawahat: returned from their pastures to their resting place, or were struck by the wind. Al-hadaj is the slow, feeble walk. Al-ri'al are young ostriches. Takubbuhunna: throws them upon their chests on the ground. Al-shamal: the wind blowing from the north. He compares the movement of the camels returning to their resting place to the swaying gait of young ostriches, a feeble walk, meaning that at that time the camels sway in their march like young ostriches when the north wind drives them.

The point of evidence is in his saying "takubbuhunna shamalan", for "shamalan" is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz), transferred from the subject; the original is "takubbuhunna shamalu" (with the subject in the nominative). It is parallel to the accusative of "kalimatan" in His saying, "Kabura kalimatan," for "kalimatan" is in the accusative as a specifier of relation, transferred from the subject, the original being "kabura kalimatun" (with the nominative).]]

That is, the winds overturn them to the north, as if he had said: "That word is enormous." It is reported from some Meccan readers that they recited it with the nominative, ﴿kabura kalimatun﴾, as one says "Your saying has become great" and "Your affair has become enormous." When read thus, there is no hidden pronoun in ﴿kabura kalimatun﴾, and "kalimatun" is an attribute of the subject.

The correct recitation in my view is that of the one who recited ﴿kabura kalimatan﴾ with the accusative, because the reciters as a consensus of proof have agreed upon it. So the meaning of the speech is: "Enormous is the word, a word that comes out of the mouths of these people who say: 'Allah has taken a son,' and 'the angels are the daughters of Allah.'"

As [it has been reported]:

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, regarding ﴿kabura kalimatan takhruju min afwahihim﴾: their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. And His saying ﴿They say not except a lie﴾: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: these speakers who say "Allah has taken a son" say by their statement nothing but a lie and a fabrication they have invented against Allah.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 6–8:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over them, [O Muhammad], if they do not believe in this message, [out of] sorrow.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is upon the earth adornment for it that We may test them [as to] which of them is best in deed.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We will make that which is upon it into barren, dry ground.﴾

He, may He be exalted in remembrance, means by this: Perhaps you, O Muhammad, would be killing yourself and destroying it over the traces of your people, who said to you, ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, in defiance of their Lord, if they do not believe in this Book which We have sent down to you, so that they would affirm that it is from Allah, [you would be consumed] with grief, anguish and longing, because of their turning away from you, their aversion to what you have brought them, and their refusal to believe in you. It is said of this: Bakhaʿa fulan nafsahu, yabkhaʿuha, bakhʿan and bukhūʿan (a man killed himself, killing himself by grief), and from it is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

Unless, O you who would destroy himself through passion
for a thing that the decrees have turned away from his hands.

[The verse is in the Diwan of Dhu al-Rummah, Cambridge edition of 1919, p. 251, from the thirty-second qasida, which has seventy-eight verses. Al-bākhiʿ means the killer; naḥatahu means diverted and turned away it. The verse is among the evidences cited by Abu ʿUbayda in Majaz al-Quran (1:393), who said: "Fa-laʿallaka bākhiʿun nafsaka": killing yourself. Dhu al-Rummah said: "Alā ayyuhādhā... " the verse.

That is, naḥatahu with emphasis. It is said bakhaʿtu lahu nafsī wa-naṣḥī: I exerted myself for him to the utmost. Al-Farrāʾ said in Maʿānī al-Quran (folio 183 of the University microfilm no. 24059): bākhiʿun nafsaka means one who brings himself out (of grief) and kills himself. And in (Lisan, bkhʿ): nafsahu yabkhaʿuha bakhʿan wa-bukhūʿan: he killed it with rage or grief. In the revelation (Fa-laʿallaka bākhiʿun nafsaka ʿalā āthārihim), al-Farrāʾ said: that is, one who distresses himself and kills himself. Dhu al-Rummah said "Alā yahdhaʾ... with a thing..." the verse. Al-Akhfash said: bakhaʿtu laka nafsī wa-naṣḥī: I exerted it, bakhaʿa bukhūʿan.]]

He means: naḥatahu, lightened.

Those who interpret the Quran have said, in line with what we have said regarding His words: ﴿bākhiʿ﴾.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself﴾ he said: killing yourself.

- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, the same.

As for His words: ﴿asafan﴾, the people of interpretation differed about its meaning. Some of them said: its meaning is: Perhaps you would kill yourself if they do not believe in this message, in anger.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿if they do not believe in this message, [out of] sorrow﴾ he said: anger.

Others said: grief (jazaʿan).

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us [transition], and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of Allah ﴿asafan﴾, he said: anguish (jazaʿan).

- Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

Others said: its meaning is: grief over them.

Mention of those who said that:

- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words ﴿asafan﴾, he said: grief over them.

He, may He be exalted in remembrance, means by this: Perhaps you, O Muhammad, would be killing yourself and destroying it over the traces of your people, who said to you, ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, in defiance of their Lord, if they do not believe in this Book which We have sent down to you, so that they would affirm that it is from Allah, [you would be consumed] with grief, anguish and longing, because of their turning away from you, their aversion to what you have brought them, and their refusal to believe in you. He means: naḥatahu, lightened.

- Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿ṣaʿīdan jurzan﴾, he said: bare-stripped (balqaʿ).

- Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, His words: ﴿And indeed, We will make that which is upon it into barren, dry ground﴾. Ṣaʿīd is land in which there is no tree or plant.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: ﴿And indeed, We will make that which is upon it into barren, dry ground﴾, meaning: the earth, for what is upon it is perishing and passing away, and the return is to Me, so do not despair, and let not what you hear and see in it grieve you.

- Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words ﴿ṣaʿīdan jurzan﴾: al-jurz is the land in which there is nothing. Do you not see that He says: ﴿Have they not seen that We drive the water to the barren land and bring forth thereby crops﴾? He said: and al-jurz: there is nothing in it, neither plant nor benefit, and ṣaʿīd: level. And he recited: ﴿You will not see therein any crookedness or unevenness﴾, he said: level. It is said: jurizat al-ardu fa-hiya majrūza, and jarazahā al-jarād wa-l-naʿam (the locusts and cattle stripped it bare), and arḍūn ajrāz: when there is nothing in them. It is said of a barren year: jurz and sinūn ajrāz, due to its dearth, dryness, and scarcity of rain. The rajaz poet said:

Indeed the years of drought have swept them away

[The verse is from the rajaz meter. It is among the evidences cited by Abu ʿUbayda in Majaz al-Quran (1:394), who said: jarazan means coarse land that grows nothing; the plural is arḍūn ajrāz. A barren year is called jurz and sinūn ajrāz, due to its dearth, dryness, and scarcity of rain. Then he cited a verse of Dhu al-Rummah, then the verse of the evidence. The verse is also among the evidences in (Lisan: jrz). He said: sanatun jurz: when it is a year of dearth. And al-jurz is a barren year. The rajaz poet said: "qad jarafatahunna..." the verse. The meaning of jarafatahunn: they were all or most of them taken away. The pronoun refers to his camels. It is possible that the meaning of jarrafatahunna, with doubled letter, is: made them lean, and removed what was in them of fat and flesh, owing to the scarcity of pasture.]]

It is said: ajraza al-qawm, when their land has become jurz, and jarazū their land, when they have eaten all its plants.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 18, Verse 9:

The interpretation (ta'wil, the explanation of the meaning) of His words: ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "Or did you think, O Muhammad, that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder? Indeed, what I created of the heavens and the earth, and what is in them of marvels, is more wondrous than the matter of the Companions of the Cave. My proof in all of that is established against these polytheists of your people and others among all My servants."

And the people of ta'wil (interpretation) said something similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us. And al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ Muhammad ibn 'Amr said in his report: "They are not a wonder compared to our most wondrous signs." Al-Harith said in his report, with their words: "Our most wondrous signs: they are not Our most wondrous signs."

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ He said: "They used to say: they are a wonder."

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ He says: "Among Our signs there has been what is more wondrous than that."

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, regarding ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ That is: "And what they measured of measure in what I made of the affairs of creation, and what I placed upon the servants of My proofs, is greater than that."

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: "Or did you think, O Muhammad, that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder? Indeed, what I have given you of knowledge and wisdom is better than it."

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ He says: "What I have given you of knowledge, the sunnah (prophetic practice) and the Book, is better than the matter of the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription."

We said that the first opinion is more fitting for the interpretation of the verse, because God, mighty and majestic, sent down the story of the Companions of the Cave to His Prophet as an argument against the polytheists of his people, as we mentioned in the report from Ibn 'Abbas, when they asked him about it, testing him with its answer to verify his truthfulness. So rebuking them by denying what is more binding upon them in argument than what they asked about, and they claimed that they would believe upon answering it, is more fitting than reporting what God had bestowed upon His Messenger of blessings.

As for "the Cave" (al-kahf), it is the cave of the mountain to which the people whose matter God related in this surah sought refuge.

As for "the Inscription" (al-raqim), the people of ta'wil differed regarding what is meant by it. Some of them said: it is the name of a town, or a valley, with differences among them on that.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn 'Abd al-A'la and 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Shaybani, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Ka'b claims that the Inscription is the town."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾: "The Inscription: a valley between 'Usfan and Ayla, short of Palestine, and it is near Ayla."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard my father, from 'Ata'iyya, who said: "The Inscription is a valley."

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾: "We used to relate that the Inscription is the valley in which the Companions of the Cave were."

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Simak ibn Harb, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿the Inscription﴾: He said: "Ka'b claims that it is the town."

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿the Inscription﴾: He said: "Some of them say: the Inscription is the book of their tubba' (kings of Yemen). Some of them say: it is the valley in which their cave is."

- al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say: "As for the Cave, it is the cave of the valley; and the Inscription is the name of the valley."

Others said: "The Inscription is the book."

Mention of those who said that:

- 'Ali narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Or did you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾: He says: "The book."

- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Ibn Qays, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Inscription is a slab of stone on which they wrote the story of the Companions of the Cave, then they placed it at the entrance of the cave."

- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "The Inscription is a book, and that book has a report, but God did not inform us about that book and what is in it." And he recited: ﴿And what will make you know what 'Illiyyun is? A written record, witnessed by those brought near. And what will make you know what Sijjin is? A written record.﴾

Others said: Rather, it is the name of the mountain of the Companions of the Cave.

Mention of those who said that:

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Inscription is the mountain in which the cave is."

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: It has been said that the name of that mountain is Banajlus.

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us with this, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas: "It has been said that its name is Banjlus."

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Wahb ibn Sulayman informed me, from Shu'ayb al-Jaba'i [[Shu'ayb al-Jaba'i: he is Shu'ayb ibn al-Aswad al-Jaba'i, a hadith scholar, a contemporary of Tawus, from whom Muhammad ibn Ishaq and Salama ibn Wahran took knowledge. He is attributed to al-Jaba' (with a hamza and shortened vowel), as al-Hamdani said in describing the Arabian Peninsula in several places. It is a district of Ma'afir, near al-Jund (see Mu'jam ma Ista'jam by al-Bakri, Cairo edition, under the entry al-Jaba', p. 360).]] that the name of the mountain of the cave is Banajlus, the name of the cave is Haylam, and the dog is Humran.

It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the Inscription that:

- al-Hasan narrated to us with it, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Simak, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I know the whole Qur'an except hanan (compassion), al-awwah (the one who sighs much), and al-raqim (the Inscription)."

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Amr ibn Dinar informed me that he heard 'Ikrima say: Ibn 'Abbas said: "I do not know what the Raqim is: is it a book or a building?"

The most correct of these opinions regarding the Inscription is that it means: a tablet, or a stone, or something on which a writing was inscribed. The people of reports have said that it is a tablet on which were written the names of the Companions of the Cave and their story when they took refuge in the cave.

Then some of them said: that tablet was raised into the treasury of the king. Some said: rather, it was placed at the entrance of their cave. And some said: rather, it was preserved with some of the people of their town.

The raqim is a form of the pattern fa'il (fa'il/fa'il-type adjective), its origin being marqum (inscribed), then it was changed to the form fa'il, as it is said of the wounded: jarih, and of the slain: qatil. It is said from it: raqamtu kadha wa kadha (I inscribed such and such) when I wrote it. From it comes the term raqm (embroidery mark) on cloth, because it is the mark by which its price is known. From this also the viper is called aram (spotted), because of the markings on it. The Arabs say: "Upon you is the raqmah, and leave the dafah," meaning: upon you is the raqmat al-wadi (the pool or bend of the valley) where the water is, and leave the dafah (the side). The two dafatan are the two sides of a valley. I think that whoever said that the raqim is the valley went to this meaning, that is, to raqmat al-wadi.

The discussion on the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the youths retreated to the cave, and said, "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and prepare for us right guidance in our affair."﴾

Allah, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Or do you think that the companions of the cave and the inscription were among Our signs as a wonder?﴾ When the youths, the companions of the cave, retreated to a mountain cave, fleeing with their religion to Allah, they said when they took refuge there: ﴿Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself﴾, desiring from their Lord that He provide them with mercy from Him. As for His saying, ﴿and prepare for us right guidance in our affair﴾, it means: they said, "Make easy for us what we seek and what we ask of Your pleasure, and the flight from disbelief in You and from the worship of the idols to which our people call us." ﴿Right guidance﴾ means: uprightness in acting upon what You love.

The people of knowledge have differed about the reason these youths went to the cave that Allah mentioned in His Book. Some of them said: the reason was that they were Muslims upon the religion of Jesus, and they had a worshipping king, an idolater, who called them to worship idols. So they fled with their religion from him, fearing that he would tempt them away from their religion or kill them, and they hid from him in the cave.

Mentioning those who said this:

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir related to us, saying: ʿAmr related to us concerning His saying, ﴿the companions of the cave and the inscription﴾: The youths were upon the religion of Jesus, upon Islam. Their king was an unbeliever, and he brought out an idol for them, but they refused and said: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never call upon any god besides Him; for then we would have uttered an excessive transgression.﴾ He said: So they withdrew from their people to worship Allah. One of them said: "My father had a cave where he kept his sheep. Come, let us go to it and stay in it." They entered it, and they were lost in that time, and they were sought. It was said: "They entered this cave." Their people said: "We do not want for them any punishment or torment worse than that we seal this cave over them." So they built it over them and sealed it. Then Allah sent over them a king upon the religion of Jesus, and that building which had been sealed over them was removed. Then some of them said to others: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ They said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day...﴾ until He reached ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾. The silver of that time was large coins. They sent one of them to bring them food and drink. When he went out, he saw on the entrance of the cave something he did not recognize, so he wanted to return, but then he went on until he entered the city, and he was surprised at what he saw. Then he took out a dirham, and they looked at it and did not recognize it, and they did not recognize the dirham. They said: "From where do you have this? This is silver of a time other than this one." They gathered around him, asking him, and they did not stop with him until they took him to their king. The people had a tablet on which they wrote what would happen. They looked into that tablet, and the king questioned him, and he informed him of his matter. They looked into the book to see when they had disappeared, and they rejoiced about him and his companions. It was said to him: "Come, show us your companions." He set out, and they set out with him to show them. He entered before the people, and Allah struck upon their ears. Then those who prevailed in their affair said: ﴿We will surely take over them a place of worship.﴾

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: The affair of the People of the Gospel fell into disorder, their sins grew great among them, and kings transgressed among them, until they worshipped idols and sacrificed to the tyrants. Among them, however, remained remnants upon the command of Jesus son of Mary, holding fast to the worship of Allah and His oneness. Among their kings who did this was a king of the Romans called Daqyanus, who had worshipped idols and sacrificed to the tyrants, and who killed whoever opposed him in that among those who adhered to the religion of Jesus son of Mary. He would travel through the villages of the Romans and would not leave in any village he entered anyone who professed the religion of Jesus son of Mary without killing him, until they worshipped idols and sacrificed to the tyrants. Then Daqyanus arrived at the city of the youths, the companions of the cave. When Daqyanus entered it, that weighed heavily upon the people of faith, so they hid from him and fled in every direction. Daqyanus had ordered, upon his arrival, that the people of faith be pursued and gathered for him. He appointed police from the disbelievers of the city, and they began to pursue the people of faith in their hiding places, bringing them out to Daqyanus. He would bring them to the assemblies where sacrifices were made to the tyrants, and he would give them the choice between being killed or worshipping the idols and sacrificing to the tyrants. Some would desire life and be terrified of being killed, and so they were tempted. Others would refuse to worship other than Allah and would be killed. When the steadfast among the people of faith in Allah saw this, they began to surrender themselves to torment and killing, so they were killed and their limbs were cut off. Then the pieces of their bodies were tied together and hung on the walls of the city on all sides and at every one of its gates, until the trial became severe upon the people of faith. Some of them disbelieved and were left alone, and some were crucified upon their religion and killed. When the youths, the companions of the cave, saw this, they grieved intensely, until their complexions changed and their bodies became emaciated. They sought help through prayer, fasting, charity, praising, glorifying, declaring the oneness of Allah, magnifying Him, weeping, and humbling themselves before Allah. They were youths, young and free, from the sons of the nobles of the Romans.

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: I have been told that upon some of them, because of their youth, was the glow of silver. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They remained thus in the worship of Allah, night and day, weeping to Allah and imploring Him. They were eight men: Maksilmina, who was the eldest, and he is the one who spoke to the king on their behalf; Muhsaymilina; Yamlikha; Marṭus; Kashuṭush; Bayrunus; Dinmus; and Yaṭunus Qalus. [Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (10:360): As for the names of the People of the Cave, they are non-Arabic, and the chain for knowing them is weak; he transmitted them from al-Tabari.]

When Daqyanus resolved to gather the people of the town to worship idols and sacrifice to the tyrants, they wept to Allah and humbled themselves before Him, saying: "O Allah, Lord of the heavens and the earth, we will never call upon any god besides You; ﴿for then we would have uttered an excessive transgression.﴾ Lift from Your servants, the believers, this trial, and repel from them the calamity, and bestow favor upon Your servants who believed in You, and who are prevented from worshipping You except secretly, hiding this, until they worship You openly." While they were in this state, their informants from among the disbelievers, those who used to gather the people of the city to worship idols and sacrifice to the tyrants, discovered them and reported their matter. They had been in a place of prayer of theirs where they worshipped Allah and humbled themselves before Him, and they expected that they would be mentioned to Daqyanus. Those disbelievers set out until they entered upon them in their place of prayer, and they found them prostrating on their faces, humbling themselves, weeping, and longing to Allah to save them from Daqyanus and his trial. When those disbelieving informants saw them, they said: "What has kept you from the king's command? Come with us to him!" Then they left them and raised their matter to Daqyanus, saying: "You gather the people to sacrifice to your gods, and these are youths from your own household, mocking you, ridiculing you, disobeying your command, and abandoning your gods. They have made for themselves a place of prayer, along with the companions of Jesus son of Mary, where they pray and humble themselves to their god and the god of Jesus and the companions of Jesus. Will you leave them doing this while they are within your authority and your kingdom? They are eight men, their leader is Maksilmina, and they are the sons of the great men of the city." When they said this to Daqyanus, he sent for them, and they were brought from the place of prayer where they had been, their eyes flowing with tears and their faces covered in dust. He said to them: "What has prevented you from witnessing the sacrifice to our gods that are worshipped in the land, and from making yourselves an example for the leading people of your city and for whoever among us is present?" He said: "Choose from me: either you sacrifice to our gods as the people sacrifice, or I will kill you!" Maksilmina said: "We have a God whom we worship, whose greatness fills the heavens and the earth. We will never call upon any god besides Him, and we will never acknowledge what you call us to, ever. Rather, we worship Allah, our Lord; to Him belong praise, magnification, and glorification, sincerely from ourselves forever. Him alone we worship, and from Him alone we seek deliverance and good. As for the tyrants and their worship, we will never acknowledge them, ever. We will not be worshippers of the devils, nor will we make ourselves and our bodies worshippers of them, after Allah has guided us to Him. Fear of you, or dread of your servitude, do what you will with us." Then the companions of Maksilmina said to Daqyanus the same as he had said. He said: When they said that to him, he ordered them to be stripped of the garments they wore, which were the clothes of their great men. Then he said: "As for you, since you have done what you have done, I will postpone you from being among the people of my kingdom and my inner circle and the people of my land. I will be free for you, and I will carry out for you what I have promised you of punishment. What prevents me from hastening that for you is only that I see you as youths, young in age, and I do not want to destroy you until I give you time, and I will set for you a term in which you may remember and reconsider your minds." Then he ordered that the adornments of gold and silver they wore be removed from them, and they were removed. Then he ordered them to be taken out from his presence. Daqyanus went to another city, other than their city, near it, for some matter he intended.

When the youths saw that Daqyanus had left their city, they hurried to act, fearing that if he came back to their city he would mention them. They agreed among themselves that each one of them would take an allowance from his father's house, to give some of it in charity and to take provisions with what remained, then set out to a cave near the city on a mountain called Banjalus, where they would remain and worship Allah, until Daqyanus returned, and they would come to him and stand before him, and he would do with them what he wished. When some of them said this to others, each youth went and took an allowance from his father's house and gave some of it in charity, and they set out with what remained of their provisions. A dog of theirs followed them until they reached that cave on that mountain. They stayed in it, having no occupation except prayer, fasting, glorification, magnification, and praising, seeking the face of Allah, the Exalted, and the life that does not end. They placed their provisions in the care of a youth among them called Yamlikha, who was in charge of their food, buying their provisions from the city secretly from its people. This was because he was among the most handsome and strongest of them. Yamlikha would do this: when he entered the city, he would put off the fine clothes he wore and take garments like those of the poor who beg for food. Then he would take his silver, go to the city, buy food and drink for them, listen and spy to learn the news, whether he and his companions had been mentioned among the people of the city, then return to his companions with their food and drink, and inform them of what he had heard of the news of the people. They remained in this state for as long as they remained. Then Daqyanus the tyrant came to the city from which he had gone out to his own city, and it is the city of Afamus. He ordered its great men, and they sacrificed to the tyrants. The people of faith were terrified at this, so they hid in every hiding place. Yamlikha was in the city buying food and drink for his companions with some of their allowance. He returned to his companions weeping, with a little food, and informed them that the tyrant Daqyanus had entered the city, and that they had been remembered and sought, and that they were being searched for along with the great men of the city, so that they would sacrifice to the tyrants. When he informed them of this, they were seized with great terror and fell prostrate on their faces, calling upon Allah, humbling themselves before Him, and seeking refuge in Him from the trial. Then Yamlikha said to them: "O my brothers, lift your heads, eat of this food which I have brought you, and put your trust in your Lord." They raised their heads, their eyes flowing with tears out of fear and dread for themselves, and they ate from it. That was at sunset. Then they sat talking and reviewing, and some of them reminding others, in sorrow, concerned about the news their companion had brought them. While they were in this state, Allah struck upon their ears in the cave for a counted number of years, and their dog stretched its forelegs at the entrance of the cave. What befell them befell them while they were believers, certain, affirming the promise. Their provisions were placed with them. When the next day came, Daqyanus missed them, searched for them, and did not find them. He said to the great men of the city: "The affair of these youths who have gone has grieved me greatly. They thought that I was angry with them for what they did at the beginning of their matter, because of their ignorance of what they were ignorant of about me. I would never have been unjust to them in my soul, nor would I punish any of them for anything, if they repent and worship my gods. Had they done so, I would have left them and not punished them for anything that had passed from them." The great men of the city said to him: "You are not deserving of mercy for a people who are wicked, rebellious, disobedient, persisting in their wrongdoing and disobedience. You had given them a term and postponed them from the punishment with which you struck others. Had they wished, they could have returned within that term, but they did not repent, did not desist, and did not regret what they had done. Since you set out, they have been squandering their wealth in the city, and when they learned of your coming they fled and have not been seen since. If you wish to bring them, send to their fathers and examine them, and press them until they show you where they are, for they are hiding from you." When they said this to Daqyanus the tyrant, he became exceedingly angry. Then he sent for their fathers, and they were brought. He asked them about their sons and said: "Tell me about your sons, the rebels who disobeyed my command and abandoned my gods. Bring them to me and inform me of their whereabouts." Their fathers said to him: "As for us, we have not disobeyed your command or opposed you. We have worshipped your gods and sacrificed to them. Do not kill us on account of rebellious people who have taken our wealth and squandered it and ruined it in the markets of the city, then went off and climbed a mountain called Banjalus, with a distant land between it and the city, fleeing from you." When they said this, he let them go. He began to deliberate what to do with the youths. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, cast into his soul that he should order the cave to be sealed over them, as an honor from Allah. He wished to honor them and honor the bodies of the youths, so that nothing would move them or pass over them. He wished to give them life and make them a sign for a nation that would succeed them, and to show them that the Hour is coming with no doubt, and that Allah raises those in the graves. So Daqyanus ordered the cave to be sealed over them, and he said: "Leave these youths, the rebels who abandoned my gods, to die as they are in the cave, of thirst and hunger, and let their chosen cave be their grave." That enemy of Allah did this to them, believing that they were awake and knew what was being done to them. But Allah had taken their souls in the sleep of death, and their dog stretched its forelegs at the entrance of the cave, and Allah covered them with what covered them. They were turned to the right and to the left.

Then two believing men who were in the household of the king Daqyanus, concealing their faith, whose names were: one named Bayduruṣ, and the other named Rūnās, agreed to write the story of the youths, the companions of the cave, their lineages, their names, their fathers' names, and the account of their story, on two leaden tablets. Then they would make a copper coffin for them and place the two tablets in it, and inscribe it at the mouth of the cave amid the buildings, and seal the coffin with their seal. They said: "Perhaps Allah will make manifest these youths to a believing people before the Day of Resurrection, so that whoever opens it will know their story when he reads this writing." They did so, then built over it within the building. Daqyanus and the generation who were with him remained as long as Allah willed for them to remain. Then Daqyanus died, along with the generation that was with him, and many generations after him, and one generation succeeded another.

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAbdullah ibn Kathir, from Mujahid, who said: The companions of the cave were the sons of the great men of their city and the nobles of their people. They went out and gathered behind the city without prior arrangement. A man among them, the eldest, said: "I find within myself something which I do not think anyone else finds." They said: "What do you find?" He said: "I find within myself that my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." They said: "We find the same." So they all stood up and said: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never call upon any god besides Him; for then we would have uttered an excessive transgression.﴾ They agreed to enter the cave. Over their city at that time was a tyrant called Daqyanus. They remained in the cave for three hundred years and nine more.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 10 (part 2 of 2):

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Abi Rawwad, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: The People of the Cave (Ashab al-Kahf) were young men, kings, wearing torques and bracelets, with locks of hair. A hunting dog of theirs was with them. They went out to a great festival of theirs, in splendour and procession, and they brought out with them the idols they worshipped. But Allah cast faith into the hearts of the youths, and they believed, and each one of them concealed his faith from his companion. They said to themselves, without any of them revealing his faith to the others: "Let us leave from among this people, lest the punishment strike us for their crime." So a young man among them went out until he reached the shade of a tree and sat down in it. Then another came out and saw him sitting alone, and he hoped that he was in the same state as himself, without it being apparent from him, so he came and sat with him. Then the others came out and came and sat with the two of them, and they gathered together. Some of them said: "What brought you together?" Another said: "Rather, what brought you together?" Each one was concealing his faith from his companion, out of fear for himself. Then they said: "Let two youths from among you go out, and let them be alone, and let them make a pact that neither of them will reveal to the other, and then let each of them reveal his matter to his companion, for we hope that we are upon a single matter." So two youths from among them went out and made a pact, then they spoke, and each one of them mentioned his matter to his companion. They returned to their fellows, joyful, having agreed upon one matter, and behold, they were all upon faith. And behold, there was a cave in the mountain near them. Some of them said to others: "Go to the cave; your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a plan in your affair" (﴿Your Lord will spread for you of His mercy and will prepare for you a course of ease in your affair﴾ [18:16]). So they entered the cave, with their hunting dog, and they slept. Allah made it a single sleep for them, and they slept three hundred years and added nine. He said: Their people lost them, so they sought them and sent out scouts, but Allah blinded their traces and their cave from them. When they could not find them, they wrote their names and lineages on a tablet: so-and-so son of so-and-so, and so-and-so son of so-and-so, sons of our kings, whom we lost at such-and-such festival, in such-and-such month, in such-and-such year, in the kingdom of so-and-so son of so-and-so. They placed the tablet in the treasury. Then that king died, and a Muslim king prevailed over them, along with the Muslims, and generation followed generation, and they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine.

Others said: Rather, their going to the cave was out of flight from the authority's pursuit, which had been on account of a claim of a crime that was alleged against a companion of theirs, that he had committed it.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, saying: Isma'il ibn Shurus informed me, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: A disciple (hawari) of ʿIsa ibn Maryam came to the city of the People of the Cave and wished to enter it, but it was said to him: "At its gate is an idol; no one enters it without prostrating to it." He disliked entering it, so he came to a bathhouse near that city and worked there, hiring himself out to the owner of the bathhouse. The owner of the bathhouse saw blessing in his bathhouse, and provision flowed to him, so he began to present Islam to him, and he (the disciple) would confide in him. Some youths of the city became attached to him, and he would inform them of the news of the heavens and the earth and the news of the Hereafter, until they believed in him and affirmed him, and they were in the same state as his in goodly appearance. He stipulated with the owner of the bathhouse that "the night is mine; let nothing come between me and the prayer when it comes." He remained so until the son of the king came with a woman and entered the bathhouse with her. The disciple reproached him, saying: "You are the son of the king, and you enter with you this wretched woman?" He was ashamed and went away, then returned another time, and he said to him the same thing; he cursed him and rebuked him, and he did not turn aside until he entered and the woman entered with him, and both of them died together in the bathhouse. The king was informed, and it was said to him: "The owner of the bathhouse has killed your son." So he (the owner) was sought, but he could not be found, having fled. The king said: "Who used to accompany him?" They named the youths, and they were sought, and they left the city. They passed by a companion of theirs in his field of crops, who was in the same state as their affair, and they mentioned that they were being sought, so the dog went with them, until night overtook them at the cave. They entered it, saying: "We will spend the night here, then we will rise in the morning, God willing, and you will see your opinion." So He struck upon their ears, and the king went out with his companions following them, until they found that they had entered the cave. Whenever a man wished to enter, he was struck with terror, and no one could bring himself to enter it. Then a speaker said: "Did you not, had you been able to capture them, kill them?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then wall up the entrance of the cave over them, and leave them in it to die of thirst and hunger." And so he did.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 11–12:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So We sealed their ears in the cave for a number of years﴾ [11] ﴿Then We woke them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the time they had stayed﴾ [12]

He, may His praise be exalted, means by His words ﴿So We sealed their ears in the cave﴾: We struck upon their ears with sleep in the cave, meaning We cast sleep upon them, just as one says to another, "May God strike you with paralysis (al-falaj)," meaning God afflicted him with it and sent it upon him.

* *

As for His words ﴿for a number of years﴾:

He means numbered years, and "ʿadadan" (numbered) is in the accusative by His words ﴿So We sealed﴾.

* *

As for His words ﴿Then We woke them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise﴾:

He says: Then We raised these youths who took refuge in the cave, after We had sealed their ears therein for a number of years from their slumber, so that My servants would look and know, through inquiry, which of the two groups that disputed about the length of the youths' stay in their cave, while they slept, was more accurate ﴿in computing the time they had stayed﴾. He says: more correct regarding the measure of their stay therein, "amad" (a term). By "amad" is meant the limit (al-ghayah), as al-Nabigha said:

*Except for one like you, or one whom you outstrip,*
*Outstripping as the racehorse does when it reaches the finish (al-amad).*

[The verse is by al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani, in (Mukhtar al-Shi'r al-Jahili, with the commentary of Mustafa al-Saqqa, Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi and Sons edition, p. 152), from his ode beginning: "O abode of Mayya at al-Ulya, then al-Sind," which has fifty verses; the witness is the twenty-sixth of them. Its commentator said: al-amad is the limit to which one runs (and on this the author cited it). He says: he does not harbor hatred and anger except toward one who is like you among people, or close to you.]

It has been mentioned that those who disagreed about that matter, from among their own people, were a group from the people of the youths. Some of them said: both parties were disbelievers. Others said: rather, one of them was a Muslim and the other a disbeliever.

Mention of those who said both parties were from the people of the youths: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿which of the two parties﴾: from the people of the youths.

* Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

* al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding his words ﴿Then We woke them that We might know which of the two parties was more precise in computing the time they had stayed﴾, he says: neither group had knowledge, neither their disbelievers nor their believers.

As for His words ﴿amadan﴾, the people of interpretation differed about its meaning. Some of them said: its meaning is "far" (ba'idan).

Mention of those who said that:

* ʿAli narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿for what they stayed, a term (amadan)﴾, he says: far.

Others said: its meaning is "number" (ʿadadan).

Mention of those who said that: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿amadan﴾, he said: numbered.

* al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Regarding the accusative case of His words ﴿amadan﴾ there are two possibilities. The first is that it is in the accusative as a specification (tafsir) of His word ﴿aḥṣā﴾, as if it were said: which of the two parties was more correct in number for the measure of their stay.

This is the more correct of the two views on this matter, because the interpretation of the exegetes has come to be so.

The other is that it is in the accusative by the governing of His words ﴿labithu﴾ upon it, as if He said: which of the two parties was more precise for their stay as a limit.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 13–14:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We relate to you their story with truth. They were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance﴾ (13) ﴿And We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke besides Him any deity. We would have certainly spoken then an excessive transgression."﴾ (14)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ):

"We, O Muhammad, relate to you the account of these young men who sought refuge in the cave, with truth", meaning: with sincerity and certainty about which there is no doubt. ﴿Indeed, they were young men who believed in their Lord﴾: meaning, the young men who took refuge in the cave, about whose account the chiefs of the polytheists among your people asked you, were young men who believed in their Lord. ﴿And We increased them in guidance﴾: meaning, We increased them in faith in addition to their belief in their Lord, and insight into their religion, to the point that they endured abandoning the abode of their people and fleeing from among them with their religion to God, and parting from what they had been in of comfortable and soft living, for the harshness of dwelling in a mountain cave.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says:

"And We inspired them with patience, and We fortified their hearts with the light of faith, until their souls turned away from what they had been in of comfortable living."

As:

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾: he said: "With faith."

* *

And His saying: ﴿When they stood up and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth"﴾

He says: when they stood before the tyrant Decius (Daqyanus), and said to him when he reproached them for abandoning the worship of his gods: ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, he says: they said, "Our Lord is the King of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and your gods are created, and it is not permissible for us to abandon the worship of the Lord and worship the created." ﴿We will never invoke besides Him any deity﴾: he says: "We will never invoke, besides the Lord of the heavens and the earth, any deity, because there is no deity other than Him, and everything besides Him is His creation." ﴿We would have certainly spoken then an excessive transgression﴾: he, may His praise be exalted, says: "If we were to invoke a deity other than the God of the heavens and the earth, we would have then, by invoking other than Him, spoken an excessive transgression" — shatatan min al-qawl, meaning: a extreme lie, exceeding its measure in falsehood and extravagance — as the poet said:

*Alā yā li-qawmī qad ashaṭat ʿawādhilī... wa-yazʿumna an awdā bi-ḥaqqī bāṭilī*
(The line is by al-Ahwas ibn Muhammad, and it is among the evidences cited by Abu ʿUbaydah in *Majaz al-Qur'an* (1:394), where he said: "(Qulna idhan shatatan): i.e., injustice and excess." He cited: "Alā yā li-qawmī qad ashaṭat ʿawādhilī..." the line, and after it he mentioned another line: "Wa-yalḥaynī fī al-lahwi an lā uḥibbuhu... wa-lil-lahwi dāʿin dāʾibun ghayru ghāfilī." In *Lisan al-ʿArab* (root sh-t-t): "Al-shatat: exceeding the measure in selling or seeking or judging or whatever else derives from it." He also said: "Shadda fī salʿatihi wa-ashatta: exceeded the measure, and distanced himself from the truth. Shadda ʿalayhi fī ḥukmihi yashuṭṭu shaṭaṭan: he was unjust in his judgment. Ishtaṭṭa and ashaṭṭa: he acted unjustly in his judgment." Abu ʿUbaydah said: "Shaṭaṭtu ashuṭṭu, with the shin vowelled with a damma, and Ashaṭtu: I acted unjustly." Ibn Barri said: "Ashaṭṭa means: went far, and shaṭṭa means: was far." The evidence for ashaṭṭa meaning "went far" is the saying of al-Ahwas: "Alā li-qawmī qad ashaṭat ʿawādhilī..." the line.)

It is said of it: "Fulan has exceeded the measure in asking the price (ashaṭṭa fi al-sawm) when he went beyond the due amount and rose above it, yashuṭṭu ishtiṭāṭan and shaṭaṭan." As for distance, it is said: "The dwelling of so-and-so is far (shaṭṭa manzilu fulānin), yashuṭṭu shuṭūṭan." And as for length: "The young woman became tall (shaṭṭat al-jāriyah), yashuṭṭu shiṭāṭan and shiṭāṭatan," when she grew tall.

In accordance with what we have said regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿shaṭaṭan﴾, the people of interpretation have spoken.

Those who said that: Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿We would have certainly spoken then an excessive transgression﴾: he said, "a lie."

Those who said that: Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿We would have certainly spoken then an excessive transgression﴾: he said, "a lie."

⁕ Yunus narrated to us, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿We would have certainly spoken then an excessive transgression﴾: he said, "We would have certainly spoken then an error. Al-shatat: the error in speech."

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are our people; they have taken gods besides Him. Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?  Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾

He, mighty is His remembrance, says, relating the statement of the youths from among the companions of the cave: "These are our people; they have taken gods besides Allah, worshipping them apart from Him." ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾ That is: why do they not bring, for their worship of them, a clear proof? In the speech there is an omission, and what is apparent has been sufficient in place of what has been omitted. This is in His saying: ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾ The pronoun "them" (hum) in "upon them" (alayhim) refers to the gods, and the gods are not brought authority, nor is authority sought for them. Rather, it is their worshippers who are asked for authority for their worship of them. Thus, since the matter is so, it is known that the meaning of the speech is: "Why do they not bring, upon their worship of them and their taking them as gods besides Allah, a clear authority?"

In keeping with what we have said concerning the meaning of "authority" (sultan), the people of interpretation have said likewise.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾: he says, "with a manifest excuse."

By His saying, mighty is His remembrance, ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ is meant: and who is more transgressive and more associating (others) with Allah than one who invents and fabricates a falsehood against Allah, and associates with Allah in His authority a partner whom he worships apart from Him and takes as a god.

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship other than Allah, then take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy and will prepare for you of your affair an easy provision.﴾ (18:16)

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says, reporting the words of some of the youths to one another:

"And when you withdraw, O youths, from your people who have taken gods besides Allah" ﴿and what they worship other than Allah﴾. He says: and when you withdraw from your people who worship gods other than Allah. Here "mā" (what), given that this is its meaning, is in the accusative position, being coordinated with the pronoun "hum" (them) in the words ﴿and when you withdraw from them﴾.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And when you withdraw from them and what they worship other than Allah﴾. In the codex of Abdullah it is: "wa-ma ya'buduna min dun Allah" (and what they worship other than Allah); this is its explanation.

As for His words ﴿then take refuge in the cave﴾, He means by it:

Betake yourselves to the cave in the mountain that is called Najlus. ﴿Your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy﴾ means: your Lord will extend for you of His mercy by facilitating for you the way out of the matter with which you have been afflicted by the unbeliever Decius (Daqyanus) and his seeking you in order to make you face trial.

* *

As for His words ﴿then take refuge in the cave﴾:

It is the answer to "idh" (when), as if the meaning of the speech is: "And when you withdraw, O people, from your people, then take refuge in the cave," just as one says: "When you have sinned, then seek forgiveness of Allah and turn to Him in repentance."

* *

As for His words ﴿and will prepare for you of your affair an easy provision﴾:

He says: and will make easy for you, of your affair in which you are in distress and anguish out of fear for yourselves and your religion, a mirfaq (provision/means of relief). By mirfaq he means: that by which you obtain relief (irtifaq) from something. Regarding mirfaq, whether of the hand or otherwise, there are two dialects: kasr the mīm with fath the fā' (mirfaq), and fath the mīm with kasr the fā' (marfiq). Al-Kisa'i would reject, for the elbow of a person which is in the hand, anything other than fath the fā' and kasr the mīm; al-Farra' would report both, I mean in mirfaq of the matter and of the hand, both dialects, and he would recite in support of that the saying of the poet:

"I spent the night keeping my elbow away from my elbow [[This is a verse of rajaz, which the author cites to show that mirfaq, the means by which one gains relief and benefit, may be pronounced with fath of the mīm together with kasr of the rā', and kasr of the mīm with fath. Likewise the elbow of the hands, and this agrees with what al-Farra' said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 184 of the Jami'a microfilm): He said: "min amrikum mirfaqan" with kasr of the mīm was recited by al-A'mash and al-Hasan, and fath of it by the people of Madinah and 'Asim; so it seems that those who pronounced the mīm with fath and the fā' with kasr intended to distinguish between mirfaq of the matter and mirfaq of a person. Most of the Arabs use kasr of the mīm both for the matter and for a person. The Arabs also use fath of the mīm for the elbow of a person; there are two dialects in them. End quote. As for Abu 'Ubaydah, in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:95 dh), he said: al-mirfaq is that by which one gains relief, and some people read it marfaq (i.e., with fath), but for the two arms it is mirfaq. I did not find this verse cited by al-Farra', nor by Abu 'Ubaydah, nor in Lisan al-'Arab. "Ajafi" means: I keep away.]]"

He says: kasr of the mīm in it is better.

Some of the grammarians of Basra used to say regarding His words ﴿from your affair, a mirfaq﴾: something by which you gain relief, like "miqta'" (that by which one cuts); and mirfaqan he made a noun like "masjid" (mosque), and it may be a dialect, they say: "rafaqa yarfuqu mirfaqan"; and if you wish, "mirfaqan" meaning "rifqan" (gentleness), though it is not recited so.

The readers have differed regarding the recitation of this. The common readers of Madinah recited it: "wa-yuhayyi' lakum min amrikum mirfaqan" with fath of the mīm and kasr of the fā', and the common readers of Iraq in both cities recited ﴿mirfaqan﴾ with kasr of the mīm and fath of the fā'.

The correct position on this matter is to say: they are two readings with one meaning; each of them has been recited by readers from among the people of the Qur'an, so whichever of the two the reader recites is correct. Nevertheless, although that is so, the one I choose in the recitation of this: ﴿and will prepare for you of your affair a mirfaq﴾ with kasr of the mīm and fath of the fā', because that is the more eloquent and more widely known of the two dialects among the Arabs; and likewise for everything by which one gains relief from something.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them on the left, while they were in a spacious place within it. That is among the signs of Allah. He whom Allah guides is the [one] guided; but he whom He leaves astray - you will not find for him a guiding ally.﴾ [18:17]

Says the Exalted: ﴿And you would see the sun﴾ - O Muhammad - ﴿when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾. By His saying ﴿tazāwaru﴾: it deviates and inclines, from al-zawr, which is crookedness and inclination. It is said of it: "in this land there is zawar" when there is crookedness in it, and "in so-and-so, from so-and-so, izwirār" when there is aversion from him in it. From this is the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Khāzim:

"The guides bring their camels toward water-palms... and in them, from the two Abān, is an izwirār."

[The verse is by Bishr ibn Khāzim. Al-Bakri mentioned it in Mu'jam mā ista'jam (Cairo edition, Lajnat al-Ta'lif, edited by Mustafa al-Saqqa) under the entry "Abān". He said: Abān is a mountain. There are two Abāns: Abān al-Abyad and Abān al-Aswad, a farsakh apart, with the Wadi al-Rimma cutting between them. Abān al-Abyad belongs specifically to the Banu Jarid of the Banu Fazara, and al-Aswad to the Banu Waleba of the Banu al-Harith ibn Tha'laba ibn Dawdan ibn Asad. Bishr said about them, "and in them, from the two Abān, is an izwirār." Al-Asma'i said: he meant one Abān, and made it dual out of necessity. Nakhl, as in Mu'jam mā ista'jam, is in the form of the plural of nakhla; Ya'qub said it is a village in a valley called Shadakh, belonging to Fazara, Ashja', Anmar, Quraysh and the Ansar... two nights from Medina, or it is water between al-Qissa and al-Thamiliya. "Yu'amu bihā" means: they aim with the camels toward it. Al-Hudāt is the plural of hādi, the driver of camels who drives them and sings to them. Al-Izwirār is inclination, turning away and aversion from a thing, as the author cited it at His saying, "inclining away from their cave" - that is, it leans and deviates from it.]

That is, aversion and avoidance.

The reciters differed regarding the recitation of this. The majority of the reciters of Medina, Mecca and Basra recited it as "tazzāwaru" with a shaddah on the zāy, meaning "tatazāwaru" with two tā's, and one of the two tā's was assimilated into the zāy, as in "tazzāharūn 'alayhim." The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited ﴿tazāwaru﴾ with the tā and zāy both unshaddah, as if it meant the form tafā'ala from al-zawr. It is related from some of them: "tazwarr" with the tā unshaddah, the zāy sukūn and the rā shaddah, like "tahmarr," and some of them: "tazwārr," like "tahmārr."

The correct position regarding the recitation of this, in our view, is to say: these are two recitations - I mean ﴿tazāwaru﴾ with the zāy unshaddah and "tazzāwaru" with it shaddah - both well-known, widely transmitted by the reciters of the provinces, close in meaning; whichever of them a reciter reads, he is correct. As for the other two readings, they are recitations I do not consider recitable, although they have an understandable basis in Arabic, because they deviate from what the reciters of the provinces follow.

In accordance with what we have said regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿tazāwaru ʿan kahfihim﴾, the people of interpretation have said.

Those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: ﴿And you would see the sun when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right﴾ - he said: it inclines.

- Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿inclining away from their cave to the right﴾ - he says: it inclines away from them.
