- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And you would see the sun when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right and when it set, passing them on the left﴾ - he says: it inclines away from their cave to the right and to the left.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿inclining away from their cave to the right﴾ - he says: it inclines to the right, leaving them on the right.

- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿inclining away from their cave to the right﴾ - he said: it inclines away from their cave to the right.

- It was related to me from Yazid ibn Harun, from Sufyan ibn Husayn, from Ya'la ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: If the sun were to rise upon them it would burn them, and if they were not turned they would be consumed by the earth. He said: and that is His saying: ﴿And you would see the sun when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right and when it set, passing them on the left﴾.

- Muhammad ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz related to me, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Muslim ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: ﴿inclining away from their cave﴾ - inclines.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and when it set, passing them on the left﴾

The Exalted says: and when the sun sets, it leaves them on their left side. The meaning of the speech is: you would see the sun when it rises inclining away from their cave, so it rises on their right side, lest it strike the youths; for if it rose facing them it would burn them and their garments, or discolor them. And when it sets it leaves them on the left side, so it does not strike them. It is said of it: "qaradtu mawdi'a kadhā" when I cut across it and passed beyond it. Thus some scholars of Arabic from Basra would say. As for the Kufans, they claim it means facing directly (al-muhādhāh), and they mention that they heard from the Arabs: "qaradtuhu qubulan wa-dubura" and "hadhawtuhu dhāt al-yamīn wa-l-shimāl," and "qubulan wa-dubura" meaning: I was opposite it. They say: qarḍ and ḥadhw have the same meaning. The root of qarḍ is cutting; it is said of it: "qaradtu al-thawb" when I cut the cloth, and from it the scissors (miqrāḍ) is so called because it cuts; and from it "the mouse cut (qarada) the cloth." From it is the verse of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Toward caravans passing the edges of Mushrif, leaving on the left and on their right the horsemen..."

[The verse is in the Diwan of Dhu al-Rumma (Cambridge edition, 1919), p. 313, of poem no. 41, whose verses number 51. That is, I looked toward caravans passing, i.e., turning away from them. Al-Fawaris are sand dunes in al-Dahna'. The verse is among the evidences of Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:396), where he said: "tuqriduhum dhat al-shimal" means they leave them behind on the left and pass them and cut across them, leaving them on its left. It is said: "Have you passed by such and such a place?" and the respondent says: "I passed it on the right by night." Dhu al-Rumma said: "Toward caravans passing the edges of Mushrif..." the verse. Mushrif and al-Fawaris are two places in Najd, as in Mu'jam mā ista'jam, and he cited the verse in the entry "al-Fawaris," attributing it to Dhu al-Rumma. Al-Zu'n is the plural of zu'ayna, the woman in the howdah on her camel or she-camel.]

By His saying "yaqridna" he means: they cut across.

In accordance with what we have said regarding that, the people of interpretation have said.

Those who said that:

- Ali related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to me, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿and when it sets, passing them on the left﴾ - he says: it leaves them.

- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: ﴿and when it sets, passing them﴾ - it leaves them on the left.

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿taqriduhum﴾ - he said: it leaves them.

- Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada: ﴿and when it sets, passing them on the left﴾ - he says: it leaves them on the left.

- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿passing them on the left﴾ - he said: it leaves them on the left.

- Ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz related to us, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Muslim ibn Abi al-Wadda' informed us, from Salim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿and when it sets, passing them﴾ - he said: it leaves them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿while they were in a spacious place within it﴾

He says: and the youths who took refuge in it were in a wide space within it; its plural is fajawāt, and fijā', with the madd.

In accordance with what we have said regarding that, the people of interpretation have said.

Those who said that:

- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada: ﴿while they were in a spacious place within it﴾ - he says: in an open area of the cave. Allah said: ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾.

- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿while they were in a spacious place within it﴾ - he said: the inner place.

- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid: ﴿while they were in a spacious place within it﴾ - he said: the open place.

- Ibn Sinan related to me, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Muslim Abu Sa'id ibn Abi al-Wadda' related to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿within it﴾ - he said: in an inner place.

* *

And His saying: ﴿That is among the signs of Allah﴾

He, Mighty is His remembrance, says: We did this which We did to these youths whose matter We have related to you, in making them such that, when We willed to place a covering over their ears, the sun inclines away from their resting place on the right when it rises and leaves them on the left when it sets, while they are in a spacious place, such that the sun does not burn them and make them pale, nor do their garments wear out from the length of their sleep and rot upon their bodies - [this is] among the proofs of Allah and His arguments over His creation, and the evidences by which those of understanding are guided to the greatness of His power and dominion, and that nothing He wills is beyond Him. And His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah guides is the one guided﴾ - the Mighty and Majestic says: whomever Allah enables to be guided by His signs and proofs to the truth which He made as evidence for it, he is the guided one: that is, he is the one who has hit upon the path of truth. ﴿And whomever He sends astray﴾ - that is, whomever Allah leaves astray from His signs and proofs, so that He does not enable him to draw guidance from them toward the path of rectitude. ﴿Then you will not find for him a guiding ally﴾ - that is, you will not find for him, O Muhammad, a close friend or ally who guides him to reach it, because success and abandonment are in the hand of Allah; He grants success to whom He wills of His servants and forsakes whom He wills. That is: so do not let the turning away of those who turn from you among your people, and their denial of you, grieve you; for if I willed, I would guide them so that they believe, and guidance and misguidance are in My hand.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 18:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And you would think them awake, while they are asleep. And We turn them to the right and to the left, and their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold. If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them.﴾ (18)

Allah, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "And you would think, O Muhammad, these youths whose story We have related to you, if you saw them in the state in which We had struck upon their ears in their cave to which they had retreated, that they were awake." The word "ayqaz" (awake) is the plural of "yaqiz" (alert), and from it is the verse of the rajaz poet:

"And they found their brothers awake... and the sword of Ghayyaz, a sword of theirs, [striking]..."

[The two verses (in the Diwan of al-Ajjaj, in the appendix to his Diwan, pp. 81–82) are from a rajaz poem of 19 verses. Their numbers in it are 8 and 16. They are among the evidences cited by Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Quran (1:397), who said concerning "and you would think them awake": its singular is "yaqiz", and one says "rijal ayqaz" (alert men); likewise the plural of "yaqzan" is "ayqaz", treating it as the plural of "yaqiz".

Ru'ba said: "And they found... the two verses," and he attributed them to Ru'ba, but they are in the Diwan of al-Ajjaj. Their poems became intermingled for the transmitters and the philologists. "Ghayyaz" is the name of a man.]

And His words: ﴿while they are asleep﴾ mean: while they are sleeping. "Ruqud" is the plural of "raqid" (sleeper), like "julus" is the plural of "jalis" (sitting), and "qu'ud" is the plural of "qa'id" (sitting).

His words: ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾ mean: exalted is His remembrance; We turn these youths in their sleep, at times to the right side and at times to the left side.

As follows:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾: "This turning was during their first sleep." He said: "It was mentioned to us that Abu 'Iyad said: for them there are two turnings each year."

* It was related to me from Yazid, who said: Sufyan ibn Husayn informed us, from Ya'la ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left﴾: He said: "If they were not turned, the earth would consume them."

* * *

And His words: ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾

The interpreters differed concerning whom Allah meant by His words: ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs﴾. Some said: it was a dog of theirs that was with them, and we have mentioned many who said that earlier. Others said: it was a man from among the people, a cook for them, who followed them.

As for "al-wasid" (the threshold), the interpreters differed in its explanation. Some said: it is the courtyard (al-fina').

Those who said that:

* Ali narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿bi-l-wasid﴾: he said: "by the courtyard."

* Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi al-Wadda' narrated to us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾: he said: "at the courtyard."

* Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, ﴿bi-l-wasid﴾: he said: "by the courtyard."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, ﴿bi-l-wasid﴾: he said: "by the courtyard." Ibn Jurayj said: "He holds the door of the cave."

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾: he said: "at the courtyard of the cave."

* al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿bi-l-wasid﴾: he said: "at the courtyard of the cave."

* It was related to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words: ﴿bi-l-wasid﴾: he said: "meaning, by the courtyard."

Others said: "al-Wasid" is "al-sa'id" (the surface of the earth).

Those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾: he meant their courtyard, and it is said: "al-wasid" is "al-sa'id."

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub narrated to us, from Harun, from Antarah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His words: ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾: he said: "al-wasid is al-sa'id."

* Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Amr, concerning His words: ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾: he said: "al-wasid is al-sa'id, the dust."

Others said: "al-Wasid" is "the door."

Those who said that:

* Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from Shabib, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿And their dog stretches out his forelegs at the threshold﴾: he said: "by the door," and they said "by the courtyard."

The most correct of these opinions, in our view, is the saying of the one who said: "al-wasid" is the door, or the courtyard of the door where the door is closed. This is because the door is "yuw'sad" (shut), and its "ii'sad" is its closing and locking, from the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Upon them will be a closed vault (mu'sadah)﴾. In it there are two dialects: "al-asid," which is the dialect of the people of Najd, and "al-wasid," which is the dialect of the people of Tihama. It is reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', who said: it is the dialect of the people of Yemen. This is like their saying: "warrakhtu al-kitab" and "arrakhtuhu" (I dated the letter), and "wakkadtu al-amr" and "akkadtuhu" (I confirmed the matter). Whoever says "al-wasid" says: "awsadtu al-bab fa-ana uwsiduhu" (I shut the door, so I shut it), and it is "muwsad." Whoever says "al-asid" says: "a'sadtu al-bab fa-huwa mu'sad." So the meaning of the statement is: "And their dog stretches out his forelegs in the courtyard of their cave, at the door, guarding its door for them."

* * *

And His words: ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned from them in flight﴾

That is: if you had looked upon them in the sleep they slept in their cave, you would have turned your back on them, fleeing from them. ﴿And you would have been filled with dread of them﴾ means: your soul would have been filled with terror from looking upon them, because Allah had clothed them in awe, so that no one would reach them and no hand would touch them, until the Decree reached its term concerning them, and His power and authority awakened them from their sleep at the time He willed, to make them a lesson for whomever He willed of His creation, and a sign for whoever wished to argue by them against His servants, so that they would know that the promise of Allah is true, and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt in it.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His words: ﴿And you would have been filled with dread of them﴾. The majority of the readers of Medina recited "lamullitta" with a doubled lam, meaning that he would be filled again and again. The majority of the readers of Iraq recited "lamulita" with a single lam, meaning: you would have been filled once. Both are, in our view, widely transmitted recitations, close in meaning, and whichever reading the reader uses is correct.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 18, Verses 19–20 (Part 1 of 3)**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We raised them up, that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him see which of them has the purest food, and bring you provision from it, and let him be discreet, and let him not make anyone aware of you (19). For if they gain control over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion, and then you will never succeed (20)."﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Just as We put these youths to sleep in the cave, guarding them from anyone reaching them and from any watcher's eye looking at them, and by Our power preserving their bodies from decay over the length of time and their garments from mildew over the passing of days, so likewise We raised them from their sleep and woke them from their slumber. We did this so that We might make them know the greatness of Our dominion and the wondrous nature of Our action in Our creation, and that they might increase in insight regarding their affair, in which they stood, namely their disavowal of the worship of idols and their sincere devotion to the worship of God alone, without partner, when they perceived how long the time had been upon them while they remained in the same state in which they had fallen asleep.

As for His words, ﴿that they might question one another﴾, it means: that some of them might ask others. ﴿A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?"﴾: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: So they questioned one another, and one speaker among them said to his companions, ﴿"How long have you remained?"﴾ This was because they were astonished at their own long sleep. ﴿They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ He says: The others answered him, saying, "We have remained a day or part of a day," supposing that this was indeed the case. Then the others said, ﴿"Your Lord knows best how long you have remained,"﴾ thereby entrusting knowledge to God.

* *

As for His words, ﴿"So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city"﴾: it means their city from which they had fled, which is called Afsus. ﴿"And let him see which of them has the purest food, and bring you provision from it"﴾: it is mentioned that they had awoken from their sleep hungry, and therefore they sought food.

Mention of those who said this, and mention of the reason for which it is reported that they were raised from their sleep when they were raised:

◆ Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: Isma'il ibn Bashrus informed me, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "They remained [in the cave], meaning the youths of the Companions of the Cave, after the door of the cave had been walled up over them, for a long period of time, after a long period of time. Then a shepherd, caught by rain near the cave, said, 'If I were to open this cave and bring my sheep in out of the rain!' He kept working at it until he opened what he had shut in. God returned their souls to their bodies on the following morning, when they woke. They sent one of them with silver to buy food. When he came to the gate of their city, he saw something he found strange, until he entered upon a man and said, 'Sell me food for these dirhams.' The man said, 'From where do you have these dirhams?' He said, 'I and my companions went out yesterday, and the night overtook us, and then we awoke, and they sent me.' The man said, 'These dirhams were in the time of the kingship of so-and-so, so how do you have them?' They brought him up before the king, who was a righteous king, and the king said, 'From where do you have this silver?' He said, 'I and my companions went out yesterday, until the night overtook us in such-and-such a cave, and then they commanded me to buy food for them.' He said, 'And where are your companions?' He said, 'In the cave.' He said, 'So they set out with him until they came to the door of the cave. He said, "Let me enter to my companions before you." When they saw him, and he drew near to them, his ear and their ears were struck [by sleep], and whenever a man entered they were stricken with terror, so they were unable to reach them. Then they built a church near them, which they took as a place of prayer.'"

◆ Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, on the authority of Qatada, on the authority of Ikrima, who said: "The Companions of the Cave were sons of the kings of Rome, whom God granted Islam. They sought refuge in their religion and withdrew from their people until they reached the cave. God then struck their hearing, and they remained a long age until their nation had perished, and a Muslim nation came, and their king was a Muslim. They differed concerning the spirit and the body. One speaker said, 'The spirit and the body will both be raised together.' Another speaker said, 'Only the spirit will be raised; as for the body, the earth will consume it, and it will become nothing.' This disagreement weighed heavily on their king, so he went and put on coarse garments, sat upon ashes, and then called upon God, exalted is He, saying, 'O Lord, You see the disagreement of these people, so raise up for them a sign that will make it clear to them.' God then raised the Companions of the Cave, and they sent one of them to buy food for them. He entered the marketplace and began to take note of the faces, recognizing the roads, and seeing faith openly displayed in the city. He went on, concealing himself, until he came to a man from whom he wished to buy food. When the man looked at the silver, he disapproved of it. He said, 'I think he said: it is like the soles of young camels, meaning small camels.' The youth said to him, 'Is your king not so-and-so?' He said, 'No, our king is so-and-so.' This continued between them until he was brought up before the king, and the king questioned him. The youth informed him of the story of his companions. The king sent to the people and gathered them, and said, 'You have differed concerning the spirit and the body, and God has sent you a sign. This man is from the people of so-and-so,' meaning their former king. The youth said, 'Take me to my companions.' So the king mounted, and the people mounted with him, until they reached the cave. The youth said, 'Let me enter to my companions.' When he saw them, his ear and their ears were struck [by sleep]. When they were slow in returning, the king entered, and the people entered with him, and they found bodies of which they could find nothing strange, except that there were no spirits in them. The king said, 'This is a sign which God has sent to you.'"

Qatada said: And from Ibn Abbas: he had campaigned with Habib ibn Maslama, and they passed by the cave, and there were bones in it. A man said, "These are the bones of the Companions of the Cave." Ibn Abbas said, "Their bones have decayed for more than three hundred years."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, regarding what was mentioned of the narrative of the People of the Cave. He said: Then the people of those lands were ruled by a righteous man called Tidhusis. When he became king, his reign lasted sixty-eight years. The people split into factions during his rule, and they became parties. Some of them believed in God and knew that the Hour is true, while others denied it. This weighed heavily on the righteous king Tidhusis. He wept to God and humbled himself before Him, and he grieved intensely when he saw the people of falsehood increasing and prevailing over the people of truth, and saying: "There is no life but this worldly life. Only souls are resurrected, not bodies," and they forgot what was in the Book. So Tidhusis began sending for those he thought well of, and who were considered leaders in the truth. But they went on denying the Hour, until they nearly turned the people away from the truth and from the religion of the Disciples (al-Hawariyyin).

When the righteous king Tidhusis saw this, he entered his chamber and shut himself in. He put on a hair shirt, placed ashes beneath himself, and sat upon them. He continued this by night and by day for a period of time, humbling himself before God and weeping to Him over what he saw among the people. Then the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, who dislikes the destruction of His servants, willed to manifest the young men of the Cave, to make their condition clear to the people, to make them a sign for them and a proof against them, so that they might know that the Hour is coming without doubt. He also willed to answer His righteous servant Tidhusis, to complete His blessing upon him, so that his kingship and the faith He had given him would not be taken away, and that God would be worshipped without associating anything with Him, and that He would gather those believers who had been scattered. So God cast into the heart of a man from the people of that town where the Cave was, (the mountain of Banjalus in which the Cave lay belonged to that man, and that man's name was Awliyas), the notion to demolish the structure that was over the mouth of the Cave, so that he could build with its stones a pen for his sheep. He hired two workers, and they began removing those stones and building that pen with them, until they had removed what was over the mouth of the Cave and opened the entrance of the Cave for them. God had shielded them from the people by means of awe. It is claimed that the bravest person who wished to look at them could only go as far as the entrance of the Cave, and then he would advance until he saw their dog lying before them at the entrance of the Cave, asleep. When they had removed the stones and opened the entrance of the Cave for them, God, the Possessor of power, greatness and dominion, the Giver of life to the dead, permitted the young men to sit among the inside of the Cave. They sat there joyful, their faces radiant and their souls at ease. They greeted one another, as though they had awakened at the very hour they used to wake up when they rose in the morning after spending their night there. Then they stood up to pray and prayed as they used to do. They did not notice, nor was anything visible in their faces, their skin, or their complexions that they would find strange, just as they had been when they lay down the previous evening. They believed that their king Daqyanus the tyrant was seeking them out and searching for them.

When they had finished their prayer as they usually did, they said to Yamlikha, who was their provider, the one who used to buy their food and drink from the city and who had brought them the news that Daqyanus was searching for them and asking about them: "Tell us, brother, what did the people say about our affair the previous evening, in the presence of this tyrant?" They thought that they had slept just as they used to sleep at times, and it seemed to them that they had slept as long as they ever slept on the night they awoke. So they questioned one another, and some of them said to others: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ They said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ Others said: ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained.﴾ All of this, in their own minds, was insignificant.

Yamlikha said to them: "You have been missed, and they have been searching for you in the city. He wants you brought to him today, so that you will be slaughtered for the idols (tawaghit, i.e., tyrants or false deities), or he will kill you, and then whatever God wills." Then Maksalmina said to them: "O brothers, know that you will meet Him. Do not disbelieve after your faith when the enemy of God calls you, and do not deny the life that does not perish, after your belief in God, and the life after death." Then they said to Yamlikha: "Go to the city and listen to what is being said about us there today, and what we are being mentioned for before Daqyanus. Be discreet and do not let anyone notice you. Buy food for us and bring it to us, for the time has come for you. Add to the food you brought us earlier, for it was little, and we have awakened hungry."

Yamlikha did as he used to do. He put on his clothes and took the garments in which he used to disguise himself. He took some silver coins from their provisions, which had been stamped with the seal of King Daqyanus, and he set out. When he passed the entrance of the Cave, he saw that the stones had been removed from the mouth of the Cave. He was amazed by it, but then he passed on and paid it no heed, until he reached the city, concealing himself and keeping away from the road, fearing that someone from its people might see him and recognize him, and then take him to Daqyanus. The righteous servant did not realize that Daqyanus and the people of his era had perished three hundred and nine years earlier, or whatever number God wills, since the time between their falling asleep and their awakening was three hundred and nine years.

When Yamlikha saw the city gate, he raised his eyes and saw above the top of the gate a sign that belongs to the people of faith, when it was visible there. When he saw it he was amazed, and he kept looking at it while concealing himself. He looked right and left and wondered to himself. Then he left that gate and went to another of its gates, and he looked and saw there something like this covering the whole city, and he saw the same on every gate. He began to imagine that the city was not the city he knew. He saw many people who were newly arrived, whom he had never seen before. He walked on, amazed, and he imagined that he was bewildered. Then he returned to the gate by which he had entered, wondering to himself and saying: "Would that I knew! Last evening, the Muslims used to conceal this sign and hide it, and now it is openly displayed. Perhaps I am dreaming," and then he realized that he was not sleeping. He took his cloak and placed it over his head, then entered the city. He walked through the middle of its market, and he heard many people swearing by the name of Jesus, son of Mary. This increased his fear, and he realized that he was bewildered. He stood leaning his back against one of the city walls, saying to himself: "By God, I do not know what this is! Last evening there was not a person on earth who mentioned Jesus, son of Mary, without being killed, and now I hear them, and everyone who mentions the matter of Jesus is not afraid." Then he said to himself: "Perhaps this is not the city I know. I hear the speech of its people and I do not recognize any of them. By God, I do not know of any city near our city." He stood like a bewildered man, not facing any direction. Then he met a young man from the city and said to him: "What is the name of this city, young man?" He replied: "Its name is Afsus." So he said to himself: "Perhaps something has touched me, or something has affected my mind. By God, I have every right to hasten out of it before I am disgraced in it or some harm befalls me and I perish." Yamlikha told his companions this when it became clear to them what was happening to him.

Then he came to his senses and said: "By God, if I had hurried out of the city before anyone noticed me, it would have been wiser for me." He approached those who sold food, took out the silver coins he had with him, and gave them to a man among them, saying: "Sell me food with these coins, servant of God." The man took them and looked at the stamp and engraving on them, and he was amazed by them. Then he threw them to one of his companions, who looked at them. Then they began passing them among themselves from one man to another, marvelling at them. Then they began to consult with one another, and some of them said to others: "This man has found a hidden treasure in the earth from a long time and a long age ago." When he saw them consulting over him, he was overcome with great fear and began to tremble, thinking that they had noticed him and recognized him, and that they only wanted to take him to their king Daqyanus and hand him over to him. Other people kept coming to him and recognizing him. He said to them, while greatly afraid of them: "Leave me alone. You have taken my silver. Keep it, and as for your food, I have no need of it." They said to him: "Who are you, young man, and what is your matter? By God, you have found a treasure from the treasures of the ancients, and you want to conceal it from us. Come with us and show it to us and share it with us, and we will keep quiet about what you have found. For if you do not do this, we will bring you to the authorities, and they will hand you over to him, and he will kill you." When he heard what they said, he was amazed in his soul and said: "I have fallen into everything I was afraid of." Then they said: "Young man, by God, you cannot conceal what you have found, and do not think that your situation will remain hidden." Yamlikha did not know what to say to them or how to answer them. He was so frightened that he could not find an answer for them. When they saw that he was not speaking, they took his cloak and put it around his neck, and then they began leading him through the streets of the city by his collar, until word of him reached everyone in it. It was said: "A man has found a treasure," and the people of the city, young and old, gathered around him. They looked at him and said: "By God, this young man is not from the people of this city. We have never seen him here, and we do not know him." Yamlikha did not know what to say to them, given what he heard from them. When the people of the city gathered around him, he was overcome with fear, so he fell silent and did not speak. Even if he had said that he was from the people of the city, they would not have believed him. He was certain that his father and brothers were in the city, and that his family was among the city's nobles, and that they would come to him when they heard. He was also certain that he had known many of its people the previous evening, but that today he did not know anyone of them.

While he stood there like a bewildered man, waiting for someone of his family, his father or one of his brothers, to come and rescue him from their hands, they seized him and took him to the two leaders and administrators of the city who managed its affairs. They were two righteous men, one named Aryus and the other named Istiyus. When they brought him to them, Yamlikha thought that he was being taken to the tyrant Daqyanus, their king, from whom they had fled. He began looking right and left, and the people mocked him as one mocks a madman or a bewildered man. Yamlikha wept, then raised his head to the heavens and to God and said: "O God, Lord of the heavens and the earth, send into me a spirit from You today, to strengthen me before this tyrant." He kept weeping and saying to himself: "I have been separated from my brothers. Would that they knew what I have suffered and that I am being taken to the tyrant Daqyanus. If only they knew, they would come, and we would all stand together before Daqyanus, for we had pledged to be together, not to disbelieve in God, not to associate anything with Him, and not to worship the tyrants besides God. I have been separated from them, and they will never see me, nor will I ever see them. We had sworn that we would never be parted, in life or in death. Would that I knew what he will do to me! Will he kill me or not?" This is what Yamlikha said to himself, as he later reported to his companions when he returned to them.

When he reached the two righteous men, Aryus and Istiyus, Yamlikha saw that he was not being taken to Daqyanus. He came to his senses and stopped weeping. Aryus and Istiyus took the silver coins, looked at them, and were amazed by them. Then one of them said: "Where is the treasure you found, young man? This silver testifies against you that you have found a treasure." Yamlikha said to them: "I have found no treasure, but these coins are the coins of my fathers, and the engraving and stamp are of this city. But by God, I do not know what has happened to me, nor do I know what to say to you." One of them said to him: "Who are you?" Yamlikha said: "I do not know." He said: "I used to think that I was from the people of this village." They said: "Then who is your father, and who knows you here?" So he named his father, but they found no one who knew him or his father. One of them said to him: "You are a liar and do not tell us the truth." Yamlikha did not know what to tell them, but he lowered his gaze to the ground. Some of those around him said: "This man is mad." Others said: "He is not mad, but he is deliberately feigning madness so that he can slip away from you." One of them looked at him with a stern look and said: "Do you think that by pretending to be mad we will let you go and believe you when you say this is your father's wealth and that these coins, with their engraving and stamp, were minted more than three hundred years ago? You are just a young man who thinks he can deceive us, and we are old men as you see, and around you are the nobles of the city and its rulers. I think I will order that you be tortured severely, and then I will bind you until you confess to this treasure you found." When he said this, Yamlikha said: "Tell me about something I will ask you, and if you do, I will tell you the truth about what I know. Do you know what Daqyanus, the king who was in this city the previous evening, did?" The man said to him: "There is no man on the face of the earth named Daqyanus. There was only a king who perished a long time and a long age ago, and many generations perished after him." Yamlikha said to him: "By God, then I am bewildered, and no one will believe what I say. By God, I know: we fled from the tyrant Daqyanus, and I saw him the previous evening when he entered the city of Afsus. But I do not know whether this city is Afsus or not. Come with me to the Cave in the mountain of Banjalus, and I will show you my companions." When Aryus heard what Yamlikha was saying, he said: "O people, perhaps this is a sign from God, which He has made for you through this young man. Come with us, so that he can show us his companions," as he said. So Aryus and Istiyus set out with him, and the people of the city, young and old, went along with them toward the People of the Cave to look at them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 19–20 (part 3 of 3):

When the young men, the Companions of the Cave, saw that Yamlikha had been delayed with their food and drink, beyond the time he usually took, they thought that he had been seized and taken to their king Daqyanus, from whom they had fled. While they were thinking this and fearing it, they heard voices and the clatter of horses coming up toward them. They thought that they were messengers of the tyrant Daqyanus, whom he had sent to bring them. So when they heard that, they stood up for prayer, greeted one another, and counselled one another, saying: "Let us go to our brother Yamlikha, for he is now before the tyrant Daqyanus, waiting for when we will come to him." While they were saying this, sitting in the middle of the cave, they saw nothing but Ariyus and his companions standing at the mouth of the cave. Yamlikha had gone ahead of them, entered upon them weeping. When they saw him weeping, they wept with him. Then they asked him about his condition, and he informed them of his news and related to them the whole account. At that, they knew that they had been asleep by God's command all that time, and that they had only been woken so that they would be a sign for the people and a confirmation of the Resurrection, and so that they would know that the Hour is coming, with no doubt about it.

Then Ariyus entered after Yamlikha and saw a coffin of copper, sealed with a seal of silver. He stood at the door of the cave, then summoned men from the notables of the city, and the coffin was opened in their presence. They found in it two tablets of lead, on which a writing was inscribed. He read them and found in them [[There is much disagreement among its transmitters concerning the number of these names, and their vocalisation. In manuscript no. 100 (Tafsir), they are undotted.]] that Maksalmina, Mahsalmina, Yamlikha, Marutunus, Kasatunus, Yabur, Yakrunus, Yatbiyunus and Qalush were young men who had fled from their king Daqyanus, the tyrant, for fear that he would tempt them away from their religion. They entered this cave, and when their whereabouts were reported, he ordered that the cave be sealed up against them with stones. We have written down their situation and the account of their news, so that whoever comes after them may know of it, should they be discovered.

When they had read it, they were astonished and praised God, who had shown them a sign of the Resurrection among them. Then they raised their voices in praise and glorification of God. Then they entered upon the young men in the cave and found them sitting in its midst, their faces radiant, their clothes not worn out. Ariyus and his companions fell prostrate and praised God, who had shown them one of His signs. Then they spoke to one another, and the young men informed them about what they had suffered from their king Daqyanus, that tyrant from whom they had fled.

Then Ariyus and his companions sent a messenger to their righteous king Tidhusiyus, saying: "Hasten, perhaps you will look upon one of the signs of God, which God has placed in your kingdom and made a sign for the worlds, to be a light and a radiance for them, and a confirmation of the Resurrection. So come quickly to young men whom God has raised up, though He had caused them to die more than three hundred years ago." When the news reached King Tidhusiyus, he rose from the seat on which he had been sitting, his mind and reason returned to him, his anxiety left him, and he turned back to God, the Mighty and Majestic, and said: "O God, I praise You, Lord of the heavens and the earth. I worship You, I praise You, and I glorify You. You have been gracious to me and shown me mercy by Your mercy, and You have not extinguished the light which You placed for my forefathers and for the righteous servant, King Qastantinus." When the people of the city were informed, they rode out to him and went with him until they came to the city of Afsus. The people of the city met them, and they went with him until they climbed toward the cave and came to it. When the young men saw Tidhusiyus, they rejoiced at him and fell prostrate on their faces. Tidhusiyus stood before them, then embraced them and wept, while they sat before him on the ground, glorifying God and praising Him. And he said: "By God, I can liken you to nothing but the disciples when they saw the Messiah." And he said: "May God relieve you, as if you were those who are called and then gathered from the graves." Then the young men said to Tidhusiyus: "We bid you farewell. Peace be upon you and the mercy of God. May God protect you and protect your kingdom in peace. We seek refuge for you in God from the evil of the jinn and of men."

[[The passage from his saying "Then he ordered a food of khalar and nashil..." up to here is omitted from this report in ʿAra'is al-Majalis of the exegete al-Tha'labi, p. 427: "Al-khalar: a grain eaten as food, said to be the chickpea. Al-nashil: milk in the hour it is milked." The passage appears, from what is evident, to be part of the speech of the Companions of the Cave.]] "Then he ordered a food of khalar and nashil, for the worst thing that enters a person's belly is that he should know nothing, except a dignity if he is honoured by it, or a humiliation if he is humiliated by it."

While the king was standing, they returned to their resting places, lay down, and God took their souls by His command. The king approached them, placed his garments over them, and ordered that a coffin of gold be made for each man among them. When evening came and he slept, they came to him in a dream and said: "We were not created from gold or silver, but we were created from dust, and to dust we shall return. So leave us as we were in the cave, on the dust, until God raises us from it." Then the king ordered a coffin of teak, and they were placed in it. God veiled them with awe when they left from among them, so no one could approach them. The king ordered that their cave be made a mosque in which to pray, and he made for them a great festival, and ordered that people come to it every year. This is the account of the Companions of the Cave.

◆ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad, from Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, who said: God raised them up — meaning the young men, the Companions of the Cave — when a Muslim king had come to rule over them, meaning over the people of their city. God had caused hunger to afflict the young men. Then one of them said: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ They said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ He said: They referred the knowledge of that to God. ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾, and they had with them silver coins struck in the reign of the king of their time, ﴿and let him bring you a provision from it﴾, meaning food, ﴿and let him not alert anyone to you.﴾ So one of them went out and saw the landmarks had changed until he reached the city. People greeted him, and he did not recognise any of them, so he went out while they did not recognise him, until he came to the food seller and bought food from him. The food seller said: "Give me your silver." So he brought out the silver to him. He said: "From where do you have this silver?" He said: "This is our silver and the silver of the people of our land." He said: "Impossible! This silver was struck by so-and-so, son of so-and-so, three hundred and nine years ago. You have found a treasure, and I shall not leave you until I bring you before the king." So he brought him before the king, and the king was a Muslim, and his companions were Muslims. He rejoiced and was delighted, revealed his affair to them, and informed them of the news of his companions. Then they sent for the tablet in the treasury, brought it, and it agreed with what had been described of their affair. The polytheists said: "We have a better claim to them, these are the sons of our fathers." The Muslims said: "We have a better claim to them; they are Muslims from among us." So they went with him to the cave. When they reached the mouth of the cave he said: "Let me enter upon my companions first, so that I may bring them good news, for if they see you with me they will terrify them." He entered and gave them good news, and God took their souls. He said: God blinded them to their place, so they could not find it. The polytheists said: "We shall build a structure over them, for they are the sons of our fathers, and we shall worship God in it." The Muslims said: "We have a better claim to them; they are of us. We shall build a mosque over them in which to pray and worship God."

The most correct opinion, in my view, concerning this is the statement of the one who said: God, exalted is He, raised them from their sleep so that they might question one another among themselves, as we have explained before, because God, mighty is His remembrance, informed His servants of this in His Book. God caused the people whom He caused to find them to find them, so that it would be confirmed to them, by God's raising these young men from their sleep after its long duration, in the same form they had been on the day they slept, their hair not whitened over the passing of days and nights, nor did they grow old over the course of ages and times, that God has power to raise whom He caused to die in this world from his grave to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection. For God, mighty is His remembrance, has informed us of this, saying: ﴿And thus We caused them to be found, so that they would know that the promise of God is true and that the Hour is not in doubt.﴾

The reciters differed concerning the recitation of His words: ﴿so send one of you with this silver of yours﴾. The majority of the reciters of Medina, and some of the Iraqis, recited ﴿بِوَرِقِكُمْ﴾ (biwariqikum) with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ra and the qaf. The majority of the reciters of Kufa and Basra recited ﴿بَورْقِكُمْ﴾ (bawriqikum) with a sukun on the ra and a kasra on the qaf. Some of the Meccans recited it with a kasra on the ra and the qaf assimilated into the kaf. All these readings have the same meaning, though their wording differs, and they are well-known dialects of the speech of the Arabs. However, the original form is with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the ra and the qaf, because it is al-warq (the silver), and whatever else differs from it has entered upon it the desire for lightening. There is also another dialect, al-warq (وَرْق), just as they say kabid (كَبِد) for kabd (كَبْد) for the liver. When this is the original, recitation with it is more pleasing to me, without the other two being rejected as to their soundness. We have mentioned the report that the one who was sent with the silver to the city was named Yamlikha.

Ubayd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri related to me, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Muqatil: ﴿so send one of you with this silver of yours﴾: his name was Yamlikh.

As for His words: ﴿let him see which of them has the best food﴾, the people of ta'wil (exegesis, the interpretation of meaning) differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: its meaning is, let him see which of the people of the city has more food.

Mention of those who said this:
◆ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Husayn, from Ikrima, concerning ﴿which of them is purer in food﴾: more.
◆ And al-Hasan related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Abu Husayn, from Ikrima, the like of it, except that he said: ﴿أيُّهُ أكْثَرُ﴾ (ayyuhu aktharu).

Others said: rather, its meaning is: which of them is more lawful as food.

Mention of those who said this:
◆ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿which of them is purer in food﴾: more lawful.
◆ al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the like of it.

Others said: rather, its meaning is: which of them is better as food.

Mention of those who said this:
◆ al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Mu'ammar informed us, from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿purer in food﴾: better in food.

The most correct opinion in my view, concerning this, is the statement of the one who said: the meaning of that is: more lawful and purer. This is because there is no sense in choosing the one with more food to buy from, unless it means that when he has more food, the better of it is more likely to be found with him. And if the one sent is required to buy from the seller of the better food, then he has been commanded to buy what is good, whether what the buyer has of that is little or much. Those who understood the interpretation of "purer" as "more" did so because they found the Arabs say: the wealth of so-and-so has zaka (زكا), meaning it has increased, and as the poet said:

"Our tribes are seven, and you are three,
and the seven are purer (azka) and better than three."

[[The verse is by al-Qital al-Kilabi. Sibawayh cited it in (al-Kitab 2: 181), and it is among the witnesses of Abu Ubayda in (Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 237, 397). In the second place he said: "ayyuha azka ta'aman" means "more." He said: "Our tribes are seven..." (the verse). In the first place he said: he mentioned "thalatha" (three) by taking it to mean "a clan," then made it feminine, because he took it to mean a tribe. I say: The grammarians permit both masculine and feminine for numerals when the counted noun is not mentioned, and this is evidence for that. In (Lisan al-Arab: zaka), al-zaka' (with mad) means growth and increase; zaka yazku zaka'an and zakwan.]]

in the sense of "more." Even so, lawful good food, however little, is more than unlawful wicked food, however much. It has been said that His words: ﴿let him see which of them﴾ are linked to the pronoun of the city, and what is meant is its people, for the sense of the speech is: let him see which of its people has purer food, since the hearer knows what is intended by the speech. It may also be that by His words ﴿which of them is purer in food﴾ they meant: which of them is more lawful, because they had left their people, who were idol worshippers, and so they did not consider it permissible to eat their slaughter.

* *

As for His words: ﴿let him bring you a provision from it﴾:
He says: let him bring you food from it, a sustenance on which you may live and which you may eat.
As:
◆ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad, from Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr: ﴿let him bring you a provision from it﴾: food.

* *

As for His words: ﴿and let him be discreet﴾:
He says: let him be gentle in what he buys, in his route, and in his entering the city. ﴿and let him not alert anyone to you﴾: He says: let him not let anyone among the people know of you.

As for His words: ﴿for if they discover you, they will stone you﴾: by this they mean Daqyanus and his companions. They said: if Daqyanus and his companions discover you, and learn your whereabouts, they will stone you, meaning, they will abuse you with words.
As:
◆ al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His words: ﴿for if they discover you, they will stone you﴾: he said: they will revile you with words, and harm you.

* *

As for His words: ﴿or return you to their religion﴾:
He says: or they will send you back to their religion, so that you become unbelievers by worshipping idols.
﴿and then you will never succeed⁠—ever﴾: He says: you will never attain success, which is lasting survival and eternity in the Gardens. Then: that is, if you return to their religion forever, for the days of your lives.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 18, Verses 19–20 (Part 1 of 3)**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We raised them up, that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?" They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day." They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained. So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city, and let him see which of them has the purest food, and bring you provision from it, and let him be discreet, and let him not make anyone aware of you (19). For if they gain control over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion, and then you will never succeed (20)."﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Just as We put these youths to sleep in the cave, guarding them from anyone reaching them and from any watcher's eye looking at them, and by Our power preserving their bodies from decay over the length of time and their garments from mildew over the passing of days, so likewise We raised them from their sleep and woke them from their slumber. We did this so that We might make them know the greatness of Our dominion and the wondrous nature of Our action in Our creation, and that they might increase in insight regarding their affair, in which they stood, namely their disavowal of the worship of idols and their sincere devotion to the worship of God alone, without partner, when they perceived how long the time had been upon them while they remained in the same state in which they had fallen asleep.

As for His words, ﴿that they might question one another﴾, it means: that some of them might ask others. ﴿A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?"﴾: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: So they questioned one another, and one speaker among them said to his companions, ﴿"How long have you remained?"﴾ This was because they were astonished at their own long sleep. ﴿They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ He says: The others answered him, saying, "We have remained a day or part of a day," supposing that this was indeed the case. Then the others said, ﴿"Your Lord knows best how long you have remained,"﴾ thereby entrusting knowledge to God.

* *

As for His words, ﴿"So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city"﴾: it means their city from which they had fled, which is called Afsus. ﴿"And let him see which of them has the purest food, and bring you provision from it"﴾: it is mentioned that they had awoken from their sleep hungry, and therefore they sought food.

Mention of those who said this, and mention of the reason for which it is reported that they were raised from their sleep when they were raised:

◆ Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: Isma'il ibn Bashrus informed me, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "They remained [in the cave], meaning the youths of the Companions of the Cave, after the door of the cave had been walled up over them, for a long period of time, after a long period of time. Then a shepherd, caught by rain near the cave, said, 'If I were to open this cave and bring my sheep in out of the rain!' He kept working at it until he opened what he had shut in. God returned their souls to their bodies on the following morning, when they woke. They sent one of them with silver to buy food. When he came to the gate of their city, he saw something he found strange, until he entered upon a man and said, 'Sell me food for these dirhams.' The man said, 'From where do you have these dirhams?' He said, 'I and my companions went out yesterday, and the night overtook us, and then we awoke, and they sent me.' The man said, 'These dirhams were in the time of the kingship of so-and-so, so how do you have them?' They brought him up before the king, who was a righteous king, and the king said, 'From where do you have this silver?' He said, 'I and my companions went out yesterday, until the night overtook us in such-and-such a cave, and then they commanded me to buy food for them.' He said, 'And where are your companions?' He said, 'In the cave.' He said, 'So they set out with him until they came to the door of the cave. He said, "Let me enter to my companions before you." When they saw him, and he drew near to them, his ear and their ears were struck [by sleep], and whenever a man entered they were stricken with terror, so they were unable to reach them. Then they built a church near them, which they took as a place of prayer.'"

◆ Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, on the authority of Qatada, on the authority of Ikrima, who said: "The Companions of the Cave were sons of the kings of Rome, whom God granted Islam. They sought refuge in their religion and withdrew from their people until they reached the cave. God then struck their hearing, and they remained a long age until their nation had perished, and a Muslim nation came, and their king was a Muslim. They differed concerning the spirit and the body. One speaker said, 'The spirit and the body will both be raised together.' Another speaker said, 'Only the spirit will be raised; as for the body, the earth will consume it, and it will become nothing.' This disagreement weighed heavily on their king, so he went and put on coarse garments, sat upon ashes, and then called upon God, exalted is He, saying, 'O Lord, You see the disagreement of these people, so raise up for them a sign that will make it clear to them.' God then raised the Companions of the Cave, and they sent one of them to buy food for them. He entered the marketplace and began to take note of the faces, recognizing the roads, and seeing faith openly displayed in the city. He went on, concealing himself, until he came to a man from whom he wished to buy food. When the man looked at the silver, he disapproved of it. He said, 'I think he said: it is like the soles of young camels, meaning small camels.' The youth said to him, 'Is your king not so-and-so?' He said, 'No, our king is so-and-so.' This continued between them until he was brought up before the king, and the king questioned him. The youth informed him of the story of his companions. The king sent to the people and gathered them, and said, 'You have differed concerning the spirit and the body, and God has sent you a sign. This man is from the people of so-and-so,' meaning their former king. The youth said, 'Take me to my companions.' So the king mounted, and the people mounted with him, until they reached the cave. The youth said, 'Let me enter to my companions.' When he saw them, his ear and their ears were struck [by sleep]. When they were slow in returning, the king entered, and the people entered with him, and they found bodies of which they could find nothing strange, except that there were no spirits in them. The king said, 'This is a sign which God has sent to you.'"

Qatada said: And from Ibn Abbas: he had campaigned with Habib ibn Maslama, and they passed by the cave, and there were bones in it. A man said, "These are the bones of the Companions of the Cave." Ibn Abbas said, "Their bones have decayed for more than three hundred years."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, regarding what was mentioned of the narrative of the People of the Cave. He said: Then the people of those lands were ruled by a righteous man called Tidhusis. When he became king, his reign lasted sixty-eight years. The people split into factions during his rule, and they became parties. Some of them believed in God and knew that the Hour is true, while others denied it. This weighed heavily on the righteous king Tidhusis. He wept to God and humbled himself before Him, and he grieved intensely when he saw the people of falsehood increasing and prevailing over the people of truth, and saying: "There is no life but this worldly life. Only souls are resurrected, not bodies," and they forgot what was in the Book. So Tidhusis began sending for those he thought well of, and who were considered leaders in the truth. But they went on denying the Hour, until they nearly turned the people away from the truth and from the religion of the Disciples (al-Hawariyyin).

When the righteous king Tidhusis saw this, he entered his chamber and shut himself in. He put on a hair shirt, placed ashes beneath himself, and sat upon them. He continued this by night and by day for a period of time, humbling himself before God and weeping to Him over what he saw among the people. Then the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, who dislikes the destruction of His servants, willed to manifest the young men of the Cave, to make their condition clear to the people, to make them a sign for them and a proof against them, so that they might know that the Hour is coming without doubt. He also willed to answer His righteous servant Tidhusis, to complete His blessing upon him, so that his kingship and the faith He had given him would not be taken away, and that God would be worshipped without associating anything with Him, and that He would gather those believers who had been scattered. So God cast into the heart of a man from the people of that town where the Cave was, (the mountain of Banjalus in which the Cave lay belonged to that man, and that man's name was Awliyas), the notion to demolish the structure that was over the mouth of the Cave, so that he could build with its stones a pen for his sheep. He hired two workers, and they began removing those stones and building that pen with them, until they had removed what was over the mouth of the Cave and opened the entrance of the Cave for them. God had shielded them from the people by means of awe. It is claimed that the bravest person who wished to look at them could only go as far as the entrance of the Cave, and then he would advance until he saw their dog lying before them at the entrance of the Cave, asleep. When they had removed the stones and opened the entrance of the Cave for them, God, the Possessor of power, greatness and dominion, the Giver of life to the dead, permitted the young men to sit among the inside of the Cave. They sat there joyful, their faces radiant and their souls at ease. They greeted one another, as though they had awakened at the very hour they used to wake up when they rose in the morning after spending their night there. Then they stood up to pray and prayed as they used to do. They did not notice, nor was anything visible in their faces, their skin, or their complexions that they would find strange, just as they had been when they lay down the previous evening. They believed that their king Daqyanus the tyrant was seeking them out and searching for them.

When they had finished their prayer as they usually did, they said to Yamlikha, who was their provider, the one who used to buy their food and drink from the city and who had brought them the news that Daqyanus was searching for them and asking about them: "Tell us, brother, what did the people say about our affair the previous evening, in the presence of this tyrant?" They thought that they had slept just as they used to sleep at times, and it seemed to them that they had slept as long as they ever slept on the night they awoke. So they questioned one another, and some of them said to others: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ They said: ﴿We have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ Others said: ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained.﴾ All of this, in their own minds, was insignificant.

Yamlikha said to them: "You have been missed, and they have been searching for you in the city. He wants you brought to him today, so that you will be slaughtered for the idols (tawaghit, i.e., tyrants or false deities), or he will kill you, and then whatever God wills." Then Maksalmina said to them: "O brothers, know that you will meet Him. Do not disbelieve after your faith when the enemy of God calls you, and do not deny the life that does not perish, after your belief in God, and the life after death." Then they said to Yamlikha: "Go to the city and listen to what is being said about us there today, and what we are being mentioned for before Daqyanus. Be discreet and do not let anyone notice you. Buy food for us and bring it to us, for the time has come for you. Add to the food you brought us earlier, for it was little, and we have awakened hungry."

Yamlikha did as he used to do. He put on his clothes and took the garments in which he used to disguise himself. He took some silver coins from their provisions, which had been stamped with the seal of King Daqyanus, and he set out. When he passed the entrance of the Cave, he saw that the stones had been removed from the mouth of the Cave. He was amazed by it, but then he passed on and paid it no heed, until he reached the city, concealing himself and keeping away from the road, fearing that someone from its people might see him and recognize him, and then take him to Daqyanus. The righteous servant did not realize that Daqyanus and the people of his era had perished three hundred and nine years earlier, or whatever number God wills, since the time between their falling asleep and their awakening was three hundred and nine years.

When Yamlikha saw the city gate, he raised his eyes and saw above the top of the gate a sign that belongs to the people of faith, when it was visible there. When he saw it he was amazed, and he kept looking at it while concealing himself. He looked right and left and wondered to himself. Then he left that gate and went to another of its gates, and he looked and saw there something like this covering the whole city, and he saw the same on every gate. He began to imagine that the city was not the city he knew. He saw many people who were newly arrived, whom he had never seen before. He walked on, amazed, and he imagined that he was bewildered. Then he returned to the gate by which he had entered, wondering to himself and saying: "Would that I knew! Last evening, the Muslims used to conceal this sign and hide it, and now it is openly displayed. Perhaps I am dreaming," and then he realized that he was not sleeping. He took his cloak and placed it over his head, then entered the city. He walked through the middle of its market, and he heard many people swearing by the name of Jesus, son of Mary. This increased his fear, and he realized that he was bewildered. He stood leaning his back against one of the city walls, saying to himself: "By God, I do not know what this is! Last evening there was not a person on earth who mentioned Jesus, son of Mary, without being killed, and now I hear them, and everyone who mentions the matter of Jesus is not afraid." Then he said to himself: "Perhaps this is not the city I know. I hear the speech of its people and I do not recognize any of them. By God, I do not know of any city near our city." He stood like a bewildered man, not facing any direction. Then he met a young man from the city and said to him: "What is the name of this city, young man?" He replied: "Its name is Afsus." So he said to himself: "Perhaps something has touched me, or something has affected my mind. By God, I have every right to hasten out of it before I am disgraced in it or some harm befalls me and I perish." Yamlikha told his companions this when it became clear to them what was happening to him.

Then he came to his senses and said: "By God, if I had hurried out of the city before anyone noticed me, it would have been wiser for me." He approached those who sold food, took out the silver coins he had with him, and gave them to a man among them, saying: "Sell me food with these coins, servant of God." The man took them and looked at the stamp and engraving on them, and he was amazed by them. Then he threw them to one of his companions, who looked at them. Then they began passing them among themselves from one man to another, marvelling at them. Then they began to consult with one another, and some of them said to others: "This man has found a hidden treasure in the earth from a long time and a long age ago." When he saw them consulting over him, he was overcome with great fear and began to tremble, thinking that they had noticed him and recognized him, and that they only wanted to take him to their king Daqyanus and hand him over to him. Other people kept coming to him and recognizing him. He said to them, while greatly afraid of them: "Leave me alone. You have taken my silver. Keep it, and as for your food, I have no need of it." They said to him: "Who are you, young man, and what is your matter? By God, you have found a treasure from the treasures of the ancients, and you want to conceal it from us. Come with us and show it to us and share it with us, and we will keep quiet about what you have found. For if you do not do this, we will bring you to the authorities, and they will hand you over to him, and he will kill you." When he heard what they said, he was amazed in his soul and said: "I have fallen into everything I was afraid of." Then they said: "Young man, by God, you cannot conceal what you have found, and do not think that your situation will remain hidden." Yamlikha did not know what to say to them or how to answer them. He was so frightened that he could not find an answer for them. When they saw that he was not speaking, they took his cloak and put it around his neck, and then they began leading him through the streets of the city by his collar, until word of him reached everyone in it. It was said: "A man has found a treasure," and the people of the city, young and old, gathered around him. They looked at him and said: "By God, this young man is not from the people of this city. We have never seen him here, and we do not know him." Yamlikha did not know what to say to them, given what he heard from them. When the people of the city gathered around him, he was overcome with fear, so he fell silent and did not speak. Even if he had said that he was from the people of the city, they would not have believed him. He was certain that his father and brothers were in the city, and that his family was among the city's nobles, and that they would come to him when they heard. He was also certain that he had known many of its people the previous evening, but that today he did not know anyone of them.

While he stood there like a bewildered man, waiting for someone of his family, his father or one of his brothers, to come and rescue him from their hands, they seized him and took him to the two leaders and administrators of the city who managed its affairs. They were two righteous men, one named Aryus and the other named Istiyus. When they brought him to them, Yamlikha thought that he was being taken to the tyrant Daqyanus, their king, from whom they had fled. He began looking right and left, and the people mocked him as one mocks a madman or a bewildered man. Yamlikha wept, then raised his head to the heavens and to God and said: "O God, Lord of the heavens and the earth, send into me a spirit from You today, to strengthen me before this tyrant." He kept weeping and saying to himself: "I have been separated from my brothers. Would that they knew what I have suffered and that I am being taken to the tyrant Daqyanus. If only they knew, they would come, and we would all stand together before Daqyanus, for we had pledged to be together, not to disbelieve in God, not to associate anything with Him, and not to worship the tyrants besides God. I have been separated from them, and they will never see me, nor will I ever see them. We had sworn that we would never be parted, in life or in death. Would that I knew what he will do to me! Will he kill me or not?" This is what Yamlikha said to himself, as he later reported to his companions when he returned to them.

When he reached the two righteous men, Aryus and Istiyus, Yamlikha saw that he was not being taken to Daqyanus. He came to his senses and stopped weeping. Aryus and Istiyus took the silver coins, looked at them, and were amazed by them. Then one of them said: "Where is the treasure you found, young man? This silver testifies against you that you have found a treasure." Yamlikha said to them: "I have found no treasure, but these coins are the coins of my fathers, and the engraving and stamp are of this city. But by God, I do not know what has happened to me, nor do I know what to say to you." One of them said to him: "Who are you?" Yamlikha said: "I do not know." He said: "I used to think that I was from the people of this village." They said: "Then who is your father, and who knows you here?" So he named his father, but they found no one who knew him or his father. One of them said to him: "You are a liar and do not tell us the truth." Yamlikha did not know what to tell them, but he lowered his gaze to the ground. Some of those around him said: "This man is mad." Others said: "He is not mad, but he is deliberately feigning madness so that he can slip away from you." One of them looked at him with a stern look and said: "Do you think that by pretending to be mad we will let you go and believe you when you say this is your father's wealth and that these coins, with their engraving and stamp, were minted more than three hundred years ago? You are just a young man who thinks he can deceive us, and we are old men as you see, and around you are the nobles of the city and its rulers. I think I will order that you be tortured severely, and then I will bind you until you confess to this treasure you found." When he said this, Yamlikha said: "Tell me about something I will ask you, and if you do, I will tell you the truth about what I know. Do you know what Daqyanus, the king who was in this city the previous evening, did?" The man said to him: "There is no man on the face of the earth named Daqyanus. There was only a king who perished a long time and a long age ago, and many generations perished after him." Yamlikha said to him: "By God, then I am bewildered, and no one will believe what I say. By God, I know: we fled from the tyrant Daqyanus, and I saw him the previous evening when he entered the city of Afsus. But I do not know whether this city is Afsus or not. Come with me to the Cave in the mountain of Banjalus, and I will show you my companions." When Aryus heard what Yamlikha was saying, he said: "O people, perhaps this is a sign from God, which He has made for you through this young man. Come with us, so that he can show us his companions," as he said. So Aryus and Istiyus set out with him, and the people of the city, young and old, went along with them toward the People of the Cave to look at them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 19–20 (part 3 of 3):

When the young men, the Companions of the Cave, saw that Yamlikha had been delayed with their food and drink, beyond the time he usually took, they thought that he had been seized and taken to their king Daqyanus, from whom they had fled. While they were thinking this and fearing it, they heard voices and the clatter of horses coming up toward them. They thought that they were messengers of the tyrant Daqyanus, whom he had sent to bring them. So when they heard that, they stood up for prayer, greeted one another, and counselled one another, saying: "Let us go to our brother Yamlikha, for he is now before the tyrant Daqyanus, waiting for when we will come to him." While they were saying this, sitting in the middle of the cave, they saw nothing but Ariyus and his companions standing at the mouth of the cave. Yamlikha had gone ahead of them, entered upon them weeping. When they saw him weeping, they wept with him. Then they asked him about his condition, and he informed them of his news and related to them the whole account. At that, they knew that they had been asleep by God's command all that time, and that they had only been woken so that they would be a sign for the people and a confirmation of the Resurrection, and so that they would know that the Hour is coming, with no doubt about it.

Then Ariyus entered after Yamlikha and saw a coffin of copper, sealed with a seal of silver. He stood at the door of the cave, then summoned men from the notables of the city, and the coffin was opened in their presence. They found in it two tablets of lead, on which a writing was inscribed. He read them and found in them [[There is much disagreement among its transmitters concerning the number of these names, and their vocalisation.
