He guides whoever He wills among you to right guidance, so he believes, and He leaves astray whoever He wills from guidance, so he disbelieves. None of that is up to me, and I will not drive away your desires those who follow the truth and who believe in God and in what has been revealed to me. So if you wish, believe, and if you wish, disbelieve. Indeed, if you disbelieve, your Lord has prepared for you, for your disbelief in Him, a Fire whose enclosure surrounds you. But if you believe in Him and act in obedience to Him, then for you is what God has described for the people of His obedience.

It has been related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this:

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. He said: whoever God wills for him to have faith, believes; and whoever God wills for him to disbelieve, disbelieves. This is His saying: ﴿And you will not will except that God wills, Lord of the worlds﴾. This is not a granting by God of disbelief to whoever wishes, and faith to whoever desires; it is only a threat and a warning.

That this is so is shown by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾ and the verses after it.

Likewise:

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Umar ibn Habib, from Dawud, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. He said: It is a warning from God, so [the disbeliever] cannot escape.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ and His saying ﴿Do what you will﴾: All of this is a warning, not a concession, nor a flattery, nor a delegation of authority.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾

Almighty God says: Indeed We have prepared, and it comes from "al-'udda" (preparation). For the wrongdoers: those who disbelieved in their Lord.

Likewise:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure will surround them﴾: He said: for the disbelievers. And His saying: ﴿whose enclosure will surround them﴾ means: the enclosure of the Fire which God has prepared for those who disbelieve in their Lord has surrounded them. It is said that it is a wall of fire encircling them like the sarادiq (enclosure) of a tent, which is the curtain that surrounds the tent, as Ru'ba said:

O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud,
the enclosure of grace is extended over you.

[These two verses are from a short rajaz poem of seven verses by Ru'ba, in his Diwan (Leipzig edition, 1903, among the appendices attached to the Diwan; the first and fifth verses, p. 172). The two verses are among the evidences cited by Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:399), though in his narration the second verse reads: "You are the generous son of the generous, the praised." And after it comes the second verse. He said: "Its enclosure has surrounded them": like the sarادiq of a tent, which is the curtain surrounding the tent. Ru'ba said: "O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud..."

In Lisan al-Arab (root s-r-d-q): al-sarادiq is what surrounds a building, its plural being sarادiqat. Sibawayh said: they made its plural with the feminine ending even though it is masculine, since it was not broken. In the revealed text: "Its enclosure has surrounded them", in describing the Fire, may God protect us from it. Al-Zajjaj said: a sarادiq of punishment has come to be upon them. The sarادiq is what surrounds a thing, such as the cloth at the entrance of the tent (the pavilion), or a wall enclosing a thing.]

And as Salama ibn Jandal said:

He is the one who brings Nu'man into a house whose roof
is the chests of elephants, after a fortified house.

[The verse is in the Diwan of Salama ibn Jandal al-Sa'di al-Tamimi (Beirut edition, 1910, p. 19), from a qasida of thirty verses. Abu 'Amr said: Kisra had imprisoned Nu'man in a house in which there were three elephants. The word "musardaq" means one who has a sarادiq, or one upon whom a sarادiq is placed. Abu 'Ubayda, in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:399), after citing the verse, said: that is, a house having a sarادiq. End. In Lisan al-Arab (s-r-d-q): "He sardaqa the house." Salama ibn Jandal said: [and he cited the verse]. Then al-Jawhari said: the sarادiq is singular for the sarادiqat stretched above the courtyard of a house. Every house of cotton (kirsaf) is a sarادiq. Ru'ba said: O Hakam ibn al-Mundhir ibn al-Jarud... You are the generous son of the generous, the praised. The enclosure of glory is extended over you. He said: It is also said that the rajaz is by al-Kadhdhab al-Harmazi. Al-Jawhari attributed the verse of Salama ibn Jandal to al-A'sha, and said of its occasion: he mentions Ibn Wabr and his killing of Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir. From Lisan al-Arab (s-r-d-q).]

That is: a house having a sarادiq.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure will surround them﴾: It is a wall of fire.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from one who informed him, who said: ﴿whose enclosure will surround them﴾: It is smoke that surrounds the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, and it is the one of which God said: ﴿a shadow of three branches﴾.

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) a report indicating that the meaning of His saying ﴿whose enclosure will surround them﴾ is that it surrounded them in this world, and that this enclosure is the sea.

Mention of those who said this: al-Abbas ibn Muhammad and al-Husayn ibn Nasr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Umayya, who said: Muhammad ibn Hayy ibn Ya'la narrated to me, from Safwan ibn Ya'la, from Ya'la ibn Umayya, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The sea is Jahannam." It was said to him: How is that? So he recited this verse, or read this verse: ﴿a Fire whose enclosure will surround them﴾. Then he said: By God, I will never enter it, or as long as I am alive, and not a drop of it will touch me.

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ya'mar ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, saying: Rushdin ibn Sa'd informed us, saying: Amr ibn al-Harith narrated to me, from Abu al-Samh, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The enclosure of the Fire is four walls, the thickness of each is the distance of forty years' journey."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn al-Harith informed me, from Darraj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the enclosure of the Fire has four walls, the thickness of each is the distance of forty years' journey."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, saying: Amr informed me, from Darraj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) who said: "Water like al-muhl," and he said: "Like the dregs of oil. When he brings it near to himself, the skin of his face falls off into it."

* *

And His saying: ﴿And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾

Almighty God says: And if these wrongdoers seek relief on the Day of Resurrection in the Fire, from the intensity of the thirst they suffer, and ask for water, they will be relieved with water like al-muhl.

The people of ta'wil differed regarding al-muhl. Some of them said: It is everything that has been melted and liquefied.

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us that a vessel of gold and silver was presented to Ibn Mas'ud. He ordered a trench to be dug in the ground, then firewood was thrown into it, then that vessel was thrown into it, until it foamed and liquefied. Then he said to his servant: Call whoever of the people of Kufa is present with us. He called a group, and when they entered upon him, he said: Do you see this? They said: Yes. He said: We have not seen in this world anything resembling al-muhl closer than this gold and silver, when it foamed and liquefied.

Others said: It is pus and black blood.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasa, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim, from Abu Bazza, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾: He said: pus and blood.

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿water like al-muhl﴾: He said: pus and black blood, like the dregs of oil. Al-Harith said in his narration: that is, its sediment.

Ali narrated to me, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿like al-muhl﴾: He said: It is black, in the likeness of oil.

It was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying ﴿water like al-muhl﴾: The water of Jahannam is black, and it is black, and its trees are black, and its people are black.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾: He said: It is thick water like the sediment of oil.

Others said: It is the thing whose heat has reached its extreme.

Mention of those who said this:

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Ja'far and Harun ibn 'Antara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: al-muhl is that which has reached its extreme heat.

These sayings, though their wording differs among those who said them, are close in meaning, because everything that is melted from lead, gold, or silver has reached its extreme heat, and whatever is kindled with fire upon it until it becomes like the sediment of oil has also reached its extreme heat.

It has been related to me from Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, who said: I heard al-Muntaji' ibn Nabhan say: By God, so-and-so is more hateful to me than the al-talya' [[he means by al-talya' the mangy she-camel smeared with tar or the khadkhad]] and the muhl. He said: We said to him: And what are they? He said: The mangy she-camel, and the muhl, which is the mud that runs down the sides of the bread when it is baked in the fire, like red fine sand (sahla) [[al-sahla, with a kasra, is a red sand-like earth that water brings (Lisan)]], finely ground, so it is reddish. So al-muhl is every liquid upon which fire has been kindled until it reaches the limit of its heat, or whatever is not liquid but has melted by the fire and reached the utmost degree of intense heat.

* *

And His saying: ﴿which scalds the faces﴾

Almighty God says: That water with which they are relieved scalds their faces.

Likewise:

Muhammad ibn Khalaf al-'Asqalani narrated to me, saying: Hayawa ibn Shurayh narrated to us, saying: Baqiyya narrated to us, from Safwan ibn Amr, from Abdullah ibn Busr, thus Ibn Khalaf said, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿And he is given to drink of water like pus, which he gulps down﴾: He said: It is brought near to him, and he dislikes it. When it comes near him, it scalds his face, and the skin of his head falls off. When he drinks it, it cuts his intestines. God says: ﴿And if they ask for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass, which scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink﴾.

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Taliqani and Ya'mar ibn Bishr narrated to me, both saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Safwan, from Abdullah ibn Busr, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), like this.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub narrated to us, from Ja'far and Harun ibn 'Antara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Harun said: When the people of the Fire become hungry; and Ja'far said: When the people of the Fire come, they seek relief from the tree of Zaqqum, and eat from it, so the skins of their faces are stripped off. If a passerby were to pass by them, he would recognize them by the skin of their faces in it. Then thirst is poured upon them, and they seek relief, and they are relieved with water like al-muhl, which is that whose heat has reached its extreme. When they bring it near their mouths, the flesh of their faces, from which the skin has fallen, is scalded by its heat.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Wretched is the drink﴾

Almighty God says: Wretched is the drink: this water with which these wrongdoers in Jahannam are relieved, whose description is what has been described in this verse.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and evil is the resting place﴾

Almighty God says: And evil is this Fire which We have prepared for these wrongdoers as a resting place (murtafaq). In the speech of the Arabs, al-murtafaq means the reclining place (al-muttaka'). It is said from it: irtafaqa, when one reclines, as the poet said:

She said to him, reclining: Is there not a youth
who drives the people, the gazelles of the forenoon?

[These are two verses of rajaz (mashtur), cited by Lisan al-Arab in (ghazal). The first of them differs in narration from the author's, which is: "Sulayma called a call: is there a youth" [and in another narration: "And the call of the people: is there not a youth"]. The gazelles of the forenoon: after the sun has spread and risen high. There is no evidence in the first verse for these two narrations.]

He means: she leaned upon her elbow. A man has irtafaqa when he spends the night on his elbow without sleep, and he is murtafiq, as Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

The sleeper slept, and I spent the night reclining,
as if in my eyes is the bitter aloe, slaughtered.

[This verse is in the Diwan of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali (Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyya edition, part one of the Diwan of the Hudhalis, p. 104), and it is the opening of one of his qasidas. In it, "mushtajiran" appears in place of "murtafiqan." Mushtajiran means he grips his head with his hand, meaning that he placed his head on his hands, as a garment is gripped with a stick. Al-Asma'i said: al-sab is a bitter tree with a milk that stings the eye when it touches it. Madhbuh means split; al-dhabh is the splitting. Murtafiqan means placing his elbow under his head. The verse is among the evidences of Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:400), and its beginning is: "Indeed I stayed awake and spent the night..." He said: "sa'at murtafaqan": that is, reclining. Abu Dhu'ayb said... [the verse].]

As for the root from rifq (kindness), it is said: "qad irtafaqtu bika murtafaqan" (I have been kind to you, being kind). Mujahid used to interpret His saying ﴿and evil is the resting place﴾ as meaning the gathering place.

Mention of the narration of this: Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿murtafaqan﴾: that is, gathered.

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Mu'tamir narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿and evil is murtafaqan﴾: He said: gathered.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it. I do not know of irtifaq meaning gathering in the speech of the Arabs; rather, irtifaq is an iftial form, either from al-mirfaq (elbow) or from al-rifq (kindness).

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 30:

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does best in deed﴾ [18:30].

He, Exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed, those who affirm God and His Messenger, and act in obedience to God, and submit to His command and prohibition, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does best in deed, who obeys God and follows His command and prohibition. Rather, We shall recompense him for his obedience and good deeds with Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow.

If someone asks: Where is the predicate (khabar) of the first "inna"? It is said: It is permissible that its predicate is His saying, ﴿indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does best in deed﴾, so that the meaning of the statement is: Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who performs righteous deeds. The first clause is thus left out, and reliance is placed on the second, with the intention of repetition (al-takrir), as it is said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it﴾ [2:217], meaning: about fighting in it, by way of repetition. And as the poet said:

Indeed the Caliph, indeed God has clothed him
with the garment of kingship, by which the ends are hoped for.

[[Note on the verse: al-Sirbal (the garment) means a shirt or armour (see Lisan al-Arab, under s-r-b-l). In the hadith of Uthman: "I will not take off a garment God has clothed me with," he meant by it the caliphate. The author cited it to show that the repetition in His saying, Exalted is He, "Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost..." has a parallel in the poet's words: "Indeed the Caliph, indeed God has clothed him..." the verse. The two aspects of the grammatical analysis in the repeated clause have already been explained. The verse is among the evidences cited by al-Farra' in (Ma'ani al-Qur'an, folio 185 of the University microfilm), who said: The predicate of "those who believe" in His saying "indeed We do not allow to be lost" is like the poet's words "Indeed the Caliph..." the verse, for in meaning it is: "Indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who performs righteous deeds." The first clause is left out, reliance is placed on the second, with the intention of repetition, as He said: "They ask you about the sacred month," then He said: "about fighting in it," meaning: about fighting in it, by repetition. It is also possible to take "Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds" as a conditional clause, as you would say: "Indeed whoever does righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost his reward," so the fa' is implied in His saying "fa-inna" [i.e. "then indeed"], and omitting it is permissible, and this is the most preferred aspect to me.]]

It is also transmitted as "turkha" (is hoped for). It is also permissible that ﴿Indeed those who believe﴾ is a conditional clause, so the meaning of the statement is: Indeed whoever does righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost his reward, the fa' being implied in His saying "indeed". It is also permissible that its predicate is: ﴿those, for them are Gardens of Eden﴾ [18:31], so the meaning of the statement is: Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds, those, for them are Gardens of Eden.

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Those, for them are Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein upon thrones. How excellent is the reward and good is the resting place (31).﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: For those who believed and did righteous deeds are Gardens of Eden, meaning gardens of residence in the Hereafter. ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾ means: rivers flow beneath them and before them.

And His, the Majestic's, words "from beneath them" mean: from beside them and before them. ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets﴾ means: they will wear therein, of the ornaments, bracelets of gold. The word asawir (bracelets) is the plural of iswar.

* *

His words: ﴿And they will wear green garments of sundus﴾

Sundus is a plural whose singular is sundusa, and it is what is thin of brocade (dibaj). Istabraq is what is thick and heavy of it. It has also been said that istabraq is silk (harir). Among the verses supporting this is the saying of al-Murraqish:

"You see them wearing the mashair at times, and at other times their garment is istabraq of dibaj."

[The verse is by al-Murraqish. Mashair is the plural of mash'ar, which is the undergarment that lies next to the human body, apart from anything else. In a hadith mentioning the Ansar: "They are the mash'ar, not the midthar," describing them with affection and closeness. The author has explained istabraq and dibaj. The verse is evidence for the meaning of istabraq.]

That is: and thick brocade.

* *

His words: ﴿Reclining therein upon thrones﴾

He says: reclining in the Gardens of Eden upon the arā'ik (thrones), which are couches within canopied enclosures (hijal). Its singular is arika, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Cheeks which were worn by travel until it was as if they touched the smooth ground to the touch of arā'ik."

[The verse is by Dhu al-Rumma (his Diwan, Cambridge edition, 1919, p. 422), and before it is his saying: "When they alight at a waterless place, they cover where the breaths of the wind have been worn by exhaustion..." His saying "khududan" is the object of "kasaw" in the preceding verse. Al-mi'zaa is hard, stony ground, like the carpets on the arā'ik, which are beds, singular sarir. That is: they made the place where they slept a covering for their cheeks. In Lisan (a-r-k): the exegetes said: the arā'ik are couches within canopied enclosures. Al-Zajjaj said: the arā'ik are the furnishings within canopied enclosures, and it is said they are beds, and in reality they are furnishings that were in the canopied enclosures or elsewhere. It is also said: the arika is a decorated, upholstered couch in a tent or house; if there is no couch in it, it is a hijla.]

And from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Between the pavilion and a side of its curtain, from it and between the arika of al-Anḍad."

[This verse I could not find in the Diwan of al-A'sha Maymun, nor in the rest of his poetry appended to it; I only found two verses of its meter and rhyme, p. 245, edition of Dr. Muhammad Husayn, Cairo. I found no other. Al-riwaq, with the rā' doubled and vowelled either way, is a tent. The verse is evidence, like the previous one, that the meaning of arā'ik is couches within canopied enclosures, and that its singular is arika. Al-anḍad is the plural of nadd (with a vowel change), which is what of household goods is piled up, with some placed upon others.]

And according to what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿upon the arā'ik﴾, he said: They are the hijal (canopied enclosures). Ma'mar said: and another said: the couches within the canopied enclosures.

* *

His words: ﴿How excellent is the reward﴾

That is: the excellent reward is the Gardens of Eden, and what He, the Majestic, described as having made for those who believed and did righteous deeds. ﴿And good is the resting place﴾ means: and these arā'ik in these gardens which He, may His remembrance be exalted, described in this verse, are good as a reclining place. The Majestic said: ﴿And good is [it] as a resting place (murtafaqan)﴾ and He made the verb feminine, meaning: and these arā'ik are good as a murtafaq. Had He made it masculine according to the masculine form of murtafaq, it would have been correct, because Arabs use ni'ma and bi'sa in speech only to express praise and blame, not as a verb, so they are used with a feminine noun and kept singular with the dual and plural.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 32–34:

The explanation of the words of His, the Exalted, ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: We had granted one of them two gardens of grapevines and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them fields of crops. Each of the two gardens produced its fruit and did not fall short therein in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth within them. And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): And present, O Muhammad, to these polytheists who associate others with Allah, those who asked you to drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His face, a parable: "two men, to one of whom We granted two gardens of grapevines," meaning, We granted him two gardens of vines, "and surrounded them with date palms," meaning, We encircled these two gardens with date palms.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and placed between them fields of crops﴾

meaning: We placed, in the midst of these two gardens, crops. And His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens produced its fruit﴾ meaning: each of the two gardens yielded its produce, and what was in it of plantings of date palms, vines and kinds of crops. He said "kilta al-jannatayn" (both the gardens), then said "atat" (produced), using the singular for the verb, because "kilta" is not used in the singular, its root being "kull," though the Arabs sometimes use "kilta" in the singular form and treat it as a dual. Some of the rajaz poets said on this:

"In the two feet of her, one phalanx ... both of them joined with an extra one."

[The verse is among the evidences cited by al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 186 of the University of Jami'a photocopy no. 24059), where he said: "The Arabs have sometimes used one of 'kilay' (written with a ya' for imala)." It is among the grammarians' evidences that "kilt" originally was "kilta," its alif dropped out of necessity, with the fatha on the ta' as evidence of it (Khizanat al-Adab of al-Baghdadi, 1:62). He said: I saw in the margin of al-Sihah that this verse is from a rajaz describing an ostrich, so the pronoun of "her feet" refers to the ostrich. "Salami" is on the pattern of "hubara," a bone in the foot of a camel, and small bones the length of a finger or less in the hand and foot; the plural is "salamiyat." "Farsin" is like the hoof of a horse. The pronoun in "kiltahuma" refers to the two feet. Then he said: their use of this verse as evidence for the singular is refuted by its meaning, since the meaning is the dual, as shown by its emphasis in the second hemistich. Consider this. Abu Hayyan said in his Tadhkira: this verse is a poetic necessity; "kilt" is not a singular of "kilta," but came with the meaning of "kilaa," except that he dropped the alif, relying on the kasra before it, which suffices in place of the alif inclined toward the ya'. None of the Kufans says "kilt" is the singular of "kilta," nor claims that "kila" or "kilta" has a separate singular in actual usage; if an opponent alleges it, it is a slander and a fabrication by their adversaries against their statement. End.]

He means by "kilt": "kilta." Likewise they do with "kilta," "kila," and "kull" when they are annexed to a definite noun; the verb after them may be plural or singular. His saying ﴿and did not fall short therein in anything﴾ means: it did not diminish its produce at all, but rather yielded that fully and completely. From it comes the saying of people: "So-and-so wronged so-and-so his right," when he cheated him and diminished it, as the poet said:

"He wronged me of my wealth thus, and twisted my hand ... may Allah, who is its overcomer, twist his hand."

[The verse is one of nine verses by Far'un ibn al-A'raf concerning his son Manazil (al-Hamasa with the commentary of al-Tibrizi, 4:9), whose opening is "He concealed my right unjustly and twisted my hand." "Tughammada haqqi" means he covered/concealed it. It has the meaning of "tazlimuni mali" (he wronged me of my wealth); "lawa yadi" means he twisted it and removed it from its state and form. It is among the evidences cited by Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:402), where he said: "and did not wrong from it anything": did not diminish. It is said: so-and-so wronged me of my right, meaning he diminished it for me. A man said to his son: "You wrong me of my wealth thus..." etc.

The version of the verse in Lisan al-Arab is: "tazlim mali hakadha..." the verse, without attribution. Before it he said: "wa-zalamahu haqqahu, wa-tazlamahu iyyahu," meaning that both have the same meaning.]

And the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿and did not fall short therein in anything﴾: meaning, it did not diminish anything from it.

* *

And His saying: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth within them﴾

* *

And His saying: ﴿So he said to his companion while conversing with him﴾

The Exalted says: So he who We had granted two gardens of grapevines said to his companion, who has no wealth, while speaking to him:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 32–34:

The explanation of the words of His, the Exalted, ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: We had granted one of them two gardens of grapevines and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them fields of crops. Each of the two gardens produced its fruit and did not fall short therein in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth within them. And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾

Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): And present, O Muhammad, to these polytheists who associate others with Allah, those who asked you to drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, desiring His face, a parable: "two men, to one of whom We granted two gardens of grapevines," meaning, We granted him two gardens of vines, "and surrounded them with date palms," meaning, We encircled these two gardens with date palms.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and placed between them fields of crops﴾

meaning: We placed, in the midst of these two gardens, crops. And His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens produced its fruit﴾ meaning: each of the two gardens yielded its produce, and what was in it of plantings of date palms, vines and kinds of crops. He said "kilta al-jannatayn" (both the gardens), then said "atat" (produced), using the singular for the verb, because "kilta" is not used in the singular, its root being "kull," though the Arabs sometimes use "kilta" in the singular form and treat it as a dual. Some of the rajaz poets said on this:

"In the two feet of her, one phalanx ... both of them joined with an extra one."

[The verse is among the evidences cited by al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (folio 186 of the University of Jami'a photocopy no. 24059), where he said: "The Arabs have sometimes used one of 'kilay' (written with a ya' for imala)." It is among the grammarians' evidences that "kilt" originally was "kilta," its alif dropped out of necessity, with the fatha on the ta' as evidence of it (Khizanat al-Adab of al-Baghdadi, 1:62). He said: I saw in the margin of al-Sihah that this verse is from a rajaz describing an ostrich, so the pronoun of "her feet" refers to the ostrich. "Salami" is on the pattern of "hubara," a bone in the foot of a camel, and small bones the length of a finger or less in the hand and foot; the plural is "salamiyat." "Farsin" is like the hoof of a horse. The pronoun in "kiltahuma" refers to the two feet. Then he said: their use of this verse as evidence for the singular is refuted by its meaning, since the meaning is the dual, as shown by its emphasis in the second hemistich. Consider this. Abu Hayyan said in his Tadhkira: this verse is a poetic necessity; "kilt" is not a singular of "kilta," but came with the meaning of "kilaa," except that he dropped the alif, relying on the kasra before it, which suffices in place of the alif inclined toward the ya'. None of the Kufans says "kilt" is the singular of "kilta," nor claims that "kila" or "kilta" has a separate singular in actual usage; if an opponent alleges it, it is a slander and a fabrication by their adversaries against their statement. End.]

He means by "kilt": "kilta." Likewise they do with "kilta," "kila," and "kull" when they are annexed to a definite noun; the verb after them may be plural or singular. His saying ﴿and did not fall short therein in anything﴾ means: it did not diminish its produce at all, but rather yielded that fully and completely. From it comes the saying of people: "So-and-so wronged so-and-so his right," when he cheated him and diminished it, as the poet said:

"He wronged me of my wealth thus, and twisted my hand ... may Allah, who is its overcomer, twist his hand."

[The verse is one of nine verses by Far'un ibn al-A'raf concerning his son Manazil (al-Hamasa with the commentary of al-Tibrizi, 4:9), whose opening is "He concealed my right unjustly and twisted my hand." "Tughammada haqqi" means he covered/concealed it. It has the meaning of "tazlimuni mali" (he wronged me of my wealth); "lawa yadi" means he twisted it and removed it from its state and form. It is among the evidences cited by Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:402), where he said: "and did not wrong from it anything": did not diminish. It is said: so-and-so wronged me of my right, meaning he diminished it for me. A man said to his son: "You wrong me of my wealth thus..." etc.

The version of the verse in Lisan al-Arab is: "tazlim mali hakadha..." the verse, without attribution. Before it he said: "wa-zalamahu haqqahu, wa-tazlamahu iyyahu," meaning that both have the same meaning.]

And the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said on this.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 35–36:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I should be returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return."﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: This man to whom We gave the two gardens of grapes ﴿entered his garden﴾, meaning his orchard, ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾. His wronging of himself was his disbelief in the Resurrection, his doubt about the establishment of the Hour, and his forgetting the return to Allah, the Exalted. Thereby he made deserved for himself the wrath of Allah and His painful punishment. As for His saying, ﴿He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish"﴾, He, may His praise be glorified, says: he said when he beheld his garden and saw what was in it of trees, fruits, crops, and flowing rivers, doubting the return to Allah: "I do not think that this garden will ever perish, nor be destroyed, nor be ruined. And I do not think that the Hour, in which Allah promised His creation the gathering, will come to be established and take place." Then he wished another wish, upon doubt on his part, saying: ﴿And if I should be returned to my Lord﴾, so I return to Him, while he is not certain that he will return to Him, ﴿I will surely find better than it as a return﴾. As it is related:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying, ﴿And I do not think the Hour will occur, established﴾: "He doubted." Then He said, ﴿And if I should be returned﴾, that is, if that happened, ﴿to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return﴾: "He did not give me this except that I have with Him better than that."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 35–36:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will occur. And if I should be returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return."﴾

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: This man to whom We gave the two gardens of grapes ﴿entered his garden﴾, meaning his orchard, ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾. His wronging of himself was his disbelief in the Resurrection, his doubt about the establishment of the Hour, and his forgetting the return to Allah, the Exalted. Thereby he made deserved for himself the wrath of Allah and His painful punishment. As for His saying, ﴿He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish"﴾, He, may His praise be glorified, says: he said when he beheld his garden and saw what was in it of trees, fruits, crops, and flowing rivers, doubting the return to Allah: "I do not think that this garden will ever perish, nor be destroyed, nor be ruined. And I do not think that the Hour, in which Allah promised His creation the gathering, will come to be established and take place." Then he wished another wish, upon doubt on his part, saying: ﴿And if I should be returned to my Lord﴾, so I return to Him, while he is not certain that he will return to Him, ﴿I will surely find better than it as a return﴾. He says: I will surely find with Allah something better than my garden if I am returned to Him as a place of return and a going back. That is, He has not given me this garden in the world except that I have with Him something better than it in the hereafter, if I am returned to Him.

As it is related:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself. He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish. And I do not think the Hour will occur"﴾: "Ungrateful for the blessings of his Lord, denying His meeting, wishing vainly upon Allah."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 37–38:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him: "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you into a man?"﴾ [37] ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord.﴾ [38]

God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: his companion, the one who had less wealth and children than the owner of the two gardens, said to him, ﴿while he was arguing with him﴾, meaning: while he was addressing him and speaking with him: ﴿"Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust"﴾, meaning: who created your father Adam from dust. ﴿"Then from a drop of semen"﴾, meaning: then brought you into being from the semen of a man and a woman. ﴿"Then proportioned you into a man"﴾, meaning: then made you balanced, a complete human being, a male and not a female. The meaning is: "Do you disbelieve in the One who did this to you, that He would restore you as a new creation after you become decayed bones?" ﴿"But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord"﴾, meaning: as for me, I do not disbelieve in my Lord; rather, I say: "He is Allah, my Lord." The meaning is that he says: "But I say: He is Allah, my Lord." ﴿"And I associate none with my Lord."﴾

There are two readings of this. One is ﴿lākinnā huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ with the nun doubled and the alif omitted in continuous speech, as one says "anā qā'imun" with the alif of anā dropped; this is the reading of the majority of the readers of Iraq. As for pausing, the reading in all cases retains the alif, because the nun was doubled only through the assimilation of the nun of lākinna into the nun that follows the alif of anā, when the hamza in anā has dropped. So when one pauses on it, the alif of anā appears, and it is said "lākinnā", since in pausing on anā one says it with the alif, not without it. Some people of the Hijaz read it ﴿lākinnā﴾ with the alif affirmed both in continuous speech and in pausing. Although this is said only under the necessity of poetry, as the poet said:

"I am the sword of the clan, so recognise me, / Ḥamīdan, who has climbed the hump" [The verse is among the witnesses cited by the grammarians that the retention of the alif of "anā" in continuous speech, among other than the Banu Tamim, occurs only under the necessity of poetry. (Khizānat al-Adab of al-Baghdadi, 2:390) Then he said: Ibn Jinni said in his commentary on al-Mazini's Tasrif: As for the alif in "anā" in pausing, it is extra and not original; do you not see that you say in continuous speech "an Zayd", as God the Exalted said: "Indeed I am your Lord" [Q 20:12], written with an alif after the nun, though the alif is not pronounced; it is written as in pausing, so the alif drops in continuous speech, like the dropping of the hā' which is added in pausing to show the vowel in continuous speech, and the vowel is shown by the alif as it is shown by the hā', because the hā' is close to the alif. End of quote. "Ḥamīdan" is in apposition to the yā' in "i'rifūnī", and is narrated both diminutive and augmented. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "jamīʿan" stands in place of "ḥamīdan". "Tadhdharaytu al-sanām" means I climbed its top. Yaqut attributed this verse, in the margin of al-Ṣiḥāḥ, to Ḥumayd ibn Baḥdal, a poet, who is Ḥumayd ibn Ḥurayth ibn Baḥdal, of the Banu Kalb ibn Wabara, whose lineage ends at Quḍā'a. He was an Islamic-era poet; his paternal aunt was Maysūn bint Baḥdal, the mother of Yazid ibn Mu'awiya.]

So he affirmed the alif in "anā", and that is not eloquent speech. The reading that is correct in our view is what we have mentioned from the Iraqis: omitting the alif of "lākinna" in continuous speech and affirming it in pausing.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 39:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [is so]; there is no power except in Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Why did you not, when you entered your garden and it pleased you what you saw of it, say, 'What Allah wills, that is what occurs'?" In the speech there is an omitted element, which is dispensed with because of what is manifest from it, namely the answer of the conditional, and that is "it would have been well."

When the speech is directed to this meaning that we have mentioned, then "mā" is in the accusative by the action of Allah's verb upon it, which is "shāʾa" (willed), and the omission of the answer is permissible because the meaning of the speech is known, as it is said: ﴿So if you are able to seek a shaft in the earth...﴾ and the answer is left out, since its meaning is understood. Some of the grammarians (ahl al-ʿArabiyyah) used to say that "mā" in His saying ﴿what Allah wills﴾ is in the nominative position, by supposing a hidden "huwa" (it), as if it were said: "You said, it is what Allah wills." ﴿There is no power except in Allah﴾: he says, there is no strength to what we attempt of His obedience except by Him.

* *

And His saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾

This is the saying of the believer who has no wealth and no clan, like the owner of the two gardens and his kinsmen, and he is like Salman, Suhayb and Khabbab. He says: the believer said to the disbeliever: "If you see me, O man, as less than you in wealth and children..." When you make "anā" a pronoun of separation (ʿimād), you put "aqall" in the accusative; and that is the reading we hold, because it is the reading of the major cities (qirāʾat al-amṣār). When you make it a noun, you put "aqall" in the nominative.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 40–41:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden and will send upon it a calamity from the sky, so that it becomes a barren surface, slipping away, or its water sinks into the earth so that you will not be able to seek it.﴾

His saying, exalted is His remembrance, reporting the statement of the believer who was certain of the return to God, to the disbelieving man who doubted the establishment of the Hour: "If you consider me to be less than you in wealth and children in this world, then perhaps my Lord will grant me something better than this garden of yours." ﴿And He will send upon it﴾, meaning upon the garden of the disbeliever, about which he had said: "I do not think that this will ever perish," ﴿a calamity from the sky﴾. He says: a punishment from the sky which is hurled, cast down. And al-Husban (ḥusbān) is the plural of ḥusbānah, which means projectiles.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said.

Mention of those who said this:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿And He will send upon it a calamity from the sky﴾, a punishment.

* It was related to me from Muhammad ibn Yazid, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: a punishment.

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And He will send upon it a calamity from the sky﴾, he said: a punishment. He said: al-Husban: a decree from God which He decrees.

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-Husban: the punishment.

* al-Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿a calamity from the sky﴾, he said: a punishment.

* * *

And His saying: ﴿So it becomes a barren surface, slipping away﴾

He, may His remembrance be mighty, says: so that this garden of yours, O man, becomes a smooth land with nothing in it, all that was in it of planting and vegetation having gone, and it returns to being a desolate waste, slippery, in whose soil no foot can stand because of its smoothness, and the effacement of what had been growing in it.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, His saying: ﴿So it becomes a barren surface﴾: that is, its produce has been harvested and nothing has been left in it.

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So it becomes a barren surface﴾, he said: like the juruz (barren land).

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿So it becomes a barren surface﴾, he said: a barren surface and a juruz surface are one, with nothing of vegetation in it.

* * *

And His saying: ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾

He says: or its water becomes sunken (ghā'iran), so He used ghawr, which is a verbal noun (maṣdar), in place of the active participle ghā'ir, as the poet said:

"Its horses remain mourning over him, / their reins hung with their standing-still (ṣufūnan)" [[The verse is by 'Amr ibn Kulthum, champion and chief of Taghlib, from his famous mu'allaqah. The first hemistich in al-Tibrizi's and al-Zawzani's commentaries and in Jamharat ash'ar al-'Arab (Cairo edition) reads: "We left the horses dwelling upon him." Al-Zawzani said: al-Sufun is the plural of ṣāfin. The horse ṣafana yaṣfinu ṣufūnan when it stands on three legs and bends its fourth hoof. He means: we killed him, and we held our horses over him, having hung their reins while they were standing still beside him. The verse is among the evidences cited by Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:403), where he said: "or its water becomes ghawran," meaning ghā'iran. The Arabs sometimes describe the doer by its verbal noun, and likewise the dual and plural, in the form of the verbal noun; 'Amr ibn Kulthum said: "Its horses remain nawhan (mourning) over him," meaning nā'iḥāt (wailing).]]

meaning "wailing" (nā'iḥah), and as another said:

"Pour out from their tears abundant flow, / and answer with standing lament (nawḥan qiyāman)" [[The verse is among the evidences cited by Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:404). After the previous evidence he said: a weeping mourner (wailing for Hisham ibn al-Mughira) said: "Pour out... the verse." He said: its reciter (khaffafahu) perhaps meant Hisham ibn 'Uqba ibn 'Ammara ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. End. The evidence in it is like that in the preceding verse; he means by "nawhan" wailing women, and this is common in verbal nouns. Ḍubā' is a diminutive form of Ḍubā'a, the name of a woman.]]

The Arabs use ghawr in the singular for the plural and the dual, and they use it with masculine and feminine: they say māʾ ghawr, and māʾān ghawr, and miyāh ghawr.

By His saying ﴿ghawran﴾ He means: gone, having sunk into the earth, so that it is not reached by the bucket (al-rishā').

As:

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿Or its water becomes sunken﴾: that is, gone, having sunk into the earth.

* * *

And His saying: ﴿so you will not be able to seek it﴾

He says: you will not be able, by your seeking it, to reach the water that was in your garden after its sinking.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 42–44:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed, so he began to wring his hands over what he had spent upon it, while it lay fallen on its trellises, and he said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ (42)

His exalted mention says: Destruction and calamities encompassed his fruit, meaning the varieties of fruit of his garden about which he had said: ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish﴾. So this disbelieving man, the owner of the two gardens, began to turn his palms over, back and front, in distress and regret over the loss of his expenditure that he had spent on his garden. ﴿While it lay fallen on its trellises﴾ means: while it lay empty over its plants and its structures.

And according to what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have spoken.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿so he began to wring his hands﴾: that is, he clapped (yusaffiq). ﴿over what he had spent upon it﴾, grieving over what had escaped him. ﴿And﴾ he ﴿said, "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ And he says, "Would that I...": he says, this disbeliever wishes, after his garden had been struck, that he had not associated anyone with his Lord. He means by this: this disbeliever, when he perishes and his worldly life is removed from him and he is left alone with his deeds, wishes that he had not disbelieved in God nor associated anything with Him.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And he had no company to help him against Allah, nor was he able to save himself. There, protection belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾ (43–44)

His exalted mention says: The owner of the two gardens had no company (fi'ah), meaning a group, as ʿAjjaj said:

*As the fi'ah of the kamī gathers (kamā yaḥūz al-fi'ah al-kamī)*

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His, the Exalted's, words:** ﴿وَاضْرِبْ لَهُمْ مَثَلَ الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا كَمَاءٍ أَنزلْنَاهُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ فَاخْتَلَطَ بِهِ نَبَاتُ الأَرْضِ فَأَصْبَحَ هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُقْتَدِرًا﴾ ﴿And set forth for them the parable of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, then it becomes dry stalks which the winds scatter. And Allah is ever Capable of all things.﴾ [45]

He, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "Set forth for the life of these arrogant people, who said to you, 'Drive away from you those who call upon their Lord morning and evening,' when we come to you with the worldly life from them, a parable," meaning: a likeness. ﴿كَمَاءٍ أَنزلْنَاهُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("like water which We sent down from the sky"), meaning: like rain which We sent down from the sky. ﴿فَاخْتَلَطَ بِهِ نَبَاتُ الأَرْضِ﴾ ("then the vegetation of the earth mingled with it"), meaning: the vegetation of the earth mingled with the water. ﴿فَأَصْبَحَ هَشِيمًا﴾ ("then it became dry stalks"), meaning: the vegetation of the earth became dry and crumbled. ﴿تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ﴾ ("which the winds scatter"), meaning: the winds blow it away and disperse it. It is said of this: *dharathu al-rih yadhrūhu dharwan* (the wind scattered it), *dharathu dharyan*, and *adhrathu tadhrīhi idhrā'an*, as the poet said:

*Then I said to him: "Go gently, and do not overexert him,*
*lest he bring you down from the qata's rear and you slip."*

[[The verse is by Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr (from *Mukhtar al-Shi'r al-Jahili*, Mustafa al-Babi al-Halabi edition, with the commentary of Mustafa al-Saqqa, p. 125). In its commentary: *fayudrika* means he will throw you and fell you; it is said *adhraytu al-shay' 'an al-shay'* when... and *al-qata'* is the seat of the one riding behind. The meaning: I said to the young man, "Keep the horse on a straight course, and take its ease; do not make it run fast, lest it throw you from the back of the qata'." It is also narrated as "from the top of the qata'".]]

It is said: *adhraytu al-rajul 'an al-dabbah wa al-ba'ir* (I threw the man off the riding animal or the camel), when I cast him off it.

* *

And His words: ﴿وكان الله على كل شيء مقتدرا﴾ ("And Allah is ever Capable of all things").

It means: Allah is capable of destroying the garden of this speaker, when he entered his garden, saying: ﴿مَا أَظُنُّ أَنْ تَبِيدَ هَذِهِ أَبَدًا وَمَا أَظُنُّ السَّاعَةَ قَائِمَةً﴾ ("I do not think that this will ever perish, nor do I think the Hour will come"), and capable of destroying the wealth of the owner of wealth who withholds it from its rights, and of removing the worldly life of those who disbelieve in Him from them, and of whatever else He wills. Nothing He wills is beyond His power, and no matter He intends is beyond His ability.

It means: the owner of wealth should not boast of the abundance of his wealth, nor be arrogant toward others because of it, and the people of this world should not be deceived by their worldly life. Its likeness is that of this vegetation which became lush through rain, and then, after a short while, when the water was cut off from it and it reached its end, it turned dry, scattered by the winds, rotten, and the eyes of observers turn away from it. Instead, let one work for what remains, which does not perish, and the lasting thing which does not vanish and does not change.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope﴾ (18:46).

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: "Wealth and children, O people, are what Uyayna and al-Aqra boast of and take pride in over Salman, Khabbab and Suhayb. They are part of the adornment of the life of this world, and they are not among the things of the Hereafter. ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward.﴾" That is, what Salman, Khabbab and Suhayb do of obedience to God, and their calling upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, which remains for them of righteous deeds after the life of this world has perished, is better, O Muhammad, with your Lord for reward than the wealth and children of which these polytheists boast, which perish and do not remain for their people. ﴿And better for hope﴾: what Salman, Suhayb and Khabbab hope for from that is better than what Uyayna and al-Aqra hope for from their wealth and children. These verses, from His saying ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ up to this point, are reported to have been revealed concerning Uyayna and al-Aqra.

Those who said so:

Al-Husayn ibn Amr al-ʿAnqazi related to us, saying: My father related to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr related to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Saʿid al-Azdi, who was the reciter of the Azd, from Abu al-Kanud, from Khabbab, concerning His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾. Then he mentioned the story we have mentioned in Surat al-Anʿam concerning Uyayna and al-Aqra, up to His saying: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance﴾. He said: Uyayna and al-Aqra. ﴿And follows his desire﴾. He said: He said: Then He struck for them the example of two men and the likeness of the life of this world.

The people of ta'wil (interpretation, tafsir) differed about the meaning of "the enduring good deeds," in the same way they differed about the meaning of the supplication by which God described those whom the Messenger of God ﷺ was forbidden to drive away and commanded to be patient with. Some of them said: They are the five daily prayers. Some said: They are the remembrance of God by glorifying, sanctifying and declaring His oneness, and the like. Some said: They are acting in obedience to God. Some said: They are good speech.

Those who said: They are the five daily prayers:

Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Anmati related to me, saying: Yaʿqub ibn Kasib related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Umawi related to us, saying: I heard ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Hurmuz narrate from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUtba, from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The enduring good deeds are the five daily prayers."

Zurayq ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: Qabisa related to us, from Sufyan, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "The five daily prayers."

Yahya ibn Ibrahim al-Masʿudi related to me, saying: My father related to us, from his father, from his grandfather, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Ishaq, from ʿAmr ibn Shurahbil concerning this verse: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "They are the prescribed prayers."

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The enduring good deeds are the five daily prayers."

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from al-Hasan ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ibrahim, who said: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾: "The five daily prayers."

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mansur, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Maysara: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "The five daily prayers."

Those who said: They are the remembrance of God by glorification, praise and the like. Ibn Humayd, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad and Muhammad ibn ʿUmara al-Asadi related to us, they said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid related to us, saying: Haywa informed us, saying: Abu ʿAqil Zuhra ibn Maʿbad al-Qurashi, from the Banu Taym, of the kin of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, informed us that he heard al-Harith, the client of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, say: It was said to ʿUthman: "What are the enduring good deeds?" He said: "They are: there is no god but God, glory be to God, praise be to God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor might except by God."

Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam related to me, saying: Abu Zurʿa related to us, saying: Haywa related to us, saying: Abu ʿAqil Zuhra ibn Maʿbad related to us, that he heard al-Harith, the client of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, say: It was said to ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan: "What are the enduring good deeds?" He said: "They are: there is no god but God, and glory be to God and His is the praise, God is greatest, praise be to God, and there is no power nor might except by God."

Ibn ʿAbd al-Rahim al-Barqi related to me, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam related to us, saying: Nafiʿ ibn Yazid and Rushdin ibn Saʿd related to us, they said: Zuhra ibn Maʿbad related to us, saying: I heard al-Harith, the client of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, say: They said to ʿUthman: "What are the enduring good deeds?" and he mentioned the like of it.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Hurmuz, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest."

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, saying: I heard ʿAbd al-Malik, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest."

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Talq ibn Ghannam related to us, from Zaʾida, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, the like of it.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Malik related to us, from ʿUmara ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Sayyad, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾: glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor might except by God."

Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUthman ibn Khushaym informed me, from Nafiʿ ibn Sarjis, that he informed him that he asked Ibn ʿUmar about the enduring good deeds, and he said: "There is no god but God, God is greatest, glory be to God, and there is no power nor might except by God." Ibn Jurayj said: ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah said the like of that.

Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: "The enduring good deeds: glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest."

Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar related to us, saying: Shuʿba related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest."

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Abu Sakhr related to me that ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, the client of Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah, related to him, saying: Salim ibn Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi sent me, and said: "Tell him: meet me at the corner of the grave, for I have a need of you." He said: So they met, and one of them greeted the other. Then Salim said: "What do you count as the enduring good deeds?" He said: "There is no god but God, praise be to God, glory be to God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor might except by God." Salim said to him: "When did you include in them 'there is no power nor might except by God'?" He said: "I have always included it." He said: He returned to him twice or three times, and he did not retract. He said: So he confirmed it. Salim said: "Indeed. Confirm it, for Abu Ayyub al-Ansari related to me that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ saying: 'I was taken up to the heaven, and I saw Ibrahim. He said: O Jibril, who is this with you? He said: Muhammad. He welcomed me and made it easy for me, then he said: Command your nation to plant much of the plants of Paradise, for its soil is good and its land is spacious. I said: What are the plants of Paradise? He said: There is no power nor might except by God.'"

I found in my book, from al-Hasan ibn al-Sabbah al-Bazzar, from Abu Nasr al-Tammar, from ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Muslim, from Muhammad ibn ʿAjlan, from Saʿid al-Maqburi, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest, are among the enduring good deeds."

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from al-Hasan and Qatada, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better﴾, he said: "There is no god but God, God is greatest, praise be to God, glory be to God. They are the enduring good deeds."

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: ʿAmr ibn al-Harith informed us, that Darraj Abu al-Samh related to him, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Increase your store of the enduring good deeds." It was said: "And what are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "The religion." It was said: "And what are they, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Magnifying God (takbir), declaring His oneness (tahlil), glorifying Him (tasbih), praising Him (hamd), and there is no power nor might except by God."

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Malik informed me, from ʿUmara ibn Sayyad, that he heard Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab say concerning the enduring good deeds: they are the servant's saying: "God is greatest, glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and there is no power nor might except by God."

Ibn al-Barqi related to me, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub informed us, saying: Ibn ʿAjlan related to me, from ʿUmara ibn Sayyad, who said: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab asked me about the enduring good deeds, and I said: "The prayer and fasting." He said: "You are not correct." I said: "Zakat and Hajj." He said: "You are not correct. Rather, they are the five words: there is no god but God, God is greatest, glory be to God, praise be to God, and there is no power nor might except by God."

Those who said: They are acting in obedience to God, the Mighty and Majestic: al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAta' al-Khurasani, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope﴾, he said: "The righteous deeds are: glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest."

ʿAli related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah related to us, saying: Muʿawiya related to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "They are the remembrance of God: the saying 'there is no god but God, God is greatest, glory be to God, praise be to God, blessed is God, there is no power nor might except by God, I seek God's forgiveness, and God's blessings be upon the Messenger of God,' and fasting, prayer, Hajj, charity, freeing slaves, jihad, kinship ties, and all the works of good deeds. They are the enduring good deeds, which remain for their people in Paradise as long as the heavens and the earth endure."

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying: "And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward and better for hope": "They are the righteous deeds."

Those who said: They are good words: Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾, he said: "They are good speech."

The most correct of these sayings in terms of truth is the saying of those who said: They are all deeds of goodness, as is narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas, because all of that is among the righteous deeds that remain for their doer in the Hereafter, and by them he is recompensed and rewarded. And God, may His remembrance be exalted, did not specify, in His saying ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord for reward﴾, some of them over others, either in the Book or in a report from the Messenger of God ﷺ.

If someone supposes that this is restricted by the report we narrated from Abu Hurayra from the Prophet ﷺ, then that is contrary to what he thinks. The report from the Messenger of God ﷺ only states that the saying "glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest" are among the enduring good deeds. It did not say "they are all the enduring good deeds" nor "every enduring good deed." It is permissible that these are enduring good deeds, and that other acts of righteousness are also enduring good deeds.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 47–48:

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] the Day We will set the mountains in motion, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We will gather them and leave none of them behind.﴾ [47] ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time. But you claimed that We would not appoint for you a appointment."﴾ [48]

His Exalted remembrance says:

﴿And the Day We set the mountains in motion﴾ away from the earth, so We will crumble it to dust and make it scattered dust particles (hiba' munbathth). ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾, i.e., manifest. Its being laid bare, visible to the eyes of onlookers, with nothing covering it of mountain or tree, is its barrenness.

Similar to this was said by a group of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil).

Those who said that:

* Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, who said: Abu 'Asim related to us, who said: 'Isa related to us, (and) al-Harith related to me, who said: al-Hasan related to us, who said: Warqa' related to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿and you will see the earth laid bare﴾: He said: "There is no hollow in it, no shelter, no building, and no rock in it."

* Al-Qasim related to me, who said: al-Husayn related to us, who said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

* Bishr related to us, who said: Yazid related to us, who said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding his saying: ﴿and you will see the earth laid bare﴾: there is no building or tree upon it.

It was also said: the meaning of that is: "and you will see the earth laid bare," with its people who were in its belly now on its surface.

* *

As for His saying ﴿and We will gather them﴾:

He says: We will assemble them at the place of reckoning. ﴿And We will leave none of them behind﴾, i.e., We will not leave behind, nor will We keep back from them under the earth anyone. It is said from this: "I did not leave (ghadartu) any of the people behind," and "I did not leave any of them (aghdartu)." And from aghdartu is the saying of the rajaz poet:

Do you have, while the passing one from you is departing, [a share] in a herd / from which the one who takes hold leaves (yughdiru) some remaining?

[These are two verses of rajaz meter, from a set of three verses cited in (Lisan al-Arab: 'arada). The third precedes them: "O night, may the flashing lightning give you drink."

It belongs to Abu Muhammad al-Fuq'asi, who said it addressing a woman whom he proposed to, enticing her to marry him, saying: "Are you interested in a hundred camels or more than that, since the herd begins at forty and goes up to whatever more you add, which he would make a dowry for her." He said: there is inversion in it, and the meaning is: "Are you interested in a hundred camels or more, of which the one who holds them, who drives them, is left some remainder," i.e., it remains, because he cannot drive them due to their number and strength, since they scatter from him. Then he said: "and the one who passes from you is departing," i.e., the giver of the offer of your womanhood, the giver of the exchange of your womanhood as a compensation, is departing, i.e., one who takes a return from you by marriage, which would be equal to what is offered by you. It is said: 'adtu ('a'ith) and 'udtu (a'awwidu): when one takes a compensation, and when one gives a compensation, i.e., pays. So his saying 'a'ith is from 'idtu (with kasra in the past), not from 'udtu (with damma in the past). As for the one who narrated "yughdiru," he meant "yatruku" (leaves), from their saying ghadartu al-shay' (I left the thing). Ibn Bari said: what is in his poem is "wal-'a'ith minka 'a'ith," i.e., the compensation from you is compensation, as you say: "the gift from you is a gift," meaning it has a place. End. I say: in the narration of this rajaz in Lisan it is "yas'ir," meaning "remains," in the place of "yughdir."]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾:

He, Mighty is His remembrance, says: And the creation will be presented before your Lord, O Muhammad, in rows.

﴿You have certainly come to Us as We created you the first time﴾. He, Mighty is His remembrance, says: It will be said to them when they are presented before God: "You have certainly come to Us, O people, living, in the same state as when We created you the first time." The saying "it will be said" is omitted from the speech, due to the listeners' knowledge that it is intended within the speech.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿But you claimed that We would not appoint for you an appointment﴾:

This statement came in the form of a report, while God addressed it to all of them, and what is meant by it is the specific group. That is because there will come to the Resurrection a group of prophets and messengers, and believers in God, His messengers, and the Resurrection, and it is known that it will not be said on that day to those who arrive there, from among the people who affirmed God's promise in this world and had certainty in it regarding the establishment of the Hour, but rather: "You claimed that We would not make for you the resurrection after death and the gathering to the Resurrection an appointment," and that this is only said to those who in this world denied the Resurrection and the establishment of the Hour.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it. And they will say, "Oh woe to us! What sort of book is this that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it?" And they will find what they did present. And your Lord does not wrong anyone.﴾ (18:49)

He, glorified is His mention, says: And God will place on that Day the books of His servants' deeds in their hands, so one takes his in his right hand and another takes his in his left hand. ﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾ He, glorified is His mention, says: you will see the criminals, the polytheists who associated others with God, fearful, meaning terrified and anxious about what is written in it of their evil deeds which they committed in the world, lest they be held accountable for them. ﴿And they will say, "Oh woe to us! What sort of book is this that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it"﴾ This means that when they read their book and see what has been written against them in it of the minor and major sins, they will cry out "Woe!" when they become certain of God's punishment, and will wail over the evil deeds they knew of, which their book has enumerated, and they will be unable to deny their accuracy.

As evidence:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "What sort of book is this that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it." The people complained, as you hear, of the enumeration, and no one complained of injustice. So beware of trivial sins, for they gather upon their doer until they destroy him. It has been related to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to give an example for them, saying: It is like a people who set out traveling until they halted in a desert wasteland, and the people's meal was prepared, so each man went out to gather firewood. One man would bring a stick, another would bring a stick, until they gathered a great pile and kindled a fire. Likewise, a small sin gathers upon its doer until it destroys him. It was also said that by "small" in this context he meant laughter.

Mention of those who said this:

Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Musa narrated to us, from al-Zayyal ibn Amr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding "leaves nothing small or great": he said, "Laughter."

Ahmad ibn Hazim narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: My mother Hammadah daughter of Muhammad narrated to me, saying: I heard my father Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman say, concerning this verse, in the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "What sort of book is this that leaves nothing small or great but has enumerated it," that the small thing is laughter.

By His saying: "What sort of book is this" he means: what is the matter with this book? "Leaves nothing small or great" means: it leaves behind none of our sins and deeds, neither small nor great. "But has enumerated it" means: except that it has preserved it. "And they will find what they did present" means: the deeds they did in the world are present in that book of theirs, recorded and fixed, so they will be repaid with the like of their evil deeds, and good deeds will be repaid by God with what He recompenses them. "And your Lord does not wrong anyone" means: your Lord, O Muhammad, does not repay anyone with other than what they deserve; He repays good only to the people of good, and evil only to the people of evil, and that is justice.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 50:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord. Then will you take him and his descendants as allies other than Me while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is [that] exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾ (50)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says, admonishing these polytheists about the envy of Iblis toward their father and their teacher, and about what proceeded from him of arrogance and pride toward him when He commanded him to prostrate to him, and that [Iblis] has the same enmity and envy toward them as he had toward their father: ﴿And﴾ mention, O Muhammad, ﴿when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis﴾, whom these polytheists obey and whose command they follow, opposing the command of God. He did not prostrate out of arrogance toward God and envy of Adam. ﴿He was of the jinn﴾.

The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of His words ﴿He was of the jinn﴾. Some of them said: He was from a tribe called the jinn.

Others said: Rather, he was one of the treasurers of Paradise, and so he was ascribed to Paradise (al-jannah). Others said: Rather, he was said to be of the jinn because he was of the jinn who hid from the eyes of the children of Adam.

Mention of those who said that:
