You have already received an excuse from me﴾. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Musa was shy before Allah at that point."

* Abdullah ibn Abi Ziyad narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Hamza al-Zayyat, from Abu Ishaq, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned someone and prayed for him, he would begin with himself. One day he said: "The mercy of Allah be upon us and upon Musa. Had he remained with his companion, he would have seen the wonder. But he said: 'If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion. You have already received an excuse from me'" (doubled).

**The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food, but they refused to host them. Then they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright. [Moses] said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ (18:77)**

He, the Exalted, says: So Moses and the scholar (*ḥattā idhā atayā ahla qaryatin istaṭʿamā ahlahā*) went on until they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, but they did not feed them, and they asked them for hospitality. ﴿But they refused to host them. Then they found in it a wall about to collapse﴾.

He says: They found in the town a wall that was about to fall and collapse. It is said of this verb: *inqaḍḍa al-dār* (the house collapsed) when it was torn down and fell. From it comes *inqiḍāḍ al-kawkab* (the falling of a star), which is its fall and departure from its place. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"fa-nqaḍḍa ka-l-kawkabi al-durriyyi munṣilitan"*
("So it plunged like a shining star, swooping down.")[[This is the first half of a verse by Dhu al-Rummah. In *Lisan al-ʿArab* (under *q-ḍ-ḍ*): *inqaḍḍa al-jidār* means the wall cracked without falling; it is also said that *inqaḍḍa* means it fell. In the revealed text, "*fa-wajadā fīhā jidāran yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa*" is counted by Abū ʿUbayd and others as a biliteral-root form, while Abū ʿAlī took it as triliteral from *n-q-ḍ*, so that in his view it is the form *ifʿalla* with a doubled final consonant. In *Tahdhib*: *yanqaḍḍa* means *yankasir* (breaks), as in *qaḍaḍtu al-shayʾ* (I crushed the thing) when one pounds it. *Al-munṣilit* means the one who hastens, of anything.]]

It has been related from Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar that he recited it as ﴿*yurīdu an yanqāḍḍa*﴾ (it wants to be torn away).

The scholars of the Arabic language have differed concerning the meaning of this reading when it is recited thus. Some of the Basran scholars said: *yanqāḍḍa* means that it is uprooted from its base and splits apart, in the same way as they say *qad inqāḍat al-sinn* (the tooth has come loose), meaning it split and was pulled from its root. It is said: *firāq ka-qayḍ al-sinn* (a separation like the falling out of a tooth), meaning its people do not reunite.

Some of the Kufan scholars[[This is al-Farrāʾ (see his *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān*, University of Chicago microfilm 24059, p. 190).]] said: *al-inqiyāḍ* is a split along the length of the wall, in the lining of a well, and in a man's tooth. It is said: *qad inqāḍat sinnuhu* (his tooth has split lengthwise).

It was also said that the town whose people Moses and his companion asked for food and who refused to host them was Ayla.

Those who said this:

⁕ Al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad al-Dharrāʿ told me, saying: ʿImrān ibn al-Muʿtamir, the companion of al-Karābīsī, told us, saying: Ḥammād Abū Ṣāliḥ told us, from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, who said: "They frequented Ayla, for few who come to it return disappointed. It is the land that refused to host them, and it is the farthest land of God from the sky."

⁕ Bishr told us, saying: Yazīd told us, saying: Saʿīd told us, from Qatādah, concerning His words ﴿So they set out until, when they came to a town﴾, and he recited up to His words ﴿you could have taken a wage for it﴾: "It was the worst of towns, which did not host guests and did not recognize the right of the traveler."

The scholars of the Arabic language differed concerning the meaning of the words of God, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa﴾ (it wants to fall). Some of the Basrans said: The wall has no will, nor does the ruin (*al-mawāt*), but when it is in this state of decay, that is its will. This is like the Arabs' saying about something else:

*"yurīdu al-rumḥu ṣadra Abī Barrāʾin wa-yarghabu ʿan dimāʾi Banī ʿUqayl"*
("The spear wants the chest of Abū Barrāʾ, and turns away from the blood of the Banū ʿUqayl.")[[This verse is among the evidences cited by Abū ʿUbayda in *Majāz al-Qurʾān* (1:410), where he said regarding the words "*yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa*": the wall has no will, nor does death, but when it is in this state of decay, that is its will. This is the speech of the Arabs about other things too. Al-Ḥārithī said: "The spear wants..." (the verse). In *Lisan al-ʿArab* (under *r-w-d*): His words, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿*fa-wajadā fīhā jidāran yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa fa-aqāmahu*﴾ (they found there a wall wanting to fall, so he set it up): he set it up, i.e., al-Khiḍr, and said "wants." Will (*irāda*) properly belongs to animals, and the wall does not have a true will. But because its readiness to fall has become apparent, as the actions of those who will are apparent, the wall was described with will, when the two cases are one. Such usage is common in the language and in poetry. Al-Rāʿī said: "In a desert whose headlands shook with it, shaking like axes when they want to cut..." And another said: "The spear wants the chest of Abū Barrāʾ..." (the verse).]]

Another of them said: God addressed the people in terms they understand. He said: When it drew near to falling, it was permissible to say "it wants to fall." He said: Like it is His words ﴿*takādu al-samāwātu yatafaṭṭarna*﴾ (the heavens almost split apart), and the saying "I almost fly for joy," though you have not come near that and have not intended it; rather, it is because of the great importance of the matter to you.

Some of the Kufans said: It is among the speech of the Arabs to say: "The wall wants to fall." He said: Like this is the saying of the poet:

*"Inna dahran yalaffu shamlī bi-jumlin / la-zamānun yahummu bi-l-iḥsān"*
("Indeed, a time that gathers my scattered affairs with one who is dear to me is a time that intends kindness.")[[This verse is among al-Farrāʾ's evidences in *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān* (folio 190 of the University of Chicago microfilm). He said: "*yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa*": It is asked: how can a wall want to fall? This is among the speech of the Arabs, who say: "The wall wants to fall." Similar is God's word: ﴿*wa-lammā sakata ʿan Mūsā al-ghaḍab*﴾ (when the anger subsided from Moses). Anger does not "become silent"; rather, its possessor falls silent, and its meaning is "it subsided." Also His word: ﴿*fa-idhā ʿazama al-amr*﴾ (when the matter is resolved): the matter is resolved only by its people. Another poet said: "Indeed, a time..." (the verse). Another said: "My camel complained to me..." (the verse), which will come later. The camel did not complain; rather it was said of it as though, if it could speak, it would say that. Likewise is ʿAntarah's saying: "And he recoiled from the impact of spears in his breast..." (the verse), which will come later. Abū ʿUbayda also said in *Majāz al-Qurʾān* (1:411): *jāza "an yanqaḍḍa"* is a figurative usage meaning "it falls." It is said: "The house collapsed," when it was torn down and fell. Some read *an yanqāḍḍa*, and its figurative meaning is that it is uprooted from its base and splits, like the saying: "the tooth has come loose," i.e., it has split and been pulled from its root.]]

And another's saying:

*"Yashkū ilayya jamalī ṭūla al-surā / ṣabran jamīlan fa-kilānā mubtalā"*
("My camel complains to me of the length of the journey: 'Patience, beautiful patience, for both of us is tested.'")[[The verse was discussed in the previous evidence; it is also among al-Farrāʾ's evidences in *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān*.]]

He said: The camel did not complain; rather, it was spoken of as though, if it spoke, it would say that. He said: Likewise is ʿAntarah's saying:

*"Wa-zawwara min waqʿi al-qanā bi-labānihi / wa-shakā ilayya bi-ʿabratin wa-taḥammuḥi"*
("He recoiled from the impact of spears on his chest, and complained to me with a sob and a neigh.")[[The verse was discussed in the previous evidence. *Labān* means chest; *qanā* is the plural of *qanāh*, which is the spear. It is among al-Farrāʾ's evidences.]]

He said: Among this is God's word, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿*wa-lammā sakata ʿan Mūsā al-ghaḍab*﴾ (when the anger subsided from Moses). Anger does not fall silent; rather, its possessor falls silent. Its meaning is: it subsided.

* *

And His words: ﴿*fa-idhā ʿazama al-amr*﴾ (when the matter is resolved).

Only its people resolve it. Another of them said: This is among the most eloquent of the Arabs' speech. He said: The wall's "will" is its inclination, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "*Lā tarāʾā nāruhumā*" (Their fires should not see each other). That means there are two fires, each of which is in a place where, if a person stood there, he would see the other from nearby. He said: This is like God's word about the idols: ﴿*wa-tarāhum yanẓurūna ilayka wa-hum lā yubṣirūn*﴾ (You see them looking at you, yet they do not see). He said: The Arabs say: "My house looks at the house of so-and-so," meaning that the distance between them is small. He cited the verse of Dhu al-Rummah describing a pool or an abandoned dwelling:

*"Qad kāda aw qad hamma bi-l-buyūd"*
("It almost, or nearly, came to ruin.")[[This is a verse in *rajaz* meter by Dhu al-Rummah. *Al-buyūd* is the verbal noun of *bāda yabīdu*, meaning to perish. The evidence in it is like the evidences before it.]]

He said: He made it "intend," but its meaning is that it had changed through decay. What we say about this is that God, the Mighty, in His kindness, made speech among His creatures a mercy from Him toward them, so that some might make clear to others what is in their hearts, which their eyes cannot perceive. The Arabs have understood the meaning of the speaker's words:

*"Fī mahmahin qalaqat bihi hāmātuhā / qalaqa al-fuʾūsi idhā aradna nuṣūlā"*
("In a desert whose headlands trembled with it, trembling like axes when they wish to cut.")[[This verse is by al-Rāʿī, and its discussion has been given earlier in more than one place.]]

It is understood that axes are not described with what is described with the human beings' inner thoughts of the heart, even though they are described as "wanting." And the speaker's meaning is known from his saying:

*"Ka-mithli hayli al-naqā ṭāfa al-mushāt bihi / yanhālu ḥīnan wa-yanhāhu al-thará ḥīnan"*
("Like the heaping of a sand dune, which walkers circled around, it pours down at times, and the damp earth holds it back at times.")[[*Hāl al-turāb wa-l-raml hīlan* means it poured; *ahālahu* means he made it pour, and the verb *fa-nhāla* describes it as flowing down. *Al-naqā* is a heap of clean sand. The verse is like the evidences before it, in that its words "the damp earth holds it back" mean the damp earth holds it in its heaping, making that equal to its prohibition of falling, though damp earth neither forbids nor commands. But it came thus in the language of the Arabs, just as God's word in the Qur'an came: "wants to fall." Its meaning was made clear by what is sufficient in the evidences just before.]]

He did not mean that the damp earth spoke; rather, he meant that it was soaked with dew, which prevented it from pouring down, so its holding it back from that was like the prohibition of those who speak, so it does not pour. Likewise is His word: ﴿*jidāran yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa*﴾ (a wall that wants to fall). You know that its meaning is that it was about to fall or collapse. God, may His praise be exalted, addressed through the Qur'an those to whom He sent the revelation in their own tongue, and they understood what was meant, even if the dull and the blind were confused in understanding it, and the ignorant and the stupid went astray in it.

* *

And His words: ﴿*fa-aqāmahu*﴾ (so he set it up).

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: He tore it down, then sat to build it.

⁕ Ibn Ḥumayd told us of that, saying: Salamah told us, saying: Ibn Isḥāq told us, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUmārah, from al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUtaybah, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Others said about it:

⁕ Al-Qāsim told us, saying: Al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Ḥajjāj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, concerning ﴿*fa-wajadā fīhā jidāran yurīdu an yanqaḍḍa*﴾: "He raised the wall with his hand, and it became straight."

The correct statement on this is that God, the Mighty, informed us that the companion of Moses and Moses found a wall that wanted to fall, and the companion of Moses set it up, meaning he corrected its lean until it returned upright.

It is possible that this happened through repair after demolition, and it is possible that it happened through his lifting it with his hand, so that it straightened by God's power, and its lean was removed by His kindness. There is no evidence from the Book of God, nor any reliable report, deciding which of these occurred.

* *

And His words: ﴿*qāla law shi'ta la-ttakhadhta ʿalayhi ajran*﴾ (He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it").

He means: Moses said to his companion: "If you had wished, you would not have set up this people's wall until they gave you a wage for setting it up." Some of them said: What Moses meant by the wage in his words ﴿*law shi'ta la-takhadhta ʿalayhi ajran*﴾ was hospitality, that is, that they would host us, since they had refused to host us. Others said: He meant by it the compensation and reward for setting up the leaning wall.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of Medina and Kufa read ﴿*la-takhadhta*﴾ (you would have taken), with the *ta* pointed as an *ifʿal* form of *akhadha* (to take), and some of the Basrans read ﴿*la-takhadhta*﴾ (you would have taken) with the *ta* lightened and the *kh* vowelled with a kasra, and its original form is *la-ftaʿalta*, except that they treated the *t* as though it belonged to the root of the word, because for them the discussion concerns the forms *faʿala* and *yafʿalu*: *takhidha fulānun kadhā yatkhadhuhu takhdhan* (so-and-so took such-and-such), and it is a dialect reported for the tribe of Hudhayl. One of the poets said:

*"Wa-qad takhidhat rijlī ladā janbi gharzihā / nasīfan ka-afḥūṣi al-qaṭāti al-muṭarriqi"*
("My leg has been marked near her saddle-girth with a scar like the scratched nest of the sand-grouse that is broken with traces.")[[This verse is by al-Mumazziq al-ʿAbdī, whose name is Shaʾs ibn Nihār, an ancient pre-Islamic poet. It is among Abū ʿUbayda's evidences in *Majāz al-Qurʾān* (1:411), where he said: "*law shi'ta la-takhadhta ʿalayhi ajran*": the *kh* is kasra, and its meaning is the meaning of *akhadha*, so its articulation is like *faʿala yafʿalu* (from the pattern of *fariḥa yafraḥu*). Al-Mumazziq al-ʿAbdī (of ʿAbd al-Qays) said: "And my leg has been marked..." (the verse). In *Lisan al-ʿArab*: the *gharz* for a camel is like the stirrup for a mule, and it is where the rider places his foot when mounting. *Al-afḥūṣ* is the resting place of the sand-grouse, because it scrapes the place and then lays its eggs in it; the same is true of the hen. Al-Mumazziq said: "And my leg has been..." (the verse). *Al-nasīf* is the mark left on the camel's side by the bite of the saddle-girth, from a bite or from rubbing of fur. *Al-muṭarriq* describes the sand-grouse. It is said: "The woman gave birth through difficulty" when half the child came out and then stuck; it is said: "She is in difficulty, then she was delivered." It was also said that the *taṭrīq* of the sand-grouse is when it searches for a place for its eggs, as if it makes a path for them.]]

The correct statement on this, in my view, is that they are two well-known dialects of the Arabs with the same meaning. Whichever of the two the reader recites is correct; however, I prefer reciting it with the *ta* doubled as *la-takhadhta*, because it is the more eloquent and more famous of the two dialects and the more common on the tongues of the Arabs.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 78–79:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience.﴾ (18:78)

He, the Exalted, says: The companion of Musa said to Musa: "This is what you said, when you said, ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾." ﴿Parting between me and you﴾ means: separation between me and you, i.e., one who separates me from you.

﴿I will inform you﴾ means: I will tell you ﴿of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾ means: of what the outcome of my actions that I did will lead to, so that you could not refrain from asking about them and from objecting to me concerning them. And God knows best.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it, and there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force.﴾ (18:79)

He says: As for my act concerning the boat, it was because it belonged to poor people (﴿who worked on the sea, so I wished to damage it﴾) by the hole I made in it.

As related:

Ibn Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu Asim narrated to us, he said: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾, he said: "I would make a hole in it."

Al-Harith narrated to us, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, the same.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and there was behind them a king﴾

"Behind them" means in front of them and before them, a king.

As related:

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada: ﴿and there was behind them a king﴾. Qatada said: "In front of them. Do you not see that He says: ﴿Behind them is Jahannam﴾ (14:16), and it is before them."

Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: "In the reading it was: ﴿and there was in front of them a king who seizes every sound boat by force.﴾" It has been mentioned from Ibn Uyayna, from Amr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, that he recited it: "and there was in front of them a king."

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Some scholars of the Arabic language have counted "wara'" (behind) among the words with opposite meanings (addad), claiming that it can refer to what is in front of a person and to what is behind him, and they cited for the soundness of this view the verse of the poet:

Do the sons of Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people, Tamim, and the wilderness are behind me [[The verse is by Siwar ibn al-Mudarrib (al-Lisan: w-r-y). It is among the evidences cited by Abu Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an (1:412), where he said, explaining the verse ﴿and there was behind them a king﴾: i.e., in front of them. He said: "Do the sons of Marwan... the verse": i.e., in front of me. End. In al-Lisan (w-r-y): His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and there was behind them a king﴾ means in front of them. Ibn Bari said: similar to it is the saying of Siwar ibn al-Mudarrib: "Do the sons of Marwan... the verse".]]

meaning "in front of me." But they have overlooked the correct meaning in this. Rather, what is before a person is called "behind me" because you are behind him: you encounter him just as he encounters you. So when he is encountering you, it is as if he is behind you and you are in front of him. Some grammarians of Kufa did not permit saying of a man in front of you, "he is behind me," nor, when he is behind you, saying "he is in front of me." They say that this is permitted only with regard to times and periods, as in the saying of the speaker: "Behind you is a severe cold, and in front of you is severe heat," because you are behind it; it is permissible because it is something that comes, so when it reaches you it becomes behind you, and when you reach it, it becomes in front of you. They said: therefore both usages are permissible.

* *

And His saying: ﴿who seized every boat by force﴾

Someone may say: What did the damaging of the boat by this scholar, which he boarded, avail its owners, since because of its damage he would seize all boats, both the defective and the non-defective? And what was the basis of his excuse for damaging it, that he damaged it because there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force? It is said: The meaning of that is that he seizes every sound boat by force, and leaves aside every defective one; not that he would take both its sound and unsound boats. If someone says: What is the evidence that this is so? It is said: His saying: ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾. Thereby it is made clear that he damaged it only because a defective one is not targeted, so this suffices instead of saying: "and there was behind them a king who seized every sound boat by force," and in some readings it is so.

Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, who said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every good boat by force.﴾

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: al-Hasan ibn Dinar narrated to me, from al-Hakam ibn Uyayna, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every good boat by force.﴾ And I only damaged it so that I might turn him away from it.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij: ﴿and there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force﴾. When they left it, they repaired it with pitch and benefited from it. Ibn Juraij said: Wahb ibn Sulayman informed me, from Shu'ayb al-Jaba'i, that the name of the man who seized every boat by force was Hudad ibn Budad.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 80–81:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers, so We feared that he would overwhelm them with rebellion and disbelief. (80) So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion. (81)﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, while his parents were believers. "So We knew that he would overwhelm them" means: he would cover them with "rebellion," which is arrogance toward Allah, and "disbelief" in Him. The interpreters have said what we have said regarding this, and it has been mentioned in some of the readings (ḥurūf). As for the boy, he was a disbeliever.

Those who said this:

* Al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah, regarding ﴿And as for the boy, he was a disbeliever﴾, in the reading of Ubayy, "and his parents were believers" ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: ﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers﴾ and he was a disbeliever in some readings. And His saying "fa-khashīnā" (so We feared); in the codex of ʿAbd Allah it is: ﴿So your Lord feared that he would overwhelm them with rebellion and disbelief﴾.

* ʿAmr ibn ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: Abū Qutaybah narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn ʿAbbās al-Hamdānī narrated to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The boy whom al-Khiḍr killed was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever."

Khashya (fear) and khawf (dread) are taken by the Arabs to mean suspicion (ẓann), while these words are directed to the meaning of knowledge of a thing perceived not through the senses or direct observation. We have explained this with its evidence in another place, in a way that suffices without repeating it.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: the meaning of His saying "khashīnā" in this place is "we disliked," because Allah does not fear. In some readings it is "fa-khāfa Rabbuka" (so your Lord feared), and he said: it is like the saying "I feared that the two men would support (themselves)," while he does not fear from that more than that he dislikes it for them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them﴾

The readers differed in reading this. A group of the readers of Mecca, Medina and Basra read: ﴿fa-aradnā an yubaddilahumā rabbuhumā﴾ (with the doubled dāl). Some of them argued for the soundness of this by saying that it was found doubled throughout the Qur'an, such as the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted (fa-baddala)﴾ and His saying ﴿And when We substitute (wa-idhā baddalnā) a verse in place of a verse﴾, so they joined His saying ﴿so We wished that their Lord would replace them﴾ to these. The majority of the readers of Kufa read: ﴿fa-aradnā an yubdilahumā﴾ with the single dāl. Some of the grammarians who read it thus said: abdala yubdilu (with lightness) and baddala yubaddilu (with doubling) have one meaning.

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that they are two readings close in meaning, and a group of readers have read each of them, so whichever of the two the reader recites, he is correct. It has been said that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, replaced the parents of the boy whom the companion of Moses killed with a girl.

Those who said this:

* Yaʿqūb narrated to me, saying: Hāshim ibn al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Mubārak ibn Saʿīd narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Qays, regarding His saying: ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾, said: It has reached me that it was a girl.

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Sulaymān ibn Umayyah informed me that he heard Yaʿqūb ibn ʿĀṣim say: They were given in place of the boy a girl.

Ibn Jurayj said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUthmān ibn Khuthaym also informed me that he heard Saʿīd ibn Jubayr say: They were given in place of the boy a girl.

Others said: Their Lord replaced them with a Muslim boy.

Those who said this:

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Abū Jurayj: ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾, he said: His mother was pregnant at that time with a Muslim boy.

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Abū Sufyān narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, that he mentioned the boy whom al-Khiḍr killed, and said: his parents rejoiced in him when he was born and grieved for him when he was killed; and had he lived, there would have been their ruin in him. So let a man be content with the decree of Allah, for Allah's decree for the believer in what he dislikes is better for him than His decree in what he loves.

* *

And His saying: ﴿better than him in purity﴾

He says: better than the boy whom he killed in righteousness and religion.

As:

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: ﴿so We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity﴾, he said: Islam.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾

The interpreters differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: the meaning of that is: and nearer in compassion toward his parents and more dutiful to them than the one who was killed.

Those who said this:

* al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾: more dutiful to his parents.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾, that is, nearer in goodness.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: and nearer that his parents would have compassion for him than for the one who was killed.

Those who said this:

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾: more compassionate toward him than toward the one whom al-Khiḍr killed.

Some of the grammarians used to interpret it: "and nearer that they would have compassion for him." Al-Rukhm is a verbal noun of raḥimtu, one says: raḥimtuhu raḥmah and ruḥman. Some of the Basrans said: it is from raḥim (womb) and kinship. It may also be said ruḥm and ruḥum, like ʿusr and ʿusur, and halk and haluk, and he cited for this the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

*wa-lam tuʿawwaj ruḥmu man taʿawwajā* [[The line is from the rajaz meter and belongs to al-ʿAjjāj (his Dīwān, Leipzig ed. 1903, p. 10). It is cited by Abū ʿUbayda in Majāz al-Qurʾān (1:413) in explaining His saying "and nearer in compassion": its meaning is the meaning of raḥman, like ʿusr and yusr, and halk and halk. Al-ʿAjjāj said: "wa-lam tuʿawwaj... the line." In Lisān al-ʿArab (r-ḥ-m): al-raḥm, with a ḍamma, is mercy. In the revelation: "and nearer in compassion," and it is read ruḥman (with two ḍammas). Abū Isḥāq said: that is, nearer in tenderness and closer in kinship. Al-raḥm (with the ra doubled in both, with the ḥāʾ quiescent or ḍammed) in the language means tenderness and mercy.]]

There is no sense of "womb" (raḥim) in this place, because the one whom Allah replaced his parents with was a child for the parents of the one killed; so their kinship to his parents and their nearness to him in the womb are the same. Rather, the meaning of that is: and nearer than the one killed to have compassion for his parents and to be dutiful to them, as Qatādah said. The speech may also be directed to mean "and nearer that they would have compassion for him," but no interpreter has interpreted it thus, and since no one has said it, the correct view is what we have said, for the reasons we have explained.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 80–81:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers, so We feared that he would overwhelm them with rebellion and disbelief. (80) So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion. (81)﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: As for the boy, he was a disbeliever, while his parents were believers. "So We knew that he would overwhelm them" means: he would cover them with "rebellion," which is arrogance toward Allah, and "disbelief" in Him. The interpreters have said what we have said regarding this, and it has been mentioned in some of the readings (ḥurūf). As for the boy, he was a disbeliever.

Those who said this:

* Al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah, regarding ﴿And as for the boy, he was a disbeliever﴾, in the reading of Ubayy, "and his parents were believers" ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: ﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers﴾ and he was a disbeliever in some readings. And His saying "fa-khashīnā" (so We feared); in the codex of ʿAbd Allah it is: ﴿So your Lord feared that he would overwhelm them with rebellion and disbelief﴾.

* ʿAmr ibn ʿAlī narrated to us, saying: Abū Qutaybah narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn ʿAbbās al-Hamdānī narrated to us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The boy whom al-Khiḍr killed was sealed on the day he was sealed as a disbeliever."

Khashya (fear) and khawf (dread) are taken by the Arabs to mean suspicion (ẓann), while these words are directed to the meaning of knowledge of a thing perceived not through the senses or direct observation. We have explained this with its evidence in another place, in a way that suffices without repeating it.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: the meaning of His saying "khashīnā" in this place is "we disliked," because Allah does not fear. In some readings it is "fa-khāfa Rabbuka" (so your Lord feared), and he said: it is like the saying "I feared that the two men would support (themselves)," while he does not fear from that more than that he dislikes it for them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them﴾

The readers differed in reading this. A group of the readers of Mecca, Medina and Basra read: ﴿fa-aradnā an yubaddilahumā rabbuhumā﴾ (with the doubled dāl). Some of them argued for the soundness of this by saying that it was found doubled throughout the Qur'an, such as the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But those who did wrong substituted (fa-baddala)﴾ and His saying ﴿And when We substitute (wa-idhā baddalnā) a verse in place of a verse﴾, so they joined His saying ﴿so We wished that their Lord would replace them﴾ to these. The majority of the readers of Kufa read: ﴿fa-aradnā an yubdilahumā﴾ with the single dāl. Some of the grammarians who read it thus said: abdala yubdilu (with lightness) and baddala yubaddilu (with doubling) have one meaning.

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that they are two readings close in meaning, and a group of readers have read each of them, so whichever of the two the reader recites, he is correct. It has been said that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, replaced the parents of the boy whom the companion of Moses killed with a girl.

Those who said this:

* Yaʿqūb narrated to me, saying: Hāshim ibn al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Mubārak ibn Saʿīd narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Qays, regarding His saying: ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾, said: It has reached me that it was a girl.

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Sulaymān ibn Umayyah informed me that he heard Yaʿqūb ibn ʿĀṣim say: They were given in place of the boy a girl.

Ibn Jurayj said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUthmān ibn Khuthaym also informed me that he heard Saʿīd ibn Jubayr say: They were given in place of the boy a girl.

Others said: Their Lord replaced them with a Muslim boy.

Those who said this:

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Abū Jurayj: ﴿So We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾, he said: His mother was pregnant at that time with a Muslim boy.

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Abū Sufyān narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, that he mentioned the boy whom al-Khiḍr killed, and said: his parents rejoiced in him when he was born and grieved for him when he was killed; and had he lived, there would have been their ruin in him. So let a man be content with the decree of Allah, for Allah's decree for the believer in what he dislikes is better for him than His decree in what he loves.

* *

And His saying: ﴿better than him in purity﴾

He says: better than the boy whom he killed in righteousness and religion.

As:

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: ﴿so We wished that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity﴾, he said: Islam.

* *

And His saying: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾

The interpreters differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: the meaning of that is: and nearer in compassion toward his parents and more dutiful to them than the one who was killed.

Those who said this:

* al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾: more dutiful to his parents.

* Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾, that is, nearer in goodness.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: and nearer that his parents would have compassion for him than for the one who was killed.

Those who said this:

* al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾: more compassionate toward him than toward the one whom al-Khiḍr killed.

Some of the grammarians used to interpret it: "and nearer that they would have compassion for him." Al-Rukhm is a verbal noun of raḥimtu, one says: raḥimtuhu raḥmah and ruḥman. Some of the Basrans said: it is from raḥim (womb) and kinship. It may also be said ruḥm and ruḥum, like ʿusr and ʿusur, and halk and haluk, and he cited for this the verse of al-ʿAjjāj:

*wa-lam tuʿawwaj ruḥmu man taʿawwajā* [[The line is from the rajaz meter and belongs to al-ʿAjjāj (his Dīwān, Leipzig ed. 1903, p. 10). It is cited by Abū ʿUbayda in Majāz al-Qurʾān (1:413) in explaining His saying "and nearer in compassion": its meaning is the meaning of raḥman, like ʿusr and yusr, and halk and halk. Al-ʿAjjāj said: "wa-lam tuʿawwaj... the line." In Lisān al-ʿArab (r-ḥ-m): al-raḥm, with a ḍamma, is mercy. In the revelation: "and nearer in compassion," and it is read ruḥman (with two ḍammas). Abū Isḥāq said: that is, nearer in tenderness and closer in kinship. Al-raḥm (with the ra doubled in both, with the ḥāʾ quiescent or ḍammed) in the language means tenderness and mercy.]]

There is no sense of "womb" (raḥim) in this place, because the one whom Allah replaced his parents with was a child for the parents of the one killed; so their kinship to his parents and their nearness to him in the womb are the same. Rather, the meaning of that is: and nearer than the one killed to have compassion for his parents and to be dutiful to them, as Qatādah said. The speech may also be directed to mean "and nearer that they would have compassion for him," but no interpreter has interpreted it thus, and since no one has said it, the correct view is what we have said, for the reasons we have explained.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 82:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. And I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience.﴾ (82)

Exalted is His remembrance, relating the words of Moses' companion: As for the wall that I set up, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding that treasure. Some of them said: it was scrolls (suhuf) containing buried knowledge.

Those who said this:

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, he said: my father related to me, he said: my paternal uncle related to me, he said: my father related to me from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: beneath it was a treasure of knowledge.

- Ya'qub related to us, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Husayn informed us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: it was a treasure of knowledge.

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: Abd al-Rahman related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: knowledge.

- Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: Abu Dawud related to us, he said: Shu'ba related to us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: knowledge.

- Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, he said: Abu Asim related to us, he said: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, he said: al-Hasan related to us, he said: Warqa' related to us, all from Abu Najih, from Mujahid, regarding his saying ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: scrolls for the two boys in which there was knowledge.

- al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, he said: scrolls of knowledge.

- Ahmad ibn Hazim al-Ghifari related to me, he said: Hunada bint Malik al-Shaybaniyya related to us, she said: I heard my companion Hammad ibn al-Walid al-Thaqafi say: I heard Ja'far ibn Muhammad say regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: two and a half lines, the third was not completed: "I marvel at the one who is certain of provision, how he toils; I marvel at the one who is certain of reckoning, how he is heedless; and I marvel at the one who is certain of death, how he rejoices." And He has said: ﴿And if it should be the weight of a mustard seed, We would bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾. She said: and it was mentioned that they were preserved by the righteousness of their father, and no righteousness of theirs was mentioned; and between them and the father by whose merit they were preserved there were seven generations; and he was a weaver.

- Ya'qub related to me, he said: Ibn Habib ibn Nadba related to us, he said: Salama ibn Muhammad related to us, from Nu'aym al-'Anbari, who was among the companions of al-Hasan, he said: I heard al-Hasan say regarding the saying: ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: a tablet of gold on which was written: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I marvel at one who believes, how he grieves; I marvel at one who is certain of death, how he rejoices; I marvel at one who knows the world and its turning over its people, how he finds rest in it. There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

- Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salama related to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq related to me, from al-Hasan ibn Imara, from al-Hakam, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to say: the treasure was nothing but knowledge.

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ibn Uyayna informed us, from Humayd, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: scrolls of knowledge.

- Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Abd Allah ibn Ayyash informed me, from Umar, client of Ghufra [[Umar ibn Abd Allah al-Madani, client of Ghufra, with the letter ghayn pointed; it is said she was the sister of Bilal ibn Rabah. He died in the year 145 AH (al-Khazraji).]], he said: the treasure that Allah mentioned in the surah in which the Cave is mentioned, ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾, was a solid tablet of gold, on which was written: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Wonderful is the one who knows death and then laughs; wonderful is the one who is certain of destiny and then toils; wonderful is the one who is certain of death and then feels secure. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.

Others said: rather, it was hoarded wealth.

Those who said this:

- Ya'qub related to me, he said: Hushaym related to us, he said: Husayn informed us, from Ikrima: ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: a treasure of wealth.

- Ibn Bashshar related to us, he said: Abd al-Rahman related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Husayn, from Ikrima, the like of it.

- Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, he said: Abu Dawud related to us, from Shu'ba, he said: Abu Husayn informed me, from Ikrima, the like of it. Shu'ba said: we did not hear it from him.

- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada: ﴿and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: he said: wealth belonging to them. Qatada said: the treasure was made lawful for those before us and made unlawful for us; for Allah makes lawful from His command what He wills, and makes unlawful, and these are the sunan and the obligations; He makes lawful for one community and makes unlawful for another; but Allah does not accept from anyone who has passed away except sincerity and monotheism toward Him.

The most correct of the two interpretations in this matter is the view stated by Ikrima, because what is known in the speech of the Arabs is that "kanz" is the name for wealth that is hoarded, and that everything hoarded is called a kanz; interpretation is directed toward the most common usage of those addressed by the revelation, unless there is evidence requiring that it be directed otherwise, for reasons we have explained in other places.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And their father had been righteous, so your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity﴾

He says: your Lord intended that they should attain and reach their strength and maturity, and then extract their hidden treasure, which lay beneath the wall you had set up, as a mercy from your Lord toward them. That is, I did this with the wall as a mercy from your Lord to the two orphans.

Ibn Abbas used to say about this:

- Musa ibn Abd al-Rahman related to me, he said: Abu Usama related to us, from Mis'ar, from Abd al-Malik ibn Maysara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, he said: Ibn Abbas said regarding His saying ﴿and their father had been righteous﴾: they were preserved by the righteousness of their father, and no righteousness of theirs was mentioned.

- Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Sufyan related to us, from Mis'ar, from Abd al-Malik ibn Maysara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, the like of it.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾

He says: and, O Moses, I did not do all that you saw me do by my own opinion or from my own self; rather I did it by the command of Allah to me.

As in:

- Bishr related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾: he was a servant under command, so he proceeded by the command of Allah.

- Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord﴾: I did not do all of it of my own self.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿That is the interpretation of that about which you could not have patience﴾

He says: this which I have mentioned to you of the reasons for which I did the actions you disapproved of is their interpretation, that is, what those actions lead to and return to, the actions about which you could not refrain from asking me and could not have patience in disapproving of them.

These stories which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) about Moses and his companion are a discipline from Him to him, and a directive to him to refrain from hastening the punishment of the polytheists who denied him and mocked him and his Book, and an informing from Him to him that His actions toward them, though they may proceed in what the eyes see in a manner that may sometimes proceed similarly toward His friends, their interpretation will ultimately lead to the conditions of His enemies in them, just as the actions of Moses' companion occurred contrary to soundness in appearance in Moses' view, since he did not know their outcomes, while they were proceeding in soundness in reality and leading to rectitude in the end. The following indicates the soundness of this: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy. Were He to seize them for what they have earned, He would have hastened for them the punishment; but for them is an appointed time from which they will find no refuge other than Him.﴾ Then He followed that with the story of Moses and his companion, teaching His Prophet that His, exalted is His majesty, leaving the polytheists without hastening punishment for them is not without consideration on His part for them, even if that may seem, to one without knowledge of what Allah is arranging concerning them, to be neglect; for their interpretation leads to their destruction and ruin by the sword in this world, and to their deserving from Allah in the Hereafter everlasting disgrace.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verses 83–85:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say, "I will recite to you about him a remembrance."﴾ [18:83] And again: ﴿And they ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say, "I will recite to you about him a remembrance."﴾ [18:83] ﴿Indeed, We established him upon the earth and gave him of every thing a way.﴾ [18:84] ﴿So he followed a way.﴾ [18:85]

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "And they ask you, O Muhammad, these polytheists, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, what his affair was and what his story was. So say to them: ﴿I will recite to you about him a remembrance﴾," meaning: I will relate to you a report about him. It has been said that those who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn were a people of the People of the Book.

As for the report that those who asked him about that were the polytheists of his people, we have already mentioned it before.

As for the report that those who asked him were a people of the People of the Book, Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn Habbab narrated to us from Ibn Lahi'ah, who said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An'am narrated to me, from two shaykhs of Tujayb. One of them said to his companion: "Come, let us go to Uqbah ibn Amir and talk." They both went to him and said, "We have come so that you may tell us." He said: "One day I was serving the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I went out from his presence, and a group of the People of the Book met me and said: 'We want to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so seek permission for us to see him.' I entered upon him and informed him, and he said: 'What is it to me and to them? I have no knowledge except what Allah has taught me.'" Then he said: "Pour water for me," and he performed ablution and then prayed. He said: "When he finished, I recognised the joy in his face. Then he said: 'Bring them in to me, and whoever of my companions you see.'" They entered and stood before him, and he said: "If you wish, ask, and I will inform you about what you find written in your book, and if you wish, I will inform you." They said: "Yes, inform us." He said: "You came to ask me about Dhu al-Qarnayn and what you find in your book: he was a young man from the Romans. He came and built a city, Alexandria in Egypt. When he finished, an angel came to him and lifted him up into the sky and said to him: 'What do you see?' He said: 'I see my city and cities.' Then he lifted him again and said: 'What do you see?' He said: 'I see my city.' Then he lifted him and said: 'What do you see?' He said: 'I see the earth.' He said: 'This is the sea encompassing the world. Indeed, Allah has sent me to you to teach the ignorant and to confirm the knowledgeable.' Then he brought him to the barrier, which is two soft mountains from which everything slides off. Then he went on with him until he passed Gog and Magog. Then he went on with him to another nation whose faces are the faces of dogs, who fight Gog and Magog. Then he went on with him until he crossed with him another nation fighting those whose faces are the faces of dogs. Then he went on until he crossed with him to another nation, whose names he had given."

The scholars differed concerning the reason for which Dhu al-Qarnayn was called Dhu al-Qarnayn. Some of them said:

He was called that because he was struck on his horn (qarn), and died, then was brought back to life and was struck on the other horn, and died.

Those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasah, from Ubayd al-Muktib, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he said: "He was a servant whom Allah loved, so He loved him, and who advised Allah, so He advised him. He commanded them to fear Allah, so they struck him on his horn and killed him. Then Allah raised him, and they struck him on his horn, and he died."

- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and he said: "He was a servant who advised Allah, so He advised him. He called his people to Allah, so they struck him on his horn and he died. Then Allah revived him, and he called his people to Allah, and they struck him on his horn and he died. Therefore he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn."

- Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "I heard Ali, and they asked him about Dhu al-Qarnayn, was he a prophet?" He said: "He was a righteous servant who loved Allah, so Allah loved him, and who advised Allah, so He advised him. Allah sent him to his people, and they struck him two blows on his head, so he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn, and among you today there is one like him."

Others said regarding that, with what:

Muhammad ibn Sahl al-Bukhari narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to me, saying: Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "Dhu al-Qarnayn was a king." It was said to him: "Why was he named Dhu al-Qarnayn?" He said: "The People of the Book differed about him. Some of them said: he was king of the Romans and Persia. And some of them said: there was on his head something like two horns."

Others said: He was only called that because the two sides of his head were of copper.

Those who said that:

- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ishaq narrated to me, saying: one whom I do not accuse narrated to me, from Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani, who said: "He was only called Dhu al-Qarnayn because the two sides of his head were of copper."

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, We established him upon the earth and gave him of every thing a way﴾

He says: We made the earth firm for him. ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾: He says, and We gave him of every thing, meaning that by which he could find a means, which is knowledge of it.

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said regarding that.

Those who said that:

- Ali narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾, he said: knowledge.

- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾, i.e., knowledge.

- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾, he said: "Of every thing, knowledge."

- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾, he said: "The knowledge of every thing."

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾: knowledge.

- It was narrated from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: ﴿And gave him of every thing a way﴾: "Knowledge."

* *

The Interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of black mud, and found near it a people. We said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them or treat them with kindness."﴾ (18:86)

Some of the reciters of Madina and Basra read ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiʾah﴾ (in a spring of black mud), meaning: it sets in a water spring that has mud (ḥamaʾ). A group of the reciters of Madina, and the majority of the reciters of Kufa, read (fi ʿaynin ḥamiyah) (in a spring of hot water), meaning: it sets in a spring of hot water.

The people of interpretation differed in their explanations of this according to the difference of the reciters in its recitation.

Those who said ﴿it sets in a spring of black mud﴾:

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi ʿAdiyy narrated to us, from Dawud, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿he found it setting in a spring of black mud﴾, he said: "Having mud."

Al-Husayn ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, saying: Saʿid ibn Salamah narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from ʿUthman ibn Hadir, who said: I heard ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas say: Muʿawiyah recited this verse and said: "ʿaynun ḥamiyah." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is ʿaynun ḥamiʾah." He said: So they made Kaʿb a judge between them. They sent to Kaʿb al-Ahbar and asked him, and Kaʿb said: "As for the sun, it sets in a thaʾt (wet clay)," so it was as Ibn ʿAbbas had said. Al-Thaʾt means clay.

Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Nafiʿ ibn Abi Nuʿaym told me, saying: I heard ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Aʿraj say: Ibn ʿAbbas used to say ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiʾah﴾, then he explained it: "having mud." Nafiʿ said: Kaʿb was asked about it, and he said: "You are more knowledgeable of the Qur'an than I am, but I find it in the Book that it sets in black clay."

Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, ﴿he found it setting in a spring of black mud﴾, he said: "It is the ḥamaʾ (mud)."

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiʾah﴾, he said: "Thaʾt."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraj, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah, mighty is His remembrance, ﴿it sets in a spring of black mud﴾, he said: "A thaʾtah (patch of clay)."

He said: ʿAmr ibn Dinar informed me, from ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "I recited ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiʾah﴾, and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs recited ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiyah﴾, so we sent to Kaʿb, and he said: 'It sets in black muddy clay.'"

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, ﴿it sets in a spring of black mud﴾, and al-ḥamiʾah: black mud.

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Marwan ibn Muʿawiyah narrated to us, from Warqaʾ, who said: I heard Saʿid ibn Jubayr say: "Ibn ʿAbbas used to read this word ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiʾah﴾ and say: 'black mud in which the sun sets.'"

Others said: rather, it sets in a hot spring.

Those who said that:

ʿAli narrated to me, saying: ʿAbdullah narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, ﴿he found it setting in a spring of hot water﴾, he says: "In a hot spring."

Yaʿqub narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', who said: I heard al-Hasan say ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiyah﴾, he said: "Hot."

Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Mamar informed us, from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿fi ʿaynin ḥamiyah﴾, he said: "Hot," and thus al-Hasan recited it.

The correct statement on this, in my view, is to say that both are widely transmitted readings among the regional recitations, each has a sound meaning and a clear sense, and neither of the two meanings invalidates the other. It is possible that the sun sets in a hot spring that also has mud and clay, so the reader of ﴿ḥamiyah﴾ describes it by its attribute that it has, which is heat, and the reader of ﴿ḥamiʾah﴾ describes it by its attribute that it has, which is that it has mud and clay. Reports have also been transmitted with both forms, both of which are among its attributes.

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: al-ʿAwwam informed us, saying: a client of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, from ʿAbdullah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the sun when it set and said: 'In the hot fire of Allah, in the hot fire of Allah. Were it not for what restrains it by the command of Allah, it would burn what is on the earth.'"

Al-Fadl ibn Dawud al-Wasiti narrated to me, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Dinar narrated to us, from Saʿd ibn Aws, from Mus'ab, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited to him: ﴿ḥamiʾah﴾.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and found near it a people﴾:

It is mentioned that those people were called Nasik.

* *

As for His words, ﴿We said: "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either you punish them"﴾:

He says: either you kill them if they do not enter into affirmation of the oneness of Allah and submit to you in obeying their Lord, to which you call them; ﴿or that you take them with kindness﴾, meaning: or that you capture them and teach them guidance and show them the right path.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 18, verse 87–88:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿He said, "As for one who wrongs, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment."﴾ (87)

His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿As for one who wrongs, we will punish him﴾ means: As for one who disbelieves, we will kill him.

As related:

* Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿As for one who wrongs, we will punish him﴾, he said: It is killing.

* *

As for His saying ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment﴾:

It means: then he will return to Allah, may He be exalted, after his killing, and He will punish him with a great punishment, which is the nukr (terrible punishment), and that is the punishment of Hell.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿But as for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he will have the reward of the best, and we will speak to him of Our command with ease.﴾ (88)

It means: As for those among them who affirm Allah's oneness and believe in Him, and act in obedience to Him, then with Allah is al-Husna (the best reward), which is Paradise, a reward, meaning a recompense for their faith and their obedience to their Lord.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of the reciters of Madinah and some of the people of Basra and Kufa recited ﴿fa-lahu jazaʾu l-ḥusnā﴾ with jazaʾ in the nominative and in construct with al-Husna.

When it is read thus, it has two interpretations:

The first: that al-Husna is taken to mean their faith and their righteous deeds, so the meaning, when this is intended, is: As for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he has its recompense, meaning the recompense of these good deeds.

The second: that al-Husna refers to Paradise, and the jazaʾ is attributed to it, as it is said ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter is better﴾, where the abode is the Hereafter, and as He said ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾, where the religion is the upright one.

Others recited ﴿fa-lahu jazaʾan al-ḥusnā﴾, with the meaning: "for him is Paradise as a reward," so that jazaʾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: He recompenses them with the recompense of Paradise.

The more correct of the two readings in my view is the reading of the one who recites ﴿fa-lahu jazaʾan al-ḥusnā﴾ with jazaʾ in the accusative and tanwin, according to the meaning I have described, that for them Paradise is the recompense. Thus jazaʾ is in the accusative as an explanation (tafsir).

It means: We will teach him in this world what is easy for Us to teach him, that which brings him near to Allah and makes speech gentle for him. Mujahid said similarly to what we have said.

The readers (qurra') differed over the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of Medina and some of the Kufans recited ﴿between the two barriers (al-suddayn)﴾ with a ḍamma on the sīn, and so with every instance of it in the Qur'an. Some of the Meccan readers recited it with a fatḥa throughout. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' (a reader and grammarian) used a fatḥa on the sīn in this surah and a ḍamma on the sīn in Yā Sīn, and said: al-saddu with a fatḥa is what stands as a barrier between you and a thing, while al-suddu with a ḍamma is what is a film over the eye. As for the Kufans, most of them recited the sīn with a fatḥa throughout the Qur'an, except for the words al-suddayn in this verse, where they specifically used a ḍamma.

It has been transmitted from 'Ikrima concerning this:

- Ahmad ibn Yusuf related to us, saying: al-Qasim related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Harun, from Ayyub, from 'Ikrima, who said: Whatever is the work of the children of Adam is al-sadd, meaning with a fatḥa, and whatever is the work of God is al-sudd.

al-Kisa'i (a reader) used to say: they are two dialects with one meaning.

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that they are two widely transmitted readings among the readings of the regional centers (amṣār), and two dialects agreeing in meaning without difference. So whichever of the two the reader recites is correct. There is no sense in the distinction reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and 'Ikrima between al-suddu and al-saddu, because we have found no evidence to show a difference between them as reported from those two. What confirms this is that all the people of interpretation from whom we have received explanations did not transmit from any of them a distinction between the fatḥa and the ḍamma. Had the two differed in meaning, the distinction would have been transmitted along with the interpretation, God willing. Rather, the meaning of both was not divided in their view, so they explained the letter without distinguishing between them. As for what was mentioned from 'Ikrima on this, the one who transmitted it from Ayyub and Harun is open to question, and we do not know of it from Ayyub through the reliable transmitters of his circle. Both al-sadd and al-sudd mean a barrier between two things. Here, according to what has been mentioned, they are two mountains that closed off what lay between them, and Dhu al-Qarnayn filled in with a barrier between Yajuj and Majuj and those behind them, to cut off their hostility and mischief from people.

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said:

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿between the two barriers (al-suddayn)﴾, he said: The two mountains, the rampart between Yajuj and Majuj, two peoples from beyond the rampart of Dhu al-Qarnayn. He said: The two mountains are Armenia and Adharbayjan.
- Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, concerning ﴿between the two barriers﴾, and they are two mountains.
- I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words ﴿between the two barriers﴾, meaning between two mountains.
- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, concerning His words ﴿between the two barriers﴾, he said: They are two mountains.

* * *

And His words ﴿he found beside them a people who could hardly understand speech﴾.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: he found beside the two barriers a people who could hardly understand the speech of anyone other than their own speech.

The readers differed over the recitation of His words ﴿could understand (yafqahūn)﴾. The majority of the readers of Medina and Basra and some of the people of Kufa recited ﴿yafaqahūna qawlan﴾ with a fatḥa on the qāf and the yā', from faqiha, yafqahu, fiqhan (to understand). The majority of the readers of Kufa recited ﴿yufqihūna qawlan﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā' and a kasra on the qāf, from afqahtu fulānan kadhā uf-qihuhu ifqāhan (I made someone understand that), meaning: when I made him understand it.

The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that they are two widely transmitted readings among the readings of the regional centers, neither of which negates the other. This is because the people about whom God reported this report may be people who could hardly understand speech from others about them, so the recitation with that is correct. And it is possible that they, while being so, could hardly make others understand them, for reasons either in their tongues or in their speech, so the recitation with that is also correct.

* * *

And His words ﴿Indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land﴾.

The readers differed over the recitation of His words ﴿Indeed Gog and Magog (inna Ya'jūja wa Ma'jūja)﴾. The readers of the Hijaz, Iraq and elsewhere recited ﴿inna Yājūja wa Mājūja﴾ without a hamza, in the pattern fā'ūl from yajjtu and majjtu, and they took the two alifs in them to be extra letters. The exception was 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud and al-A'raj, for it has been reported that they recited it with a hamza in both, and they took the hamza in both to be original to the word. It seems they took Ya'jūj to be yaf'ūl from ajjtu, and Ma'jūj to be maf'ūl.

The recitation that is the correct one according to us is Yājūj and Mājūj with an alif and without a hamza, because the authoritative readers are in consensus on it, and because it is the known speech on the tongues of the Arabs. From it is the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj:

"Even if Yājūj and Mājūj together,
and 'Ād returned and they gathered an army against Tubba'..."

[The verse is by Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj (his Dīwān, Leipzig edition 1903, p. 92). He said: "Yājūj and Mājūj are not diptotes. Some of them add a hamza to their two alifs, and some do not add it. Ru'ba said: 'If Yājūj and Mājūj together...' and did not make them diptotes (in the Arabic sense, without tanwīn). (In Lisān al-'Arab, under ajj.) Yājūj and Mājūj are two tribes of God's creation, and the recitation came with both hamza and without hamza. He said: A ḥadīth has come: 'Creation is ten parts, nine of them are Yājūj and Mājūj.' They are two foreign names, and the derivation of similar words is from Arabic speech: it comes from ajjat al-nār (the fire blazed), and from al-mā' al-ajāj (salt water), which is extremely salty, burning from its saltiness. He said: The estimate for Yājūj would be yafʿūl, and likewise Majūj. He said: This would be their derivation if the two names were Arabic, but a foreign word is not derived from Arabic. Whoever does not add a hamza and takes the two alifs to be extra says: Yājūj is from yajjtu, and Mājūj is from majjtu, and they are not diptotes. Ru'ba said: 'If Yājūj and Mājūj together... and 'Ād returned and they gathered an army against Tubba'.' End of quote.]

They are two peoples beyond the barrier.

* * *

And His words ﴿corrupters in the land﴾.

The people of interpretation differed over the meaning of the corruption with which God described these two peoples. Some of them said: They used to eat people.

Those who said that:

- Ahmad ibn al-Walid al-Ramli related to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Ayyub al-Khuzani related to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim related to us, saying: I heard Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz say concerning His words ﴿Indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the land﴾, he said: They used to eat people.

Others said: Rather, the meaning is that Yajuj and Majuj would corrupt the land in the future, not that they were corrupting it at that time.

Those who said that, and the description of Dhu al-Qarnayn's following of the causes which God mentioned in this verse, and the account of the reason for his building the barrier: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Some of those who narrate the stories of the non-Arabs from the People of the Book, who had become Muslim, related to me, from what they had inherited of the knowledge of Dhu al-Qarnayn, that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a man from the people of Egypt named Marzaba ibn Mardaba al-Yunani, from the descendants of Yawnan ibn Yafith ibn Nuh.

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from Thawr ibn Yazid, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan al-Kala'i, and Khalid was a man who had met people: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about Dhu al-Qarnayn and he said: 'A king who swept the earth from beneath it with the causes (asbāb).'" Khalid said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard a man say: "O Dhu al-Qarnayn!" So he said: "O God, forgive us! Are you not content to be named after the prophets, until you name yourselves after the angels? If the Messenger of God said that, then the truth is what he said, and falsehood is what contradicts it."'

- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: Someone whom I do not suspect related to me, from Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani, who had knowledge of the earlier narratives, that he used to say: Dhu al-Qarnayn was a man from the Romans, the son of an old woman from among their old women, who had no child other than him. His name was Iskandar (Alexander). He was only called Dhu al-Qarnayn because the two sides of his head were of copper. When he reached maturity, and he was a righteous servant, God, mighty and majestic, said to him: "O Dhu al-Qarnayn, I am sending you to the peoples of the earth, and they are peoples of differing tongues, and they are all the people of the earth. Among them are two peoples between whom is the length of the whole earth. Among them are two peoples between whom is the breadth of the whole earth. And a community in the middle of the earth, among them are the jinn, the humans, and Yajuj and Majuj. As for the two peoples between whom is the length of the earth: one people is at the west of the sun, called Nāsik. The other is at its rising, called Manasik. As for the two between whom is the breadth of the earth: one people is in the right side of the earth, called Hawil. The other, which is on the left side of the earth, is a people called Tawil."

When God said that to him, Dhu al-Qarnayn said: "My God, You have appointed me to a great matter, whose measure none but You can grasp. So inform me about these peoples to which You have sent me: with what strength shall I contend with them, with what gathering shall I outnumber them, with what stratagem shall I outwit them, with what patience shall I endure them, with what tongue shall I speak with them, and how can I understand their languages, and with what hearing shall I grasp their speech, and with what sight shall I penetrate them, with what proof shall I dispute with them, with what heart shall I understand them, with what wisdom shall I manage their affairs, with what justice shall I be fair among them, with what forbearance shall I bear with them, with what knowledge shall I distinguish between them, with what skill shall I master their affairs, with what hand shall I overpower them, with what foot shall I trample them, with what power shall I subdue them, with what army shall I fight them, with what gentleness shall I win them over? For I have nothing, O my God, of what I have mentioned that can stand against them, nor that can prevail over them or withstand them. You are the Lord, the Merciful, who does not burden any soul beyond its capacity, nor load it beyond its power, nor distress it nor overwhelm it, but You are gentle with it [[It is said: raʾafa bihi yarʾafu, if he had mercy on him. It is of the pattern faḥa, karuma and faraḥa, and it takes bi, as in Lisān al-'Arab. Perhaps here it implies the meaning of ramiḥa, so it took its object directly, or it is a distortion of tarʾamuhā.]] and merciful to it."

God, mighty and majestic, said: "I shall equip you with what I have burdened you with. I shall expand your breast, so it will embrace everything. I shall expand your understanding, so you will comprehend everything. I shall loosen your tongue, so you will speak everything. I shall open your hearing, so you will grasp everything. I shall extend your sight, so you will penetrate everything. I shall manage your affairs, so you will master everything. I shall count for you, so nothing will escape you. I shall guard over you, so nothing will be hidden from you. I shall strengthen your back, so nothing will break you. I shall strengthen your support, so nothing will overcome you. I shall strengthen your heart, so nothing will frighten you. I shall subject to you light and darkness, and make them soldiers of your army: light will guide you in front of you, and darkness will shelter you from behind you. I shall strengthen your intellect, so nothing will terrify you. I shall extend for you from before your hands, so you will overpower everything. I shall strengthen your tread for you, so you will crush everything. I shall clothe you in awe, so nothing will dare to approach you."

When he was told that, he set out aiming for the people at the west of the sun. When he reached them, he found a multitude and a number that none but God could count, and a strength and might that none but God could withstand, and differing tongues, scattered desires, and divided hearts. When he saw that, he outnumbered them with darkness. He struck around them three of the armies of darkness, which surrounded them from every direction and encircled them until they were gathered in one place. Then he took them with light, and invited them to God and to worship Him. Some of them believed in him, and some turned away. He then targeted those who had turned their backs on him, and brought darkness upon them. It entered their mouths, their noses, their ears and their bellies, and entered their houses and their homes, and covered them from above, from below and from every side. They surged within it and became bewildered. When they feared they would perish in it, they cried out to him with one voice. He lifted it from them and took them forcibly, so they entered his call. He then gathered from the people of the west great nations, and made them one army. Then he set out, leading them, while darkness drove them from behind and guarded them on every side, and light was in front of them, leading and guiding them. He was travelling along the right side of the earth, intending the people on the right side of the earth called Hawil.
